100.name: The Civilising Mission
100.hitokoto: It was resolved that "not yet ready" is no reason.
body: From the end of the 19th century to the middle of the 20th, colonial rule was spoken of as the duty of civilised nations. The standard starting point is the General Act of the Berlin Conference of 1885, by which the powers settled the procedure for dividing Africa. The premise that there is a side that leads and a side that is led had become the vocabulary of diplomatic documents.

On 14 December 1960, at the 947th plenary meeting of the 15th session of the UN General Assembly, the Declaration on the Granting of Independence to Colonial Countries and Peoples, proposed by 43 states, was adopted. The vote was 89 to 0, with 9 abstentions. Not one vote was cast against. Khrushchev had raised the matter on 23 September that year, but what was adopted was a different text, put forward by Cambodia on behalf of 26 Asian and African states.

What made the adoption possible was the change in the makeup of the Assembly. Sixteen states joined in 1955 and nineteen in 1960 alone, and the membership had nearly doubled. The norm ended, that is, because those who did not support it became the majority. It is a rare case in which the date a criterion went out of stock survives as a count of votes.

made.label: 1885 The Berlin Conference
made.fact: The standard account is that the powers settled the procedure for dividing Africa by the General Act of the Berlin Conference of 1885. The date of signature of the Act (given as 26 February 1885) could not be confirmed against a primary source in this session, so only the year is set down, as an approximation.

discontinued.label: 1960 UN Resolution 1514
discontinued.fact: On 14 December 1960, at the 947th plenary meeting of the 15th session of the UN General Assembly, the Declaration on the Granting of Independence to Colonial Countries and Peoples (Resolution 1514 (XV)), proposed by 43 states, was adopted by 89 votes to 0, with 9 abstentions. Not one vote was cast against.

keyfacts.text: Resolution 1514 (XV) was adopted on 14 December 1960 at the 947th plenary meeting of the 15th session of the General Assembly. The vote was 89 to 0, with 9 abstentions. Not one vote was cast against. The president was H. Boland of Ireland.

The item was raised on 23 September 1960 by Khrushchev, Chairman of the Council of Ministers of the USSR, in his address to the Assembly, and submitted the same day as a letter (A/4501) with a draft declaration (A/4502). What was adopted in the end was a different text (A/L.323), put forward by Cambodia on 28 November on behalf of 26 Asian and African states and later co-sponsored by 43. The Soviet draft and the amendments to it were rejected.

Nineteen states joined the General Assembly in 1960. The admission of 16 states at once in 1955 had brought the membership to 76, and this change in the composition of the Assembly made the adoption possible. That the faces in the Assembly had changed was the condition for the norm going out of stock.

One reason the form of a "declaration" was chosen was a tactical calculation: it turned votes against into abstentions, which have no legal effect. The type of document was itself a product of the negotiation.

Resolution 1514 gave rise to a line of later resolutions: Resolution 1515 (XV) of 15 December 1960, on the sovereign right of every state to dispose of its wealth and natural resources, and Resolution 1803 (XVII) of 14 December 1962, on permanent sovereignty over natural resources. Resolution 1654 (XVI) of 27 November 1961 set up a special committee of 17 states to watch over implementation.

101.name: Divorce Forbidden
101.hitokoto: 9,114 votes. That is the margin by which Ireland made divorce possible, in 1995.
body: Article 41.3.2 of the Irish Constitution of 1937 was worded in an unusual way: "No law shall be enacted providing for the grant of a dissolution of marriage." It did not forbid divorce itself; it shut off any legislation that would allow it. Because parliament could not move unless the Constitution was changed, this value sat in the text of the Constitution for 58 years.

The first referendum was held on 26 June 1986 and was defeated, 36.52% for against 63.48%. The second was on 24 November 1995: 818,842 for, 809,728 against, turnout 62.15%. The margin was 9,114 votes. In nine years the yes vote moved 14 points and turned the result over by a hair. The Fifteenth Amendment of the Constitution Act was signed on 17 June 1996.

The statute took a little longer. The Family Law (Divorce) Act 1996 came into force on 27 February 1997, but the first divorce was granted on 17 January 1997, before that date, on the constitutional amendment as direct authority. It was a case of hurrying the remarriage of a man who was terminally ill. Malta allowed divorce fourteen years later still, on 1 October 2011.

made.label: 1937 Article 41.3.2
made.fact: Article 41.3.2 of the Irish Constitution of 1937 provided that "No law shall be enacted providing for the grant of a dissolution of marriage." It did not forbid divorce; it forbade the making of any law that would grant one. The wording bound the hands of the legislature.

discontinued.label: 1995 Referendum, by 9,114 votes
discontinued.fact: At the referendum of 24 November 1995, 818,842 voted for (50.28%) and 809,728 against (49.72%), on a turnout of 62.15% (1,633,942 votes in all). The margin was 9,114 votes. The Fifteenth Amendment of the Constitution Act was signed on 17 June 1996; the Family Law (Divorce) Act 1996 was signed on 27 November 1996 and came into force on 27 February 1997. The first divorce was granted on 17 January 1997, to a man who was terminally ill, on the constitutional amendment as direct authority.

keyfacts.text: Article 41.3.2 of the 1937 Constitution provided that "No law shall be enacted providing for the grant of a dissolution of marriage." What was forbidden was not divorce itself but legislation allowing it.
The first referendum, on 26 June 1986 (the Tenth Amendment of the Constitution Bill), was defeated: 538,279 for (36.52%), 935,843 against (63.48%), turnout 60.84%.
The second referendum, on 24 November 1995, was 50.28% for and 49.72% against, a margin of 9,114 votes. In nine years the yes vote moved from 36.52% to 50.28%.

The Fifteenth Amendment of the Constitution Act was signed on 17 June 1996 and the Family Law (Divorce) Act 1996 on 27 November 1996, coming into force on 27 February 1997. The first divorce, however, was granted earlier, on 17 January 1997, on the constitutional amendment as direct authority.

In Malta, the referendum of 28 May 2011 was 53.16% in favour on a turnout of 71.57%. Parliament passed the divorce law on 25 July 2011, and the Civil Code (Amendment) Act 2011 (Act XIV of 2011) was promulgated on 29 July 2011 and came into force on 1 October 2011.
At the time of the Maltese referendum in 2011, only three states in the world had no divorce: Malta, the Philippines and Vatican City.

102.name: White Australia
102.hitokoto: After 1909, not one person passed the test.
body: The Immigration Restriction Act 1901 (Act No. 17 of 1901), assented to on 23 December 1901, put at the head of its list of "prohibited immigrants" anyone who failed to write out fifty words in a European language dictated by an officer. The word race appears nowhere in the text. The dictation test was chosen because selection that named race openly was opposed by Britain and disliked by Japan, Britain's ally.

The margin of the section notes the precedents it was modelled on: Natal Act No. 1 of 1897, Western Australia Act No. 13 of 1897, New South Wales Act No. 3 of 1898. The device itself was an import. The first draft had English only, but it was argued that this would keep European migrants away, so it became "a European language", and in 1905, out of regard for Japan, "a prescribed language".

The record of how it worked survives. The test was given 805 times in 1902-03 and 46 people passed; 554 times between 1904 and 1909, and six people passed. After 1909 nobody passed at all. It worked not as a selection but as a device for closing the gate. Amended again and again, the 1901 Act stayed in force until 1958, when the Migration Act, in force from 8 October that year, replaced it.

made.label: 1901 Immigration Restriction Act
made.fact: The Immigration Restriction Act 1901 (Act No. 17 of 1901) was assented to on 23 December 1901. Its full title was "An Act to place certain restrictions on Immigration and to provide for the removal from the Commonwealth of Prohibited Immigrants".

discontinued.label: 1958 Replaced by the Migration Act
discontinued.fact: Amended many times over, the 1901 Act stayed in force until 1958. The Migration Act 1958 (Act No. 62 of 1958) came into force on 8 October 1958 and replaced it.

keyfacts.text: The Immigration Restriction Act 1901 (Act No. 17 of 1901) was assented to on 23 December 1901. Section 3(a) listed as a prohibited immigrant "any person who when asked to do so by an officer fails to write out at dictation and sign in the presence of the officer a passage of fifty words in length in a European language directed by the officer".

The margin of the Act notes the precedents it was modelled on: section 3 of Natal Act No. 1 of 1897, section 2 of Western Australia Act No. 13 of 1897, section 3 of New South Wales Act No. 3 of 1898. The device was brought over from Natal, in South Africa.

The dictation test was chosen because selection that named race openly was opposed by Britain and disliked by Japan, Britain's ally. The first draft had English only, but it was argued that this would keep European migrants away and favour Japanese and African Americans, so it became "a European language". In 1905, out of regard for Japan, it was changed to "a prescribed language".
The dictation test was given 805 times in 1902-03, with 46 passes, and 554 times between 1904 and 1909, with six. After 1909 not one person passed. Those who failed were refused entry or deported.

From 1932 the test could be set any number of times during the first five years after entry. The 1901 Act was "amended many times and remained in force until 1958". What replaced it was the Migration Act 1958 (Act No. 62 of 1958), in force from 8 October 1958.

The 1901 Act did not stand alone but was part of a run of legislation excluding non-European immigrants. It included the Pacific Island Labourers Act of the same year and section 15 of the Post and Telegraph Act (mail ships subsidised by the Commonwealth were to employ white labour only).

103.name: Section 127
103.hitokoto: The Constitution said "aboriginal natives shall not be counted". Until 1967.
body: Section 127 of the Australian Constitution read: "In reckoning the numbers of the people of the Commonwealth, or of a State or other part of the Commonwealth, aboriginal natives shall not be counted." It was not a ban on something or a denial of a right in so many words, but an exclusion written as a rule about how to take statistics. The Commonwealth was founded in 1901, and the section was there from the start.

There was a second provision. Section 51(xxvi) gave the federal parliament power to make special laws for "the people of any race, other than the aboriginal race in any State". Because they were excluded, the Commonwealth could not legislate for Aboriginal people at all. Not counted in, and not covered: the exclusion ran on two tracks.

At the referendum of 27 May 1967, about 90% voted yes, the largest yes vote in Australian history. The amendment was made as the Constitution Alteration (Aboriginals) 1967, Act No. 55 of 1967, on 10 August that year, and section 127 was deleted. The smallest change there was to make, counting people in, carries a figure of 90%.

made.label: 1901 Section 127
made.fact: Section 127 of the Australian Constitution provided that "in reckoning the numbers of the people of the Commonwealth, or of a State or other part of the Commonwealth, aboriginal natives shall not be counted". The Commonwealth was founded in 1901.

discontinued.label: 1967 Constitution Alteration (Aboriginals)
discontinued.fact: At the referendum of 27 May 1967 about 90% voted yes, and the amendment was made as the Constitution Alteration (Aboriginals) 1967, Act No. 55 of 1967, on 10 August 1967. Section 127 was deleted, and the words "other than the aboriginal race in any State" were struck out of section 51(xxvi).

keyfacts.text: Section 127 read "In reckoning the numbers of the people of the Commonwealth, or of a State or other part of the Commonwealth, aboriginal natives shall not be counted". It was an exclusion written as a rule about how to take statistics.

Section 51(xxvi) gave the federal parliament power to make special laws for "the people of any race, other than the aboriginal race in any State". Because they were excluded, the Commonwealth could not legislate for Aboriginal people.
At the referendum of 27 May 1967, about 90% voted yes. It is the largest yes vote in Australian history.

The amendment was made as the Constitution Alteration (Aboriginals) 1967, Act No. 55 of 1967, on 10 August 1967. Two and a half months separate the day of the referendum from the day the Act was made.

The question at the referendum is explained as "changing the Constitution so that Aboriginal people would be counted in the census". The smallest change there was to make, counting people in, carries a figure of 90%.

104.name: English Only
104.reading: oyake no kotoba wa eigo dake
104.hitokoto: The right to speak Māori in court was made by a statute, in 1987.
body: Section 3 of the Maori Language Act 1987 (1987 No 176) is headed "Māori language to be an official language of New Zealand". Section 4 is headed "Right to speak Māori in legal proceedings". That there is a section creating a right means that until then the right did not exist in law.

Section 5 of the Act set out the effect of that recognition, and sections 6 onward established the Māori Language Commission, its functions and powers, down to the issue of certificates of competency in Māori. It was not a declaration alone but came with administrative machinery. The status of official language was built as an institution, not put up as a sign. The Act has since been replaced by a successor statute.

The exclusion of Māori from schools and public life is usually dated to the Native Schools Act 1867, but the text of that statute could not be checked here. What is certain is that a language with no place in public life for some 120 years was put back by statute in 1987. The discontinuing and the restocking stand side by side in the same Act.

made.label: From the colonial era
made.fact: The exclusion of Māori from schools and public life is usually dated to the Native Schools Act 1867. The text of that Act could not be verified from a primary source in this session, so the year is approximate. What can be said with certainty is that the Act of 1987 was the first to give Māori the status of an official language and the right to be spoken in legal proceedings; that is, that until then that status and that right did not exist.

discontinued.label: 1987 Māori Language Act
discontinued.fact: Section 3 of the Maori Language Act 1987 (1987 No 176) made Māori an official language of New Zealand, and section 4 gave the right to speak Māori in legal proceedings. The Act established the Māori Language Commission.

restocked.label: 1987 te reo Māori
restocked.fact: By section 3 of the Maori Language Act 1987 (1987 No 176), Māori became an official language of New Zealand. The Act has since been replaced by Te Ture mō Te Reo Māori.

keyfacts.text: The heading of section 3 of the Maori Language Act 1987 (1987 No 176) is "Māori language to be an official language of New Zealand". By that section, Māori became an official language of New Zealand.

The heading of section 4 of the same Act is "Right to speak Māori in legal proceedings". The right to speak Māori in legal proceedings was made by statute in 1987. Put the other way round, until then that right did not exist in law.

Section 5 of the same Act set out the effect of the recognition, and sections 6 onward established the Māori Language Commission, its functions and powers, and the issue of certificates of competency in Māori. It was built as an institution.
The 1987 Act has now been repealed and replaced by a successor statute, Te Ture mō Te Reo Māori. The New Zealand legislation database shows it as "Repealed".

105.name: The Wife Incompetent
105.reading: tsuma wa otto no kyoka de ugoku
105.hitokoto: A wife's legal capacity was limited by the same provision as a spendthrift's or a deaf person's.
body: Article 14 of Book 1 of the Civil Code, promulgated on 27 April 1896, provided that for a wife to borrow money or give surety, to acquire or lose rights in immovable property, to bring an action, or to make a gift or a settlement, she "must obtain the permission of her husband". An act done without permission could be rescinded. By Imperial Ordinance No. 123 of 1898 it came into force on 16 July 1898.

What Article 14 cited was items 1 to 6 of Article 12, paragraph 1: the list of acts for which a quasi-incompetent person needed the consent of a curator. Article 11 defined the quasi-incompetent as "persons of unsound mind, the deaf, the mute, the blind and spendthrifts". The limits on a wife were written by borrowing the same six items. Article 19, paragraph 4, names the two in one breath: "as against a quasi-incompetent person and a wife".

The cases where no permission was needed are in the text too: where it was not known whether the husband was alive, where he had deserted his wife, where he was serving a sentence of one year's imprisonment or more, where the interests of husband and wife were in conflict. Only, that is, where the husband was effectively absent. The provision lost its effect under the Emergency Measures Act on 3 May 1947 and was gone with Act No. 222, promulgated on 22 December that year. Article 5 of the supplementary provisions of that Act states that acts done without permission in the past can no longer be rescinded.

made.label: 1898 Meiji Civil Code Article 14
made.fact: Article 14 of the Civil Code, Books 1, 2 and 3 (Act No. 89 of 1896), promulgated on 27 April 1896, provided that "for a wife to do the acts set out below she must obtain the permission of her husband", and that an act done without permission could be rescinded. Article 14, paragraph 1, item 1 cited items 1 to 6 of Article 12, paragraph 1, the list of the acts of a quasi-incompetent person, so that the acts covered were borrowing and surety, the acquisition or loss of rights in immovable property, bringing an action, gifts, settlements and arbitration agreements, and the acceptance or renunciation of an inheritance. By Imperial Ordinance No. 123 of 1898 (promulgated 21 June 1898) it came into force on 16 July 1898.

discontinued.label: 1947 The wife's incapacity deleted
discontinued.fact: The Act on Emergency Measures concerning the Civil Code Accompanying the Enforcement of the Constitution of Japan (Act No. 74 of 1947), promulgated on 19 April and in force from 3 May 1947, stopped it from applying by Article 2: "provisions limiting legal capacity or otherwise on the ground of being a wife or a mother shall not apply". The articles then went with the Act Partially Amending the Civil Code (Act No. 222, promulgated 22 December 1947, in force 1 January 1948). Article 5 of the supplementary provisions of that Act provided that "an act done by a wife before the Emergency Measures Act came into force, in breach of Article 14, paragraph 1, of the former law, cannot be rescinded", closing off any rescission reaching back into the past.

keyfacts.text: Article 14, paragraph 1, of the Meiji Civil Code: "For a wife to do the acts set out below she must obtain the permission of her husband. 1. To do the acts set out in items 1 to 6 of Article 12, paragraph 1. 2. To accept or refuse a gift or a bequest. 3. To make a contract by which she is bound in her person." Paragraph 2 of the same article: "An act contrary to the preceding paragraph may be rescinded."

Article 12, the article cited, is the provision on quasi-incompetent persons, and Article 11 provided that "persons of unsound mind, the deaf, the mute, the blind and spendthrifts may be made quasi-incompetent and given a curator". A wife's legal capacity was limited by the same six items as theirs.

Article 19, paragraph 4, read "as against a quasi-incompetent person and a wife, notice may be given within the period in the first paragraph requiring that the act be ratified with the consent of the curator or the permission of the husband", setting a wife, in the text itself, beside the quasi-incompetent as one type of "person without capacity".

Article 17 listed six exceptions in which no permission was needed: where it was not known whether the husband was alive, where he had deserted his wife, where he was himself incompetent or quasi-incompetent, where he was confined in a hospital or a private house for insanity, where he was serving a sentence of one year's imprisonment or more, and where the interests of husband and wife were in conflict.

Article 15: "A wife who has been permitted one or more kinds of business has, as to that business, the same capacity as an independent person." Permission to trade was also the husband's to give, and under Article 16 he could revoke it at any time.

On property, Article 801 of Book 4 (Act No. 9 of 1898) provided that "the husband administers the wife's property". Article 802, however, required the wife's consent for the husband to borrow on her behalf or to dispose of her property.

Article 813 of the same Book 4 listed the grounds for divorce, item 2 being "where the wife has committed adultery" and item 3 "where the husband has been sentenced for an offence of illicit intercourse". For a wife the fact of adultery was itself a ground; for a husband it became one only once he had been sentenced.

The amending text of Act No. 222 of 1947 reads "Articles 14 to 18: deleted", and struck from Article 19 the words "and a wife", "or the permission of the husband", "or the wife" and "or the permission". Article 801 went with the wholesale revision of Book 4, so it does not appear as a deleted article.

The Emergency Measures Act (Act No. 74 of 1947) stopped the wife's incapacity by Article 2, "provisions limiting legal capacity or otherwise on the ground of being a wife or a mother shall not apply", the provisions concerning the house by Article 3, and the husband's power to administer her property (former Article 801) by Article 5, paragraph 2. The article numbers are separate.

The date of entry into force is 16 July 1898, under Imperial Ordinance No. 123 of 1898 (promulgated 21 June 1898): "Books 1, 2 and 3 of the Civil Code, Act No. 89 of 1896 ... shall come into force from 16 July 1898."

106.name: Parricide
106.hitokoto: An article held unconstitutional stayed in the Penal Code for another 22 years.
body: Article 200 of the Penal Code, in force from 1 October 1908, provided that "whoever kills a lineal ascendant of himself or of his spouse shall be punished by death or by penal servitude for life". Ordinary homicide then had a minimum fixed term of three years; for killing an ascendant there was nothing but death and life. The same aggravation was set for bodily injury causing death, for abandonment, and for unlawful capture and confinement. When the offence of adultery and the offences against the Imperial House went in 1947, Article 200 was left out of the amendment.

On 4 April 1973 the Grand Bench of the Supreme Court held Article 200 void as contrary to Article 14, paragraph 1, of the Constitution. The reason lay not in the protecting of ascendants as such but in the point that the degree of aggravation was extreme and, as a means, markedly unreasonable. The same Grand Bench had held it constitutional on 25 October 1950, so the judgment turned over here.

The article actually went with Act No. 91, promulgated on 12 May 1995 and in force from 1 June that year. The reason for the 22-year gap was spoken of in the Diet. Justice Minister Isao Maeda told the Committee on Judicial Affairs of the House of Councillors on 27 April 1995 that a bill had been prepared at once at the time, but "we could not obtain the approval of the Liberal Democratic Party, which was then the governing party, and so it never came to the submission of a bill". The supplementary provisions of that amendment state that for the four articles of ascendant aggravation alone the new law applies to past acts as well.

made.label: 1907 Penal Code Article 200
made.fact: Article 200 of the Penal Code (Act No. 45), promulgated on 24 April 1907 and in force from 1 October 1908, provided that "whoever kills a lineal ascendant of himself or of his spouse shall be punished by death or by penal servitude for life". Ordinary homicide (Article 199) allowed a fixed term as an alternative, but for killing an ascendant there were only two, death and life. The aggravation was set not only for homicide but also for bodily injury causing death (Article 205, paragraph 2), abandonment (Article 218, paragraph 2) and unlawful capture and confinement (Article 220, paragraph 2).

discontinued.label: 1995 The four aggravating articles deleted
discontinued.fact: Article 200 was deleted by the Act Partially Amending the Penal Code (Act No. 91), promulgated on 12 May 1995. Under Article 1 of its supplementary provisions it came into force on the day 20 days after promulgation, that is 1 June 1995. Article 2 laid down the principle that the former law applies to acts done before that day, but its proviso, "this shall not apply to the application of Articles 200, 205, paragraph 2, 218, paragraph 2, and 220, paragraph 2, of the Penal Code before amendment by this Act", made the new law, without the aggravation, apply even to acts done before it came into force, for those four articles alone.

keyfacts.text: Article 200 of the Penal Code now stands as the single line "Article 200: deleted". What deleted it was Act No. 91, promulgated on 12 May 1995, the amendment that put the Penal Code into plain modern Japanese.

The proviso to Article 2 of the supplementary provisions of that Act, "this shall not apply to the application of Articles 200, 205, paragraph 2, 218, paragraph 2, and 220, paragraph 2, of the Penal Code before amendment by this Act", voided all four aggravating provisions at one stroke and retroactively: killing an ascendant, injuring one to death, abandoning one, and capturing and confining one.
The date of entry into force is 1 June 1995, under Article 1 of the supplementary provisions: "This Act shall come into force from the day on which 20 days have elapsed from the day of promulgation."

Article 199 as enacted read "whoever kills a person shall be punished by death or by penal servitude for life or for not less than three years", with a minimum fixed term of three years. Article 200 had only death and penal servitude for life, so that even with mitigation a sentence could not reach suspension. The present Article 199 reads "death or imprisonment for life or for not less than five years".

Act No. 124, promulgated on 26 October 1947, deleted the offence of adultery (Article 183) and the offences against the Imperial House (Articles 73 to 76). Article 200 does not appear once in that amending text and was left as it stood. The 1973 judgment itself says that "Article 200 of the Penal Code was excluded from that amendment, and from then until today no particular legislative measure has been taken with respect to it".

The old Penal Code (Grand Council Proclamation No. 36 of 1880) also had a section on "Offences against grandparents and parents" (Part 3, chapter 1, section 13), and Article 362 provided that "a child or grandchild who murders or kills his grandparent or parent shall be punished by death". Article 365 provided that "for offences of killing or wounding against a grandparent or parent, the rules on special clemency and on exemption from liability may not be applied".

The Grand Bench of the Supreme Court held Article 200 void on 4 April 1973, in case No. 1310 (a) of 1970, "Killing of an ascendant". The majority opinion reads: "Article 200 of the Penal Code, in confining the statutory penalty for killing an ascendant to death or penal servitude for life alone, goes far beyond the limit necessary to attain its legislative purpose and is found to make a markedly unreasonable discriminatory distinction as against the statutory penalty for ordinary homicide in Article 199 of the Penal Code, and is therefore void as contrary to Article 14, paragraph 1, of the Constitution." It did not hold the creating of an offence of killing an ascendant unconstitutional in itself.

Of the 15 justices taking part in the 1973 judgment, 14 held it unconstitutional and one, Takeso Shimoda, dissented for constitutionality. Eight joined the majority opinion, and six wrote separately. Those six were not of one mind either, dividing between the position that the distinction itself was unconstitutional and the position (Saburo Shimomura) that it had lost any reasonable basis with the passage of time. Quashing and deciding the case itself, the court gave two years and six months' penal servitude, suspended for three years.

The first Grand Bench judgment holding Article 200 constitutional is that of 25 October 1950 (case No. 2105 (re) of 1949, Keishu vol. 4, no. 10, p. 2126). The Grand Bench judgment of 11 October that year was not on Article 200 but on Article 205, paragraph 2 (bodily injury to an ascendant causing death), in case No. 292 (a) of 1950; the two are separate cases.

The reason for the 22 years of inaction was spoken of in the Diet. At the Committee on Judicial Affairs of the House of Councillors on 27 April 1995, Justice Minister Isao Maeda said that a bill for deletion had been prepared immediately after the 1973 judgment, but that "we could not obtain the approval of the Diet, and in particular of the Liberal Democratic Party, which was then the governing party, and so it never came to the submission of a bill".

What was done in the meantime is on the record too. At the Committee on Judicial Affairs of the House of Representatives on 28 March 1995, Mamoru Norisada, Director-General of the Criminal Affairs Bureau of the Ministry of Justice, said that "for more than twenty years since the judgment of unconstitutionality, Article 200 of the Penal Code has in fact not been applied, and even where the killing of an ascendant was involved in substance, Article 199, the general offence of homicide, has been applied". Whether a directive ordering that it not be applied exists could not be confirmed.

107.name: Half a Share
107.hitokoto: The amending Act was one sentence long. It struck out the words that said "a half".
body: Article 1004 of the Meiji Civil Code, in force from 16 July 1898, provided that where there were several lineal descendants, the share of a shoshi, an illegitimate child acknowledged by his father, and of a shiseishi, one not acknowledged, was half that of a child born in wedlock. The amendment of 1947 abolished the house system and succession to the headship, but this half survived, copied over as the proviso to Article 900, item 4.

The Grand Bench of the Supreme Court held the provision constitutional by its decision of 5 July 1995, and by its decision of 4 September 2013 held it contrary to Article 14, paragraph 1, of the Constitution. The same Grand Bench came to the opposite conclusion in 18 years. The 2013 decision gave as its reasons that a child cannot choose its own parents and that other countries had one after another done away with provisions of the same kind. Once the house system was gone, this half alone stayed on for 66 years.

The amending Act that followed is Act No. 94, promulgated on 11 December 2013, and its text is a single sentence: "In the proviso to Article 900, item 4, delete the words 'the share of a child born out of wedlock shall be one half of the share of a child born in wedlock, and'." The supplementary provisions made the amended article apply "to inheritances that commence on or after 5 September 2013". 5 September is the day after the Supreme Court's decision, and that one day is the line.

made.label: 1898 Meiji Civil Code Article 1004
made.fact: Article 1004 of the Civil Code, Books 4 and 5 (Act No. 9 of 1898), promulgated on 21 June and in force from 16 July 1898, provided that "where there are several heirs of the same rank, the share of each is equal; provided that where there are several lineal descendants, the share of a shoshi or a shiseishi is one half of the share of a child born in wedlock". Article 970, on the order of succession to the headship, likewise placed children born in wedlock and shoshi ahead of shiseishi.

discontinued.label: 2013 The first half of the proviso deleted
discontinued.fact: The Act Partially Amending the Civil Code (Act No. 94), promulgated on 11 December 2013, provided: "In the proviso to Article 900, item 4, delete the words 'the share of a child born out of wedlock shall be one half of the share of a child born in wedlock, and'." It came into force the same day. Paragraph 2 of its supplementary provisions provided that "Article 900 as amended by this Act applies to inheritances that commence on or after 5 September 2013", taking the day after the Grand Bench decision as the line.

keyfacts.text: The proviso to Article 1004 of the Meiji Civil Code: "where there are several lineal descendants, the share of a shoshi or a shiseishi is one half of the share of a child born in wedlock". The Civil Code amendment of 1947 abolished the house system and succession to the headship, but this half survived into the postwar Code as the proviso to Article 900, item 4.

The text of the amending Act is one sentence: "In the proviso to Article 900, item 4, delete the words 'the share of a child born out of wedlock shall be one half of the share of a child born in wedlock, and'." It was promulgated on 11 December 2013 and, under paragraph 1 of the supplementary provisions, came into force the same day.

Paragraph 2 of the supplementary provisions: "Article 900 as amended by this Act applies to inheritances that commence on or after 5 September 2013." 5 September is the day after 4 September 2013, when the Grand Bench of the Supreme Court decided that the first half of the proviso to Article 900, item 4, was contrary to Article 14, paragraph 1, of the Constitution.

By its decision of 5 July 1995 the Grand Bench of the Supreme Court had held the same provision constitutional. The decision of 4 September 2013 changed that, citing the changes in the forms of the family since then and the course of legislation in other countries.

Article 900, item 4, of the Civil Code now reads: "Where there are several children, lineal ascendants or siblings, the share of each is equal; provided that the share of a sibling who shares only one parent is one half of the share of a sibling who shares both." All that is left of the proviso is the half-blood sibling's share.

Article 970 of the Meiji Civil Code set the order of heirs to the headship: "as between a child born in wedlock, a shoshi and a shiseishi of the same degree, the child born in wedlock and the shoshi, even if female, come before the shiseishi", putting the manner of a person's birth into the text as what fixed the order. Article 827 defined the term: "a shiseishi whom the father has acknowledged shall be a shoshi".

The wording after the 1947 amendment was "the share of a lineal descendant born out of wedlock shall be one half of the share of a lineal descendant born in wedlock, and". It was changed to "child" by Act No. 40, promulgated on 29 March 1962.

The reason for keeping it in 1947 is on the record too. At the Committee on Judicial Affairs of the House of Councillors on 23 September 1947, the government member Kenichi Okuno said that "to make a distinction between a child born of a lawful marriage and one not so born is a treatment adopted in every country, from the standpoint of encouraging and respecting lawful marriage ... and is not necessarily contrary to the Constitution".

The holding of the 2013 decision is that "the first half of the proviso to Article 900, item 4, of the Civil Code was, by July 2001 at the latest, contrary to Article 14, paragraph 1, of the Constitution". It set the moment at which the provision became unconstitutional in July 2001, and at the same time stated expressly that divisions of estates already settled since then were not affected. It was unanimous among the 14 justices taking part, with three supplementary opinions.

The decision wrote its own link back to the Meiji Civil Code: "the provision making the statutory share of a child born out of wedlock one half of that of a child born in wedlock, as regards the inheritance of property commencing on the death of a family member (the proviso to Article 1004 of the Civil Code before the 1947 amendment), was carried over into the present Civil Code as the provision at issue here".

The decision of 5 July 1995 held it constitutional by 10 to 5 of the 15 justices taking part (the dissenters being Toshijiro Nakajima, Masao Ono, Hisako Takahashi, Yukinobu Ozaki and Mitsuo Endo). The reason was that the provision "strikes a balance between respect for legal marriage and the protection of children born out of wedlock".

108.name: The Waiting Period
108.reading: onna dake hantoshi wa saikon dekinai
108.hitokoto: The waiting period that applied to women only went on 1 April 2024.
body: Article 767 of the Meiji Civil Code, in force from 1898, provided that "a woman may not remarry until six months have passed from the day her former marriage was dissolved or annulled". No such limit applied to men. After the house system went with the Civil Code amendment of 1947, these six months stayed on as Article 733.

On 16 December 2015 the Grand Bench of the Supreme Court held the part of the six months beyond 100 days unconstitutional. The reason was that 100 days is enough to keep the presumptions of paternity from overlapping. Act No. 71, promulgated on 7 June 2016, changed "six months" to "100 days counted from", and the supplementary provisions of the same amending Act wrote in that the shape of the rule would be reviewed within about three years.

Article 733 itself was deleted by Act No. 102, promulgated on 16 December 2022, in force from 1 April 2024. It took 126 years for the article of 1898 to disappear. Look up the Civil Code now and all that stands at Article 733 is the single line "deleted".

made.label: 1898 Meiji Civil Code Article 767
made.fact: Article 767 of the Civil Code, Book 4 (Act No. 9 of 1898), promulgated on 21 June and in force from 16 July 1898: "A woman may not remarry until six months have passed from the day her former marriage was dissolved or annulled." After the Civil Code amendment of 1947 the same six months were carried over as Article 733. No such limit applied to men.

discontinued.label: 2024 Article 733 deleted
discontinued.fact: The Act Partially Amending the Civil Code and Other Acts (Act No. 102), promulgated on 16 December 2022, deleted Article 733, and came into force on 1 April 2024. Article 2 of its supplementary provisions, on transitional measures for marriages in breach of the ban on remarriage, provides that the annulment of a marriage entered into before that day "in breach of Article 733, paragraph 1, of the Civil Code before amendment" is governed by the former rules. Article 733 of the Civil Code now reads, in one line, "deleted".

keyfacts.text: The original text of Article 767, paragraph 1, of the Meiji Civil Code: "A woman may not remarry until six months have passed from the day her former marriage was dissolved or annulled." Paragraph 2 provided that where she had conceived before the dissolution of the former marriage, the preceding paragraph did not apply from the day of delivery.

On 16 December 2015 the Grand Bench of the Supreme Court held the part of the six months beyond 100 days contrary to Article 14, paragraph 1, and Article 24, paragraph 2, of the Constitution. The reason was that 100 days is enough to avoid an overlap of the presumptions of paternity.

The Act Partially Amending the Civil Code (Act No. 71), promulgated on 7 June 2016, "in Article 733, paragraph 1, replaces 'six months' with '100 days counted from'", and excepted the cases where the woman had not conceived and where she had given birth after the dissolution of the former marriage. Under paragraph 1 of the supplementary provisions it came into force on the day of promulgation.

Paragraph 2 of the supplementary provisions of the same Act provided that "the government shall, with three years from the entry into force of this Act as a target, review ... the shape of the rule on the prohibition of remarriage", writing into the text that the 100 days were provisional.

Act No. 102 of 2022, promulgated on 16 December 2022, deleted Article 733. It was part of an amendment that also reworked the presumption of legitimacy, and came into force on 1 April 2024. In the current Civil Code on e-Gov, Article 733 is shown as "deleted".

Article 2 of the supplementary provisions of that Act provides that "as regards the annulment of a marriage entered into before the date of entry into force in breach of Article 733, paragraph 1, of the Civil Code before amendment by Article 1, and an action to determine the father of a child borne by a woman who remarried in breach of that paragraph, the former rules shall continue to apply".

109.name: Preventing the Unfit
109.reading: furyo na shison wa boshi suru
109.hitokoto: The Maternal Health Law in force today is still dated 13 July 1948.
body: The Eugenic Protection Law, promulgated on 13 July 1948 and in force from 11 September that year, set out in Article 1 the purpose of "preventing the birth of inferior descendants from a eugenic standpoint". Sterilisation that did not require the consent of the person concerned went before a prefectural Eugenic Protection Board. Its predecessor was the National Eugenic Law, promulgated in 1940.

Act No. 105, promulgated on 26 June 1996, renamed the statute the Maternal Health Law and struck the word eugenic from the purpose clause. Because this was an amendment and not a repeal, the Maternal Health Law today still carries the number Act No. 156 of 1948 and the promulgation date 13 July 1948. The same statute is in use, with Article 1 rewritten. The period in which the eugenic provisions were operating was defined by the lump-sum payment Act of 2019 as "from 11 September 1948 to 25 September 1996".

The preamble to Act No. 14, promulgated on 24 April 2019, says "we sincerely reflect and offer a heartfelt and deep apology". The preamble to Act No. 70, promulgated on 17 October 2024, goes further, recording in the state's own words that it had done such things as "issuing a notice stating that there were cases in which the use of physical restraint, deception and other means was permissible" when the board-ordered operations were carried out. Article 1 of that Act lists the five Grand Bench judgments of the Supreme Court it rests on, all of 3 July 2024, each with its case number.

made.label: 1948 The Eugenic Protection Law in force
made.fact: The Eugenic Protection Law (Act No. 156 of 1948) was promulgated on 13 July 1948 and came into force on 11 September 1948. Article 1 provided that "the purpose of this Law is to prevent the birth of inferior descendants from a eugenic standpoint and to protect the life and health of the mother", and put eugenic operations that did not require the consent of the person concerned before a prefectural Eugenic Protection Board. The date of entry into force is fixed by Article 2 of Act No. 14 of 2019, which defines "the former Eugenic Protection Law" as "the Eugenic Protection Law (Act No. 156 of 1948) as in force during the period from 11 September 1948 to 25 September 1996".

discontinued.label: 1996 The eugenic provisions deleted
discontinued.fact: The Act Partially Amending the Eugenic Protection Law (Act No. 105), promulgated on 26 June 1996, renamed the statute the Maternal Health Law, and the eugenic provisions went from the purpose clause. Under the supplementary provision that "this Act shall come into force from the day on which three months have elapsed from the day of promulgation", it came into force on 26 September 1996. This matches Article 2 of Act No. 14 of 2019, which gives 25 September 1996 as the last day the former law was in force. The Act number and the promulgation date remain those of 1948 (Act No. 156 of 1948, 13 July 1948); only the text was rewritten.

keyfacts.text: Article 2, paragraph 1, of Act No. 14 of 2019: "In this Act, 'the former Eugenic Protection Law' means the Eugenic Protection Law (Act No. 156 of 1948) as in force during the period from 11 September 1948 to 25 September 1996." The eugenic provisions were operating for 48 years and 15 days.

Look up the Maternal Health Law on e-Gov and the number given is "Act No. 156 of 1948" and the promulgation date 13 July 1948. The 1996 amendment did not enact a new law; it amended and renamed the Eugenic Protection Law.

Article 1 of the present Maternal Health Law: "The purpose of this Act is to protect the life and health of the mother by providing for matters concerning sterilisation operations and the artificial termination of pregnancy and otherwise." The words of the Article 1 of 1948, "to prevent the birth of inferior descendants from a eugenic standpoint and", have been struck out.

Article 2 of the transitional provisions of the 1996 amending Act provided that "as regards the disbursement and bearing of the costs of eugenic operations carried out under Article 10 of the Eugenic Protection Law before amendment by this Act (hereinafter 'the former law'), the former rules shall continue to apply", leaving the existence of eugenic operations under the former law in the supplementary provisions of the law now in force.

Article 2, paragraph 2, of Act No. 14 of 2019 lists those covered in four periods, and as the dividing lines cites the Acts partially amending the Eugenic Protection Law (Act No. 216 of 1949, Act No. 141 of 1952, Act No. 105 of 1996) and the Act on the Abolition of the Leprosy Prevention Law (Act No. 28 of 1996). The Act abolishing the Leprosy Prevention Law also amended Article 3, paragraph 1, of the Eugenic Protection Law, so that the item numbers in that paragraph move up by one from 1 April 1996.

From the preamble to Act No. 14 of 2019: "Under the former Eugenic Protection Law enacted in 1948, or against the background of its existence, many people were compelled to undergo operations or irradiation rendering them incapable of reproduction on the ground that they had a particular disease or disability or otherwise, and suffered great pain in body and mind. For this, each of us in our own position sincerely reflects and offers a heartfelt and deep apology."

The preamble to Act No. 70, promulgated on 17 October 2024, records that the Diet and the government had done such things as "issuing a notice stating that there were cases in which the use of physical restraint, deception and other means was permissible when carrying out operations rendering a person incapable of reproduction that required the examination of a prefectural Eugenic Protection Board", and states that "with remorse and reflection we gravely acknowledge our responsibility".

Article 1 of that Act lists five Grand Bench judgments of the Supreme Court recognising the responsibility of the state, all of 3 July 2024, with their case numbers (2022 (ju) No. 1050 and No. 1411, 2023 (ju) No. 1319 and No. 1323, 2023 (o) No. 1341 and 2023 (ju) No. 1682). The preamble records that these judgments held the provisions of the former Eugenic Protection Law "contrary to Article 13 and Article 14, paragraph 1, of the Constitution of Japan".

Table 2 of the investigation report submitted to the Diet (published 19 June 2023) counts the eugenic operations from 1949 to 1996 by the provision relied on. Operations that did not require the consent of the person concerned number 14,566 under Article 4 and 1,909 under Article 12, 16,475 in all. Adding the 8,518 under Article 3, paragraph 1, items 1 to 3, which were with consent, gives a total of 24,993, of whom 6,195 were men and 18,798 women.

In the same table the peak is 1955, with 1,982 operations in the year (657 men, 1,325 women). From 1980 the annual figure is below 100, and no operation under Article 4 was carried out after 1990. The statistics come from the Ministry of Health and Welfare's Annual Health Report, its Eugenic Protection Statistics Report and the like.

The notice of the Vice-Minister of Health and Welfare of 12 June 1953, "On the enforcement of the Eugenic Protection Law" (Ministry of Health and Welfare Health Notice No. 150), stated that "it may be taken as permissible, to the extent truly unavoidable, to use physical restraint, the administration of anaesthetics, deception and other means". This is the notice the preamble to the compensation Act of 2024 points to.

Going further back, on 11 October 1949 the Director-General of the First Bureau of Legal Opinions of the Legal Affairs Agency replied to the Director-General of the Public Health Bureau of the Ministry of Health and Welfare (Legal Opinion No. 62, "On the means of carrying out compulsory eugenic operations") that "it must be taken that the operation may be carried out by force even where the person concerned has refused to undergo it".

The Grand Bench judgment of 3 July 2024 (2023 (ju) No. 1319) found that "according to the materials held by the Ministry of Health, Labour and Welfare, the number of persons who underwent sterilisation operations under the provisions at issue between 1949 and the 1996 amendment is said to be about 25,000".

The National Eugenic Law (Act No. 107 of 1940, promulgated 1 May 1940) came into force on 1 July 1941, except for Article 6, by Imperial Ordinance No. 680 of 6 June 1941. Article 6, which provided for compulsory application without the consent of the person or others, never came into force, because the imperial ordinance it needed was never made. Eugenic operations under that Law numbered 454 in all, from 1941 to 1945.
Artificial terminations of pregnancy carried out on eugenic grounds are put at about 59,000.

110.name: Lifelong Segregation
110.hitokoto: The article forbidding patients to leave the sanatorium carried a penalty.
body: The Law concerning the Prevention of Leprosy, promulgated in 1907, provided in Article 3 that the administrative authorities were to place in a sanatorium any patient who had neither means of treatment nor anyone to care for him. It came into force on 1 April 1909, two years after promulgation. Act No. 58, promulgated on 2 April 1931, retitled it the Leprosy Prevention Law and widened the scope of confinement to patients generally who were liable to spread infection.

The Leprosy Prevention Law of 1953, promulgated and in force on 15 August that year, set three stages in Article 6: persuasion, an order, and admission by the governor. Article 15 provided that "an admitted patient shall not leave the national sanatorium except in the cases set out in the following items", and Article 28 punished anyone who broke this with detention or a minor fine. Sample supplies of the drug promin were ready in April 1946, and by fiscal 1949 the state was buying it in. A ban on going out, with a penalty attached, was written after the disease had become curable.

Article 3 of the same Law reads: "No person shall, on that ground, treat a patient or a relative of a patient unjustly and discriminatorily." It was abolished by Act No. 28, promulgated on 31 March 1996, and lost its effect the next day, 1 April. The Kumamoto District Court held the state responsible on 11 May 2001, and recognised the harm done to families on 28 June 2019.

made.label: 1907 Law on the Prevention of Leprosy
made.fact: The Law concerning the Prevention of Leprosy (Act No. 11 of 1907) was assented to on 18 March 1907, promulgated in Official Gazette No. 7113 of 19 March, and came into force on 1 April 1909. Article 3 provided that "a leprosy patient who has no means of treatment and no one to care for him shall be placed in a sanatorium by the administrative authorities as provided by ordinance, and there relieved", so that it reached only patients with neither means of treatment nor a carer. Under Article 4, joint prefectural sanatoria were set up for five districts of the country; they were transferred to the state on 1 July 1941.

discontinued.label: 1996 The Leprosy Prevention Law abolished
discontinued.fact: By Article 1 of the Act on the Abolition of the Leprosy Prevention Law (Act No. 28), promulgated on 31 March 1996 - "The Leprosy Prevention Law (Act No. 214 of 1953) is abolished." - it was abolished on 1 April 1996. Article 6 of the supplementary provisions of that Act also deleted Article 3, paragraph 1, item 3, of the Eugenic Protection Law (eugenic operations on the ground of leprosy). The abolition Act itself was repealed on 1 April 2009, when the Act on the Promotion of the Resolution of the Hansen's Disease Problem (Act No. 82 of 2008) came into force.

keyfacts.text: The words "wandering" and "vagrant" do not appear in the text of the 1907 Law. In the Imperial Diet, however, they were said outright. At the plenary session of the House of Representatives on 16 February 1907, Vice-Minister of Home Affairs Saburo Yoshihara said that patients "wander about shrines, temples, parks and the like, and there is a danger of their spreading the infection", and at the special committee of the House of Peers on 5 March, the Director of the Sanitary Bureau, Seitaro Kubota, explained that those to be relieved were "chiefly those who are wandering about".

The Act Amending Act No. 11 of 1907 (on the Prevention of Leprosy) (Act No. 58, promulgated 2 April 1931, in force 1 August 1931) changed the title to the Leprosy Prevention Law and rewrote Article 3 as "where the administrative authorities find it necessary for the prevention of leprosy, they shall place a leprosy patient liable to spread the infection in a national leprosy sanatorium or in a sanatorium set up under Article 4". Even after the retitling, the number of the substantive law remained Act No. 11 of 1907.

The final report of the verification committee finds that it "deleted the previous condition for segregation and confinement, that the patient have no means of treatment and no one to care for him; that is, all patients became subject to segregation and confinement". The same report also states expressly that "it is true that the Leprosy Prevention Law contained no provision for compulsory segregation, that is, for segregating a person against his will": compulsory admission became statutory text with the Law of 1953.

The Leprosy Prevention Law (Act No. 214 of 1953) passed on 6 August 1953 and was promulgated and came into force on 15 August. Paragraph 2 of its supplementary provisions provided that "the Leprosy Prevention Law (Act No. 11 of 1907) is abolished". Article 6 set three stages: persuasion (paragraph 1), an order with a time limit (paragraph 2), and admission by the governor where the order was not obeyed or there was no time to follow the procedure (paragraph 3).

Article 15 of the same Law (restriction on going out): "An admitted patient shall not leave the national sanatorium except in the cases set out in the following items." The exceptions were only two: where the director gave permission because a relative was critically ill, had died, had suffered a disaster or the like, and where the patient was required by law to appear. Article 28 punished anyone who went out in breach of this with detention or a minor fine.

Article 16 of the same Law (maintenance of order) gave the director power to reprimand and to "confine a patient for a fixed period not exceeding 30 days", and a patient so dealt with "must stay quietly in the room the director has designated". Article 3, meanwhile, provided that "no person shall, on that ground, treat a patient or a relative of a patient unjustly and discriminatorily".

The patients' association Zenkankyo (the national council of patients of the national leprosy sanatoria) campaigned against the 1953 bill. That there was a sit-in behind the Diet building for about a week in early July 1953 is on the record: at the Committee on Health and Welfare of the House of Councillors on 23 July that year, Hisatada Hirose, chair of the subcommittee on leprosy, said that "in early July leprosy patients staged a sit-in behind the Diet in large numbers over several days to petition ... and in particular this continued for about a week".

Sample supplies of the drug promin were completed in the laboratory of Morizo Ishidate (department of pharmacy, Tokyo Imperial University) in April 1946; it was approved as an injection on 28 July 1948; and buying it in on the state budget began in earnest in fiscal 1949 (about 50 million yen). Even after the disease became curable, the law of segregation went on until 1996.

On the "no-leprosy prefecture" campaign, the final report of the verification committee records that "the term was first used in Aichi Prefecture in 1929, but it came into wide use only after the absolute segregation policy was put into effect with the promulgation of the Leprosy Prevention Law in 1931, and was stressed particularly from 1936, when the 'twenty-year eradication plan' for patients of Hansen's disease began". The Aichi campaign of 1929 was characterised in the Kumamoto District Court judgment of 2001 as a "private campaign".

Behind the campaign was the Leprosy Prevention Association. Its inaugural meeting was held at the Home Minister's official residence on 21 January 1931; Home Minister Kenzo Adachi and Eiichi Shibusawa and others were at its centre, and it was founded as a foundation with a grant from Empress Teimei and business donations as its endowment. The Sanitary Bureau of the Home Ministry announced its "policy for the eradication of leprosy" on 1 October 1930, and carried out a "twenty-year eradication plan" from fiscal 1936.

The campaign went on after the war. On 7 November 1947 the Director-General of the Prevention Bureau of the Ministry of Health and Welfare sent a circular to every prefectural governor, "On carrying out no-leprosy measures". The circular of the Director-General of the Public Health Bureau of 22 April 1950, "On leprosy prevention work for fiscal 1950", listed as methods of finding patients "letters from ordinary residents" and "surveys of vagrants and beggars". A document of 10 March 1959 from the head of the Tuberculosis Prevention Section of the Public Health Bureau to the head of the Health Department of Nagasaki Prefecture, "On the compulsory confinement of leprosy patients", also survives.

Sterilisation inside the sanatoria began before the law. The "register of patients undergoing early vasectomy" at Zensei Hospital shows the first operation performed on 24 April 1915 on a male patient of 38, with 37 in all that year. What was written into law was Article 3, paragraph 1, item 3, of the Eugenic Protection Law of 1948: "where the person or the spouse suffers from leprosy and there is a danger of its being transmitted to the descendants".

On the numbers carried out under the Eugenic Protection Law on the ground of Hansen's disease, the verification committee counted from the statistics 1,551 sterilisations and 7,696 artificial terminations of pregnancy (1949 to 1996). The figures used in the Kumamoto District Court judgment of 2001 are "more than 1,400" and "more than 3,000": two sets of figures stand side by side in the same report.

The Kumamoto District Court judgment of 11 May 2001 found that Articles 6, 15 and 28 of the Leprosy Prevention Law together provided for segregation, and that "by 1960 at the latest it had come to a state entirely lacking any ground to support its reasonableness, and its unconstitutionality had become clear". Damages were set in four steps of 14 million, 12 million, 10 million and 8 million yen according to the date of first admission and the length of stay, and the total awarded was 1,823,800,000 yen.

The government announced that it would not appeal on 23 May 2001, and a statement by the Prime Minister and a statement of the government were adopted by the Cabinet on 25 May. The statement said that "the government deeply reflects and offers a frank apology". The compensation Act (Act No. 63 of 2001) was promulgated on 22 June that year.

Responsibility towards families was recognised in the Kumamoto District Court judgment of 28 June 2019. There were 561 plaintiffs, and the judgment itself records that "the plaintiffs in this case exceed 560 in number". The Act on the Payment of Compensation to the Families of Former Hansen's Disease Patients (Act No. 55 of 2019) was promulgated on 22 November that year.

111.name: No Disgrace of Capture
111.reading: ikite ryoshu no hazukashime o ukezu
111.hitokoto: The line was not law. It was one moral precept inside an army instruction.
body: On 8 January 1941 the Senjinkun, the field service code, was issued in the name of Army Minister Hideki Tojo as Army Instruction No. 1, and distributed to units by a circular the next day. It was an instruction, neither a statute nor an imperial ordinance. Tojo himself, in his affidavit after the war, wrote "Army Ministry Instruction No. 1, the Senjinkun", and called its contents an admonition.

The famous line comes in the second half of Article 8 of Part 2, "Prize your name": "He who knows shame is strong. Think always of the honour of your home district and your house, and strive the harder to answer their expectation. Do not live to suffer the disgrace of capture; do not die leaving behind the stain of a crime." What carried a penalty was not the Senjinkun but the Army Criminal Code, and Articles 40 and 41 of it are both addressed to "a commander". There is no article punishing the surrender of a private soldier as such.

It had been otherwise before. The Rules on the Treatment of Prisoners of War of the Russo-Japanese War provided that "prisoners of war shall be treated with a spirit of benevolence, and shall on no account be insulted or ill-treated", and Japan held nearly 80,000 as prisoners of war in 29 camps. Japan signed the Geneva convention on prisoners of war in 1929 but did not ratify it. The Army Criminal Code was abolished by a cabinet order promulgated on 17 May 1947. No document abolishing the Senjinkun itself has been found.

made.label: 1941 Senjinkun, Army Instruction No. 1
made.fact: On 8 January 1941 the Senjinkun was issued as "Army Instruction No. 1" in the name of Army Minister Hideki Tojo, and distributed to units by circular Rikufu No. 54 of 9 January (Naoichi Kawahara, adjutant of the Army Ministry). The colophon of the original reads "Senjinkun, Army Instruction No. 1. This book is to serve as a means of raising morality in the field. 8 January 1941. Army Minister Hideki Tojo." Article 8 of Part 2, "Prize your name", reads "He who knows shame is strong. Think always of the honour of your home district and your house, and strive the harder to answer their expectation. Do not live to suffer the disgrace of capture; do not die leaving behind the stain of a crime."

discontinued.label: 1947 The Army Criminal Code abolished
discontinued.fact: The Army Criminal Code (Act No. 46 of 10 April 1908) was abolished by Cabinet Order No. 52 of 1947, the order abolishing the Army Criminal Code and related matters made under the Order concerning Orders Issued on the Acceptance of the Potsdam Declaration, promulgated on 17 May 1947. The Senjinkun itself was an instruction and not a law, so no document expressly abolishing it can be found. The Instructions for the National Volunteer Combat Corps, a military instruction of the same kind, was expressly abolished by Order No. 1 of the First and Second Demobilisation Ministries of 10 January 1946; nothing of that sort has been found for the Senjinkun.

keyfacts.text: The full text of Article 8 of Part 2 of the Senjinkun, "Prize your name", is: "He who knows shame is strong. Think always of the honour of your home district and your house, and strive the harder to answer their expectation. Do not live to suffer the disgrace of capture; do not die leaving behind the stain of a crime." The famous phrase is the second half of Article 8, not a provision of its own.

Article 7 immediately before, "On life and death", reads "what runs through life and death is the lofty spirit of devotion and service. Rise above life and death and press on single-mindedly to the completion of your duty." Article 8 is one of the ten articles of Part 2, with Article 7 before it and Article 9, "Simplicity and fortitude", after.

The Senjinkun was not a statute but an instruction. Tojo himself wrote in his affidavit to the International Military Tribunal for the Far East that "in January 1941 I issued Army Ministry Instruction No. 1, the Senjinkun (court exhibit No. 3069), and admonished them as to the conduct proper to the Imperial forces, servicemen and civilian employees of the army in the field".

The drafting was done by the Army Inspectorate General of Military Training over about a year and a half. Tetsujiro Inoue, Yoshio Yamada, Tetsuro Watsuji, Kenji Maki and Masami Kihira among others took part in the examination of views on the national polity, and Toson Shimazaki and Sonosuke Sato are reported to have worked on the prose (Tokyo Nichi Nichi Shimbun, 24 January 1941). Who wrote "do not live to suffer the disgrace of capture" cannot be established.

What carried a penalty was the Army Criminal Code (Act No. 46 of 1908). Article 40: "A commander who surrenders to the enemy without doing what he ought to have done, or who yields a fortress to the enemy, shall be punished by death." Article 41: "A commander who in the field surrenders to the enemy at the head of his troops shall, even where he has done all he ought to have done, be punished by imprisonment for not more than six months." Both, however, are addressed to "a commander"; there is no article in that chapter punishing the surrender of an individual private soldier as such.

The earlier norm was different. Article 2 of the Rules on the Treatment of Prisoners of War of the Russo-Japanese War (Army Ministry Order No. 22 of 14 February 1904) provided that "prisoners of war shall be treated with a spirit of benevolence, and shall on no account be insulted or ill-treated", and by the Army Ministry's published record, of 85,544 captured in all, 79,367 were treated as prisoners of war and 72,408 were held in 29 camps in Japan proper.

Japan signed the Geneva Convention relative to the Treatment of Prisoners of War on 27 July 1929 but did not ratify it. Tojo said in his affidavit that "Japan did not ratify the Geneva Convention ... in Japan it has been thought since ancient times a great disgrace to become a prisoner, and combatants have been taught to choose death rather than become prisoners ... to ratify the Geneva Convention would give rise to the misunderstanding that becoming a prisoner was being encouraged".

When ratification was considered in 1934, the Army and Navy advised against it. An individual opinion of a judge, included in the judgment of the International Military Tribunal for the Far East, gives among the reasons that "first, since no Japanese ever becomes a prisoner, the obligation is one-sided" and "fourth, it would become impossible to impose punishments on prisoners as severe as those imposed on Japanese servicemen".

The resulting proportions are on the record too. The same opinion in the judgment cites Ruth Benedict: "in the North Burma campaign the ratio of the number of prisoners to the number of the dead was 142 to 17,166", "this is a ratio of 1 to 120", while in Western armies "the proportion of those who surrender is 1 to 4". Almost all of the 142 prisoners, too, were taken wounded or unconscious.

Nineteen days after it was issued, at the plenary session of the House of Representatives on 27 January 1941, Tojo himself said "this is a passage from what was issued to the whole army the other day under the name of the Senjinkun", and at the Budget Committee of the House of Representatives on 5 February 1942 he read out the opening of its preface.

112.name: The Blood Tax
112.hitokoto: The first to use the words "blood tax" was a government proclamation.
body: On 28 November Meiji 5 (28 December 1872) an imperial rescript and the Admonition on Conscription were issued as Grand Council Proclamation No. 379. The admonition opens "in all heaven and earth there is not one thing that is not taxed", argues that a man too must give the whole strength of his mind and body in return to the state, and says "Westerners call this the blood tax, meaning a return made to the state in one's own living blood". The words blood tax were a figure of speech the government itself brought forward.

The same admonition states that reducing the stipends of the hereditary stipendiary samurai and allowing them to lay aside the sword is "the way to level high and low and to make rights equal", and that this is itself the ground for uniting soldier and farmer. Taking samurai privilege away and laying military service on commoners were, in the government's own account, one and the same argument. Those covered were "all males of the four classes throughout the country on reaching the age of twenty".

The Conscription Ordinance of 10 January 1873 had exemption provisions running to twelve articles, on height, on being the heir to a house and so on, and an article on the substitute fee, by which a payment of 270 yen bought exemption. It was narrowed to "disablement or deformity and the like" only by the amendment of 28 December 1883, and the substitute fee went at the same time. The end of the system is Imperial Ordinance No. 634, promulgated on 17 November 1945, abolishing the Military Service Law. Article 9 of the Constitution came into force a year and a half later.

made.label: 1872 The Admonition on Conscription
made.fact: Grand Council Proclamation No. 379 of 28 November Meiji 5 (28 December 1872), "The Imperial Rescript and Admonition on Conscription". The admonition says "in all heaven and earth there is not one thing that is not taxed, and with it the needs of the state are met; a man, then, must of course give the whole strength of his mind and body in return to the state. Westerners call this the blood tax, meaning a return made to the state in one's own living blood", and provides that "all males of the four classes throughout the country on reaching the age of twenty shall be entered on the military register, to be ready for use in any emergency". The Conscription Ordinance itself was issued by the Army Ministry on 10 January Meiji 6.

discontinued.label: 1945 The Military Service Law abolished
discontinued.fact: Imperial Ordinance No. 634, promulgated on 17 November 1945 (the Ordinance on the Abolition of the Military Service Law and Related Matters, made under Imperial Ordinance No. 542 of 1945, the Order concerning Orders Issued on the Acceptance of the Potsdam Declaration), abolished the Military Service Law (Act No. 47 of 1927), the Order for the Enforcement of the Military Service Law, the Temporary Special Provisions on the Deferment of Conscription for Students and others. By its supplementary provisions it came into force on the day of promulgation. Article 9, paragraph 2, of the Constitution of Japan, promulgated on 3 November 1946 and in force from 3 May 1947, provided that "land, sea, and air forces, as well as other war potential, will never be maintained".

keyfacts.text: From the text of the Admonition on Conscription: "Westerners call this the blood tax, meaning a return made to the state in one's own living blood." The figure of the tax was the government's own, and it is said that the misunderstanding it caused led to the riots against conscription in many places.

The same admonition says "the hereditary stipendiary samurai shall have their stipends reduced and be permitted to lay aside the sword, so that the four classes may by degrees obtain the rights of freedom. This is the way to level high and low and to make rights equal, and it is the ground for uniting soldier and farmer." Taking samurai privilege away and a nation in arms were, in the government's account, one and the same argument.

The Conscription Ordinance of 10 January 1873 has no statute number. In the Collection of Laws for Meiji 6 it appears among "Grand Council items outside the series and without number", with a marginal note: "The Conscription Ordinance is issued by the Army Ministry. It is nevertheless carried in the complete collection of Grand Council proclamations, and so is set out here." Grand Council Proclamation No. 272 of 1873 is the Land Tax Reform Regulations of 28 July that year.

The core of exemption is Chapter 3 of the Conscription Ordinance, the "General Rules on Exemption from the Standing Army" (12 articles): those under 5 shaku 1 sun in height (about 155 cm), those with a chronic illness or a deformity, those in the service of the government or of a prefecture, students of the military academies, students of specialist schools, those studying abroad and those studying medicine, the head of a household, an heir or a grandson succeeding to the house, an only son or only grandson, an adopted son and others. The substitute fee was set in Article 15 of Chapter 6: "whoever, being liable to conscription this year, applies of his own convenience to pay a substitute fee of 270 yen shall be exempted from both the standing and the reserve army."

Exemption was narrowed by the amendment of the Conscription Ordinance, Grand Council Proclamation No. 46 of 28 December 1883. Article 16 provided that "exemption from military service is limited to those with disablement or deformity or the like who, on examination under the Conscription Examination Regulations, are unfit for service", and heads of households, heirs, students and the like were reduced to "deferment of conscription". The provision on the substitute fee went with this amendment.

The Conscription Ordinance promulgated as Act No. 1 of 22 January 1889 provided in Article 1 that "all male subjects of the Empire of Japan from the full age of 17 to the full age of 40 are under a duty to serve in the military". From a Grand Council proclamation to a statute: the vessel changed too.

The Military Service Law was promulgated as Act No. 47 on 1 April 1927 and came into force on 1 December that year, under the supplementary provision "this Law shall come into force from 1 December 1927". It was a wholesale revision of Act No. 1 of 1889.

Imperial Ordinance No. 634, promulgated on 17 November 1945, listed: "the following Acts and imperial ordinances are abolished: the Military Service Law; the Act on Special Assistance for the Manufacture of Weapons and Other Businesses; the Order for the Enforcement of the Military Service Law; the Temporary Special Provisions on the Deferment of Conscription for Students ...". The record of the Military Service Law in the Japanese law index also notes "Imperial Ordinance No. 634 of 17 November 1945 | abolished".

The number of the war dead has been given in the Diet. At the Committee on Cabinet of the House of Representatives on 30 October 1980, Akira Ishizaki, a councillor of the Defence Agency, said that "the total number of the war dead is about 3,100,000, made up of about 2,300,000 servicemen, civilian employees of the military and the like, about 300,000 ordinary Japanese who died overseas, and about 500,000 Japanese who died in Japan proper". The period covered is from 7 July 1937 to 15 August 1945.

113.name: Nothing Until Victory
113.hitokoto: The author's name survives in the record of the Imperial Diet for 9 February 1943.
body: On 15 November 1942 the Imperial Rule Assistance Association and three newspapers, the Asahi, the Yomiuri and the Tokyo Nichi Nichi, called for entries for a "slogan of the people's resolve". The results were announced on 27 November: ten winners with a prize of 100 yen, and twenty commended entries besides. "Hoshigarimasen katsu made wa", we want nothing until we win, was one of the ten. It did not come first.

The author's name survives in an unlikely place. On 9 February 1943, at the third subcommittee of the Budget Committee of the House of Representatives, Kenryo Sato, Director of the Military Affairs Bureau of the Army Ministry, said "as I recall, it was a slogan entered by a girl named Akiko Miyake, a fifth-year pupil at Kogai National School in Azabu Ward". He put in the reservation "as I recall", however, and there is a view that her father wrote it for her, so the matter is not settled.

What held the slogan up was the statute book. The Regulations Restricting the Manufacture and Sale of Luxury Goods, promulgated on 6 July 1940, are known as the 7-7 Ban because their supplementary provision set 7 July as the day they came into force. The authority for them was not the National Mobilisation Law but Article 2 of the Act on Temporary Measures concerning Imports and Exports. The regulations lapsed under Act No. 49 of 21 December 1945. There is no document abolishing the slogan itself.

made.label: 1942 Slogan of the people's resolve
made.fact: On 15 November 1942 the Imperial Rule Assistance Association and three newspaper companies, Asahi Shimbun, Yomiuri Shimbun and Tokyo Nichi Nichi Shimbun, with the backing of the Cabinet Information Bureau, called for entries for a "slogan of the people's resolve", and on 27 November each paper announced ten winners (with a prize of 100 yen) and twenty commended entries. "Hoshigarimasen katsu made wa", we want nothing until we win, was one of the ten. It did not come first.

discontinued.label: 1945 The 7-7 Ban lapses
discontinued.fact: The Regulations Restricting the Manufacture and Sale of Luxury Goods (Ministry of Commerce and Industry and Ministry of Agriculture and Forestry Order No. 2 of 1940, known as the 7-7 Ban), the core of the consumption controls that held the slogan up, lapsed under Act No. 49 of 21 December 1945. The slogan itself was not a law, so there is no document giving notice of its abolition.

keyfacts.text: On 9 February 1943, at the third subcommittee of the Budget Committee of the House of Representatives in the 81st Imperial Diet, the government member Kenryo Sato, Director of the Military Affairs Bureau of the Army Ministry, said: "Last November, I think it was, a slogan of the people's resolve was called for, and there were some ten of them ... and last of all, as I recall, there was one entered by a girl named Akiko Miyake, a fifth-year pupil at Kogai National School in Azabu Ward, 'We want nothing until we win'." The date of the competition, the ten winners and the author's name are all on the record as a statement from the government side.

The same statement, however, carries the speaker's own reservation, "as I recall". There is a view that the author was not the girl but her father, writing for her, set out in Kei Kitsukawa, "Entertainment under the war" (Ritsumeikan Peace Research, no. 2, March 2001), p. 5. Accounts of the number of entries do not agree: some say over 320,000, others over 1,800,000.
