The earlier slogan "Luxury is the enemy!" was put out by the Headquarters for the General Mobilisation of the National Spirit, which set up 1,500 standing boards in the city of Tokyo between late July and early September 1940. The slogans came as a pair, and in the original they were in hiragana with exclamation marks: "1. Luxury is the enemy! 2. A Japanese should not be able to afford luxury!"

The formal name of the 7-7 Ban is the Regulations Restricting the Manufacture and Sale of Luxury Goods, and its number is Order No. 2 of the Ministry of Commerce and Industry and the Ministry of Agriculture and Forestry, a joint ministerial order. It was promulgated on 6 July 1940 (Official Gazette No. 4049), and its supplementary provision, "these Regulations shall come into force from 7 July 1940", gave the day that is the origin of the nickname.

The authority for the 7-7 Ban was not the National Mobilisation Law. The promulgation clause reads "under the provisions of Article 2 of Act No. 92 of 1937", citing Article 2 of the Act on Temporary Measures concerning Imports and Exports (Act No. 92 of 10 September 1937).

"Forward, one hundred million, a ball of fire" was a slogan put up by the Imperial Rule Assistance Association on 8 December 1941, with the outbreak of war, paired with "Slaughter them, America and Britain, our enemies". It was not the Cabinet Information Bureau's.

On 25 January 1941, at the Budget Committee of the House of Representatives in the 76th Imperial Diet, the member Katsu Kawasaki said of the Imperial Rule Assistance Association: "What is the voice that cries out from the camp of those people? It is the voice that says luxury is the enemy. And the camp in which the people who cry that luxury is the enemy are holed up? It is the most luxurious building in Japan." The slogan was already being mocked at the time.

The 7-7 Ban and rationing by coupon were part of the same policy package. At one and the same cabinet meeting, on 10 May 1940, the introduction of coupon rationing for matches and sugar and the restriction or prohibition of the manufacture and sale of luxury goods were decided together.

The framework of calling for slogans as national policy begins with the "Outline for the General Mobilisation of the National Spirit" (cabinet decision of 24 August 1937). The body doing the calling moved from the Central League for the General Mobilisation of the National Spirit (formed 12 October 1937) to the Committee for the General Mobilisation of the National Spirit (Imperial Ordinance No. 80 of 28 March 1939) and the Headquarters for the General Mobilisation of the National Spirit (established April 1940), and with the founding of the Imperial Rule Assistance Association in October 1940 the Headquarters was dissolved and absorbed into it.

Wartime publications carry no punctuation or interpunct in the slogan. The 1943 catalogue of the exhibition Winning the Economic Fight Through also writes "Hoshigarimasen katsu made wa" as one unbroken line.

Its opposite number, "non-national" (hikokumin), is not a term of law. The Japanese law index has no statute since 1867 with hikokumin in its title. In the Imperial Diet, too, it was treated as improper: at the plenary session of the House of Representatives on 25 March 1927, after a remark by the member Hisashi Isobe, the acting speaker asked "there was just now in your words the expression 'non-national' and so forth; I think this is not proper. Will you not withdraw it?"

114.name: Dowry
114.hitokoto: The act that banned dowry in 1961 also lists, in its own definition, the gifts that do not count.
body: The Dowry Prohibition Act received assent on 20 May 1961 and appeared in the Gazette of India the next day. Act No. 28 of 1961. Its preamble is a single line: "An Act to prohibit the giving or taking of dowry." Section 3 sets imprisonment of up to six months or a fine of up to 5,000 rupees. Section 4 punishes the demand itself.

The definition in Section 2 is the interesting part. Dowry is "property or valuable security given as consideration for the marriage"; dower or mahr under Muslim personal law is excluded, and wedding presents such as cash, ornaments and clothes do not count "unless they are given as consideration for the marriage". A prohibition act sets out, in its own text, what it does not prohibit.

So this is not a value that has lapsed. Articles on cruelty and on "dowry death" were added to the Penal Code in the 1980s, and cases registered with the Crime Records Bureau rose from 7,146 in 1998 to 8,331 in 2011 (a rise in the figures also means a rise in reporting). Only the date of the ban is clear.

made.label: Modern Given as "consideration" for the marriage
made.fact: The 1961 act defined dowry as property or valuable security given, at or before or after the marriage, by one party or by a parent or another person to the other party, "as consideration for the marriage". Until the law named and defined it, the practice had no outline in any statute. No primary source was reached for the view that it spread in modern times.

discontinued.label: 1961 The Dowry Prohibition Act
discontinued.fact: Assented to by the President on 20 May 1961 and published in the Gazette of India of 21 May 1961 (Extraordinary, Part II-Section 1, No.32). Act No. 28 of 1961. Section 3 set, for giving or taking dowry and for abetting it, imprisonment of up to six months or a fine of up to 5,000 rupees, or both. Section 1(3) left the commencement date to notification in the Gazette, and the act came into force on 1 July 1961.

keyfacts.text: The Dowry Prohibition Act was assented to by the President on 20 May 1961 and appeared in the Gazette of India of 21 May 1961 (Extraordinary, Part II-Section 1, No.32). It is Act No. 28 of 1961, and its preamble is one line: "An Act to prohibit the giving or taking of dowry."

The definition in Section 2 is "property or valuable security given at, before or after the marriage as consideration for the marriage". Dower or mahr for those to whom Muslim personal law applies is excluded, and presents such as cash, ornaments and clothes are stated not to be dowry "unless they are given as consideration for the marriage". The prohibition act writes a wide way round itself into its own text.
Section 3 sets imprisonment of up to six months or a fine of up to 5,000 rupees, or both. Section 4 punishes the demand itself.

Amendments to the Penal Code in the 1980s added cruelty by a husband or his relatives (Section 498A) and "dowry death" (Section 304B). Sources differ on the year of insertion, 1983 or 1986, and it could not be fixed here.

Dowry deaths registered with the National Crime Records Bureau (NCRB) number 7,146 in 1998, 8,172 in 2008 and 8,331 in 2011. The relevant tables on the NCRB site were not reached, and all three figures are quoted at second hand.

115.name: The Hijab, Both Ways
115.hitokoto: Over the same cloth: in 1936 the order was to take it off, in 1980 to put it on.
body: On 8 January 1936 Reza Shah issued a decree banning all veils, the hijab and the chador included. The police were ordered to remove the veil physically from women who wore it in public. The control reached men as well: making the bowler hat compulsory in the summer of 1935 brought large protests in Mashhad in which an estimated 100 to 500 people died.

After Reza Shah abdicated in 1941 the ban was relaxed, and wearing a headscarf or a chador was no longer unlawful. For some forty years after that, dress was in practice free. The direction turned with the "Islamisation of government offices" in July 1980: women without a veil were refused entry to government offices and public buildings, and at work became liable to dismissal.

Article 638 of the Islamic Penal Code now in force makes it an offence to commit openly in public an act forbidden by religion, and appearing without the hijab is treated as falling within it. In September 2024 the President said the morality police would no longer trouble women over it. Over one piece of cloth, the direction of the order has turned three times.

made.label: 1936 The unveiling decree
made.fact: On 8 January 1936 Reza Shah issued a decree banning all veils, the hijab and the chador included. The police were ordered to remove the veil physically from women who wore it in public. Traditional men's dress was banned at the same time, and making the bowler hat compulsory in the summer of 1935 brought large protests in Mashhad in which an estimated 100 to 500 people died.

discontinued.label: 1941 The ban relaxed
discontinued.fact: In 1941, after Reza Shah abdicated, the ban was relaxed under his successor Mohammad Reza Pahlavi, and wearing a headscarf or a chador was no longer unlawful.

restocked.label: 1980 Compulsory, beginning with the offices
restocked.fact: Following Khomeini's statement of March 1979, the "Islamisation of government offices" in July 1980 meant that women without a veil were refused entry to government offices and public buildings and became liable to dismissal at work. Article 638 of the Islamic Penal Code now in force makes appearing in public without the hijab an offence.

keyfacts.text: On 8 January 1936 Reza Shah issued a decree banning all veils, the hijab and the chador included. The police were ordered to remove the veil from women who wore it in public.
The control of dress reached men too. Making the bowler hat compulsory in the summer of 1935 brought large protests in Mashhad in which an estimated 100 to 500 people died.
After Reza Shah abdicated in 1941 the ban was relaxed and wearing a headscarf or a chador was no longer unlawful. Until 1979, dress was in practice free.

With the "Islamisation of government offices" in July 1980, women without a veil were refused entry to government offices and public buildings, forbidden to appear unveiled at work, and made liable to dismissal.
Article 638 of the Islamic Penal Code now in force makes it an offence to commit openly in public an act forbidden by religion, and appearing without the hijab is treated as included in it.

In September 2024 President Masoud Pezeshkian said the morality police would no longer trouble women over the hijab. Counting from 1936, the rules on the same garment have turned direction three times.

116.name: One Child
116.hitokoto: "One child" began with a single letter, on 25 September 1980.
body: Birth limitation in China was taken up as a national line at the meeting of the directors of the national family planning offices on 26 January 1979, and the regulations of the Shanghai municipality, promulgated on 22 August that year, were the first ordinance of the kind. It was established as state policy on 25 September 1980, in the "Open Letter" the Central Committee of the Chinese Communist Party addressed to every party member and every member of the Communist Youth League. To hold the population within 1.2 billion by the end of the century, it said, one couple was to be encouraged to bear only one child.

It stood on five pillars: marrying late, bearing late, bearing few, spacing births and better births. Its legal footing came in three tiers: the provisions of the Constitution, the Marriage Law as amended in 1980, and the family planning regulations of each region. A single national statute came late. The Population and Family Planning Law was passed on 29 December 2001 and came into force on 1 September 2002; Article 2 made family planning a basic state policy.

A relaxation in 2013 allowed a second child where either spouse was an only child, but take-up did not grow, and the Fifth Plenary Session of the 18th Central Committee of the Party, which closed on 29 October 2015, decided to allow a second child across the board. On 27 December the Standing Committee of the National People's Congress amended Article 18, paragraph 1 of the law to read "the state encourages a couple to bear two children", in force from 1 January 2016. On 20 August 2021 a third child was allowed.

made.label: 1980.9.25 The Party's Open Letter
made.fact: On 25 September 1980 the Central Committee of the Chinese Communist Party issued its "Open Letter to All Members of the Communist Party and of the Communist Youth League on the Question of Controlling the Growth of Our Country's Population", which stated that "in order to hold the total population of our country within 1.2 billion by the end of this century, the State Council has issued a call to the whole people, encouraging one couple to bear only one child". This is the point at which it was established as state policy.

discontinued.label: 2015.12.27 The law amended (in force 2016.1.1)
discontinued.fact: On 27 December 2015 the 18th meeting of the Standing Committee of the 12th National People's Congress decided to amend Article 18, paragraph 1 of the Population and Family Planning Law to read "the state encourages a couple to bear two children", and provided that "this decision comes into force on 1 January 2016".

keyfacts.text: A basic line at national level was first considered at the meeting of the directors of the national family planning offices on 26 January 1979, and the "only-child certificate" was tried out in Tianjin and Sichuan soon afterwards. The first ordinance was the "Certain Provisions of the Shanghai Revolutionary Committee on Promoting Family Planning", promulgated on 22 August 1979.

The policy stood on five pillars: marrying late, bearing late, bearing few, spacing (about four years between two children) and better births. Its legal footing came in three tiers: the provisions of the Constitution, the Marriage Law as amended in 1980, and the family planning regulations of each region.

On 29 December 2001 the 25th meeting of the Standing Committee of the 9th National People's Congress passed the Population and Family Planning Law of the People's Republic of China, promulgated the same day by Presidential Order No. 63 and in force from 1 September 2002. Article 2 provides that "carrying out family planning is a basic state policy".

A relaxation in 2013 allowing a second child where either spouse was an only child saw low take-up, and the communiqué of the Fifth Plenary Session of the 18th Central Committee of the Chinese Communist Party, which closed on 29 October 2015, decided to "fully implement the policy of one couple bearing two children".

On 20 August 2021 the 30th meeting of the Standing Committee of the 13th National People's Congress amended the law again (Presidential Order No. 96, in force the same day), allowing a couple to have up to three children.

Children born on or after 1 January 2016, second children included, were all to count as lawful and to be entered in the household register. On 14 January 2016 the State Council issued an opinion calling for "the complete resolution of the problem of people without household registration", covering those who had been unable to obtain it for reasons such as breach of the policy.

117.name: Red over Expert
117.hitokoto: For eleven and a half years, university entrance in China had no examination. It had recommendation.
body: "Both red and expert" is a phrase from the Sixty Articles on Higher Education of September 1961: red is the world view of the proletariat, expert is specialist knowledge and skill. Its opposite, "white expert", meant a person with technical skill whose political stand lay on the side of the bourgeoisie, and anyone who gave himself to study and took no interest in politics was criticised for "walking the white-expert road". The mathematician Chen Jingrun was one of those so called.

On 13 June 1966 the Central Committee and the State Council gave notice that the admission of new university entrants that year would be put back by six months. On 24 July, in the "Notice on Reforming the Work of Admission to Higher Education", they decided that from that year admission to higher education would cancel examinations and adopt a method joining recommendation to selection. From 1970 worker-peasant-soldier students entered in four stages: applying voluntarily, recommendation by the masses, approval by the leadership, review by the school. Their task was said to be not to study but to run the universities and remake them.

An attempt in 1973 to bring back a written test in four subjects collapsed with the blank-paper affair of Zhang Tiesheng. In August 1977 Deng Xiaoping announced, at the national forum on science and education work, direct recruitment from secondary school leavers, and on 12 October the State Council, in Guofa (1977) No. 112, endorsed and circulated the Ministry of Education's opinion and restored the unified examination. Between 28 November and 25 December that year about 5.7 million people sat it and 273,000 passed.

made.label: 1966.7.24 Examinations cancelled
made.fact: On 13 June 1966 the Central Committee and the State Council gave notice of the "Decision to Postpone by Half a Year the Work of Admitting New Students to Higher Education in 1966", and on 24 July, in the "Notice on Reforming the Work of Admission to Higher Education", decided that "from this year, admission to higher education shall cancel examinations and adopt a method combining recommendation with selection".

discontinued.label: 1977.10.12 The unified examination restored
discontinued.fact: On 12 October 1977 the State Council, in document Guofa (1977) No. 112, endorsed and circulated the Ministry of Education's "Opinion on the Work of Admission to Higher Education in 1977" and restored the system of unified examination. Between 28 November and 25 December that year about 5.7 million people sat it and 273,000 passed.

keyfacts.text: "Both red and expert" appears in the "Sixty Articles on Higher Education" issued by the Central Committee of the Chinese Communist Party in September 1961: "red" is the world view of the proletariat, "expert" is specialist knowledge and skill. The Central Committee required cadres to be both, and issued notices aimed at uniting politics with technique.

The paired term is "white expert", used from the late 1950s to the Cultural Revolution for those who gave themselves to research or study and took no interest in politics. The conduct was called "walking the white-expert road", and those so labelled were often denounced in struggle sessions. The mathematician Chen Jingrun was criticised as a "white expert" during the Cultural Revolution.

From 1970 universities admitted workers, peasants and soldiers with two or more years of practical experience and attainment at middle-school level or above as "worker-peasant-soldier students", by the method of "applying voluntarily, recommendation by the masses, approval by the leadership, review by the school". Their chief task was said to be not study but to "attend the university, run the university and remake the university with Mao Zedong Thought".

In 1973, on Deng Xiaoping's initiative, the State Council endorsed and circulated the "Opinion on the Work of Admission to Higher Education in 1973", adding a written test in four subjects: politics, language, mathematics, and physics and chemistry. But the blank-paper affair of Zhang Tiesheng followed, and because the Gang of Four made him a "blank-paper hero" the written test was stopped again.

In August 1977 Deng Xiaoping, Vice-Chairman of the Central Committee and Vice-Premier of the State Council, declared in his summing-up at the national forum on science and education work: "This year we must make up our minds to restore direct admission by examination from among secondary school leavers, and stop recommendation by the masses."

The period without a unified examination runs to eleven and a half years, from 1966 to 1977. Among the 273,000 who passed in 1977 were Li Keqiang, later Premier of the State Council, and Wang Yi, later Minister of Foreign Affairs.

118.name: Speak Mandarin only
118.hitokoto: The article ordering that dialects be reduced year by year was deleted on 2 August 1993.
body: On 2 April 1946 the Taiwan Provincial Administrative Executive Office set up the Taiwan Provincial Committee for the Promotion of the National Language and began the National Language Movement. On 25 October that year the Japanese-language editions of newspapers and magazines were abolished, leaving a transition of barely a year. On 10 July 1951 the Department of Education of the Taiwan Provincial Government ordered schools at every level to teach in the national language and strictly forbid dialects, and provided that those of low attainment in it were not to be appointed as teachers.

Under a circular of 22 July 1963, promoting the national language became an item in the head teacher's appraisal of staff, and whether a pupil spoke it affected his conduct mark. Article 1 of the rules implementing the 1966 Plan to Strengthen the Promotion of the National Language provided that teachers and pupils at schools of every level must use the national language at all times and in all places, and that pupils in breach were to be dealt with under the rules on rewards and punishments. A child who spoke a dialect on school grounds could be punished by having a tag called a gou pai, a dog tag, hung round his neck. It is the same instrument as the dialect tag in Okinawa.

Article 20 of the Radio and Television Act, promulgated on 8 January 1976, provided that the language of broadcasting for home audiences should be chiefly the national language and that dialects should be reduced year by year. The article was deleted on 2 August 1993 by presidential order. In August 1987 the provincial government had already ordered, throughout the province, that punishment by corporal punishment, fines or the dog tag cease. The Development of National Languages Act, promulgated on 9 January 2019, makes the natural languages of each of Taiwan's own ethnic groups, and Taiwan Sign Language, national languages, all of them equal.

made.label: 1946.4.2 The National Language Committee / 1951.7.10 dialects forbidden
made.fact: On 2 April 1946 the Taiwan Provincial Committee for the Promotion of the National Language was set up under the Education Department of the Taiwan Provincial Administrative Executive Office (chairman Wei Jiangong, vice-chairman He Rong), and the National Language Movement began. On 25 October that year the Japanese-language editions of newspapers and magazines were abolished. On 10 July 1951 the Department of Education of the Taiwan Provincial Government ordered schools at every level to teach in the national language and strictly forbid dialects, and made attainment in it a condition of appointment as a teacher.

discontinued.label: 1993.8.2 Article 20 deleted
discontinued.fact: Article 20 of the Radio and Television Act, enacted and promulgated on 8 January 1976, provided that "the language of a station's domestic broadcasting shall be chiefly the national language, and dialects shall be reduced year by year". On 2 August 1993 (Republic of China year 82) Article 20 was deleted by presidential order Hua-zong-yi No. 3757 of that year.

restocked.label: 2019.1.9 Development of National Languages Act
restocked.fact: On 25 December 2018 the Legislative Yuan passed the Development of National Languages Act on third reading (reported as 17 articles in all), and it was promulgated on 9 January 2019 (the text now in the national law database runs to Article 18). Article 3 provides that "the national languages in this Act mean the natural languages used by each of Taiwan's own ethnic groups, and Taiwan Sign Language", and Article 4 that "the national languages are all equal, and citizens shall not be discriminated against or restricted in using them".

keyfacts.text: Under the "Measures for Strengthening National Language Education in the National Schools of Taiwan Province" of 28 November 1952, head teachers were charged with supervision and assessment, and under the "Points for Attention in Strengthening the Promotion of the National Language in Public and Private Primary Schools in Taiwan Province" of 22 July 1963 promoting the national language became an item in the head teacher's year-end appraisal of staff, while whether a pupil spoke it affected his conduct mark.

Article 1 of the rules implementing the Taiwan Provincial Government's "Plan to Strengthen the Promotion of the National Language" of 1966 provided that "teachers and pupils at schools of every level must use the national language at all times and in all places; pupils in breach are to be dealt with under the rules on rewards and punishments". In many places a child who spoke a dialect on school grounds was punished by having a tag called a gou pai, a dog tag, hung round his neck.

From 1972 Taiwanese-language television programmes were limited to one hour a day. Article 20 of the Radio and Television Act, promulgated on 8 January 1976, provided that dialects "shall be reduced year by year", the proportion to be fixed by the Government Information Office of the Executive Yuan in the light of actual need.

In April 1983 the Ministry of Education set up a group to draft a language act, and the draft published in December 1985 would have required the use of the national language at meetings, in official business and wherever three or more people were present, with a fine of 3,000 to 10,000 yuan for a second breach. Opposition from non-party provincial assembly members and from human rights bodies led to the legislation being dropped.

In August 1987 the Taiwan Provincial Government ordered junior high schools and primary schools throughout the province that pupils who spoke a dialect on school grounds were not to be punished by such means as corporal punishment, fines or the hanging of a dog tag.

Article 9, paragraph 2 of the Development of National Languages Act requires the central education authority to place the national languages in the prescribed curriculum at each stage of basic national education. Under Article 18 that paragraph came into force three years after the twelve-year basic national education curriculum guidelines took effect, and the other articles from the day of promulgation.

119.name: Apartheid
119.hitokoto: A law that registered the race of everyone born stood for forty-one years.
body: In the election of 26 May 1948 D. F. Malan's National Party took power with 40% of the total vote and a majority of five seats. The bundle of statutes built up from there became the machinery that counted people by race, divided them and fixed where they might be. There is no single "Apartheid Act".

The frame was set in 1950. Act No. 30 of 1950, the Population Registration Act, in force from 7 July that year, classified the whole population as White, Black or Coloured, on the criteria of "appearance, social acceptance and descent". The definition of a white person extended to "habits, speech, education, deportment and demeanour". Act No. 41 of the same year, the Group Areas Act, in force the same day, fixed by group where property might be owned, where people might live and where they might work.

Nor did the repeal come at one stroke. Act No. 72 of 1985 lifted the bans on marriage and on sexual intercourse; Act No. 68 of 1986 abolished influx control; Act No. 100 of 1990 removed segregation in public places; in 1991 Act No. 114 repealed the Population Registration Act and Act No. 108 the Natives Land Act of 1913. The first democratic election was in April 1994.

made.label: 1950 Population registration and group areas
made.fact: Act No. 30 of 1950, the Population Registration Act, required the whole South African population to be classified as White, Black or Coloured, and Act No. 41 of 1950, the Group Areas Act, fixed by group where property might be owned, where people might live and where they might work. Both came into force on 7 July 1950. The starting point is the National Party's coming to power in the election of 26 May 1948.

discontinued.label: 1991 Population Registration Act repealed
discontinued.fact: Section 1 of Act No. 114 of 1991, the Population Registration Act Repeal Act, repealed the Population Registration Act, and Section 1 of Act No. 108 of 1991, the Abolition of Racially Based Land Measures Act, repealed the Natives Land Act of 1913.

keyfacts.text: In the election of 26 May 1948, D. F. Malan's National Party joined with N. C. Havenga's Afrikaner Party and won a majority of five seats on 40% of the total vote. The winner of that election put apartheid into law.

Act No. 30 of 1950, the Population Registration Act, in force from 7 July 1950, classified the whole population as White, Black or Coloured, and set the criteria of classification as "appearance, social acceptance and descent". The definition of a white person took in "habits, speech, education, deportment and demeanour".

Act No. 41 of 1950, the Group Areas Act, in force from 7 July 1950, fixed by group where property might be owned, where people might live and where they might work; it cut across established property rights and produced forced removals running into thousands. Act No. 49 of 1953, the Reservation of Separate Amenities Act, in force from 9 October 1953, divided lavatories, parks and beaches by group and further provided that they need not be of the same quality.

The repeal was piecemeal: Act No. 72 of 1985 (lifting the bans on marriage and on sexual intercourse across race), Act No. 68 of 1986 (Abolition of Influx Control Act), Act No. 100 of 1990 (Discriminatory Legislation regarding Public Amenities Repeal Act), Act No. 114 of 1991 (Population Registration Act Repeal Act) and Act No. 108 of 1991 (Abolition of Racially Based Land Measures Act).

South Africa held its first democratic election in April 1994, under an interim constitution. The ANC took 62% and Mandela became the first democratically elected President. The pass laws had been repealed in 1986.

120.name: Mixed Marriage a Crime
120.hitokoto: In 1949, the year the act was made, there were about seventy-five such marriages in the whole country.
body: Act No. 55 of 1949, the Prohibition of Mixed Marriages Act, forbade marriage between a white person and a member of another racial group. The motive stated in the parliamentary debates was concern about Coloured people passing into the white group. The next year Act No. 21 of 1950, the Immorality Amendment Act, forbade sexual intercourse between white and black, so that the law reached the stage before marriage as well.

In 1949, when the act was made, recorded "mixed marriages" numbered about 75 in the whole country. Marriages between white people that year numbered about 28,000. A statute was written for a figure under 0.3% of the whole. Act No. 21 of 1968 went further and voided marriages contracted abroad, closing the way round.

What repealed them was Act No. 72 of 1985. Of the bundle of apartheid statutes, the part about marriage and sex came off first; the Population Registration Act went six years later, in 1991. The same rule was ended in the United States by the Supreme Court in 1967, and in South Africa by Parliament in 1985.

made.label: 1949 Prohibition of Mixed Marriages Act
made.fact: Act No. 55 of 1949, the Prohibition of Mixed Marriages Act, forbade marriage between a white person and a member of another racial group. The next year Act No. 21 of 1950, the Immorality Amendment Act, forbade sexual intercourse between white and black.

discontinued.label: 1985 Act No. 72
discontinued.fact: Act No. 72 of 1985, the Immorality and Prohibition of Mixed Marriages Amendment Act, repealed a series of these provisions, Act No. 21 of 1968 among them.

keyfacts.text: Act No. 55 of 1949 forbade marriage between a white person and a member of another racial group. The motive stated in the parliamentary debates was concern about Coloured people passing into the white group.

In 1949, when the act was made, recorded "mixed marriages" numbered about 75 in the whole country, against about 28,000 marriages between white people. What it forbade came to under 0.3% of the whole.
Act No. 21 of 1950, the Immorality Amendment Act, forbade acts such as adultery, the attempt at it, and sexual intercourse between white and black. It was amended as Act No. 23 of 1957.

Act No. 21 of 1968, the Prohibition of Mixed Marriages Amendment Act, in force from 27 March 1968, voided a marriage contracted outside South Africa by a male citizen with a woman of another racial group. It was designed to close the way of marrying abroad and coming back.

What repealed these was Act No. 72 of 1985, the Immorality and Prohibition of Mixed Marriages Amendment Act. Of the bundle of apartheid statutes, the part about marriage and sex came off first. The Population Registration Act was repealed six years later, in 1991.

121.name: Women do not drive
121.hitokoto: There was no article banning it. Not issuing licences did the work for 61 years.
body: No article banning it can be found. According to the scholar David Commins, Riyadh declared the ban in 1957, but in substance it was the practice of not issuing driving licences to women. A ban without a text has nothing to repeal. To end it, then, what was needed was not the deletion of an article but the act of issuing a licence.

On 6 November 1990, 47 women drove cars in Riyadh. All were held for a day and had their passports confiscated. That date can be fixed from the sources. The day it was protested against is on the record more clearly than the day it began. A ban with no text shows its outline only when it is broken.

On 26 September 2017 King Salman issued an order allowing women to drive, and said it would be carried out by June 2018. The ban ended on 24 June 2018, and licences began to be issued to women the same day. In Japan too, the provisions of the Labour Standards Act restricting night work by women were removed on 1 April 1999.

made.label: 1957 The ban declared in Riyadh
made.fact: According to the scholar David Commins, Riyadh declared a ban on women driving in 1957. The ban was not an article reading "women shall not drive" but was kept up as the practice of not issuing driving licences to women.

discontinued.label: 2018.6.24 The ban ends
discontinued.fact: On 26 September 2017 King Salman issued an order allowing women to drive, and said that licences would be issued by June 2018. The ban ended on 24 June 2018, and licences began to be issued to women the same day.

keyfacts.text: According to David Commins, Riyadh declared a ban on women driving in 1957. No written provision stating that women shall not drive has been confirmed, however; the ban was kept up by the practice of not issuing licences.
On 6 November 1990, 47 women drove cars in Riyadh in protest. They were held for a day and had their passports confiscated.
On 26 September 2017 King Salman issued an order allowing women to drive "in accordance with the Sharia". Guidance was to be prepared and the order carried out by June 2018.
The ban ended on 24 June 2018, and licences began to be issued to women the same day: 61 years counting from 1957, 28 years counting from the protest of 1990.

Japan too had rules of the form "women do not work like this". The Labour Standards Act of 1947 restricted night work and overtime by women, and the restriction was removed by the amendment of 1997, in force on 1 April 1999. That the end of a ban has a date is the same in both.

122.name: Guardian's Permission
122.hitokoto: The rule that a daughter's or a wife's passport needed her father's or husband's permission left the statute in August 2019.
body: What had been restricted can be worked out backwards from the words of the amendment. In 2019 the passport law, the Travel Documents Law, was rewritten to say that any Saudi national may obtain a passport. Until then, in other words, a passport was not something anyone could get. A woman needed the permission of her male guardian, and was entered on the passport of a male relative.

The amendment was adopted as a decision of the Council of Ministers on 31 July 2019, published in the official gazette on 1 August and given effect by Royal Decree M/134. The Civil Status Law changed as well as the passport law: a woman could register the birth of a child, and report a death, a marriage or a divorce. The wording that a wife should live with her husband was deleted.

A guardian's approval still stands, however, for marriage, for release from prison and for leaving a shelter. This is not the abolition of the system but an amendment within three statutes: the passport law, the Civil Status Law and the Labour Law. The Meiji Civil Code in Japan had its own Article 14, by which a wife needed her husband's permission for certain legal acts; it was deleted in the amendment of the Civil Code in 1947.

made.label: 20th century Guardianship under the passport and civil status laws
made.fact: A woman needed the permission of a male guardian (wali or mahram) to obtain a passport and leave the country, and was entered on the passport of a male relative. Because the amendment of 2019 rewrote the law to say that any Saudi national may obtain a passport, the content of the earlier rule can be read back from it.

discontinued.label: 2019.8 The passport and civil status laws amended
discontinued.fact: A decision of the Council of Ministers was adopted on 31 July 2019, published in the official gazette on 1 August 2019 and given effect by Royal Decree M/134. The passport law (the Travel Documents Law) was amended to say that any Saudi national may obtain a passport, and the Civil Status Law and the Labour Law were amended as well. Implementation was reported to begin in late August 2019.

keyfacts.text: A decision of the Council of Ministers was adopted on 31 July 2019 and published in the official gazette on 1 August 2019. Royal Decree M/134 gave it effect.

The amendment of the passport law (the Travel Documents Law) made it read that any Saudi national may obtain a passport, so that a woman could apply for and obtain one without the permission of a male guardian. Until then a woman was entered on the passport of a male relative.

The amendment of the Civil Status Law allowed a woman to register the birth of a child and to report a death, a marriage or a divorce to the civil status office. Both spouses are "head of household" for their children jointly, and the wording that a wife should live with her husband was deleted.

The amendment of the Labour Law stated that "worker" includes women, forbade dismissal during pregnancy, maternity leave or a pregnancy-related illness, and provided that "citizens are equal in the right to work, without discrimination on grounds of sex".

After the amendment, the approval of a male guardian remained necessary for marriage, for release from prison and for leaving a shelter. The government announcement spoke of freedom of travel for women aged 21 and over, but the text of the Council of Ministers decision makes no express mention of freedom of travel.

In January 2021 women became able to change personal details such as their surname, a child's name and their marital status without a guardian's permission, and from June that year single, divorced and widowed women could live independently without one.

The Meiji Civil Code in Japan also had a provision, Article 14, by which a wife needed her husband's permission for certain legal acts; it was deleted in the amendment of the Civil Code in 1947. A system tying the capacity of a wife or a daughter to a guardian existed in Japan too.

123.name: Ubasute
123.hitokoto: There is no evidence of it as a village rule. What there is runs from a tenth-century tale to a novel of 1956.
body: Ubasute first appears in the tenth century, in section 156 of the Tales of Yamato, held to have been put together in the Tenryaku era. A man who has abandoned his aunt on a mountain looks at the moon, composes a poem, and brings her back; the section ends "and from then on they called it Obasute Mountain". It has the form of a tale explaining the origin of a place name. Book 30, story 9 of the Konjaku monogatarishu has the same plot, and Obasute Mountain is Mount Kamuriki in Nagano.

The type in which a parent is hidden and hard riddles are solved by that parent's wisdom is imported. Yoshihiro Otani's "On the Obasuteyama Legend" argued that this type belongs with the Chinese legend of Yuan Gu and the abandoning of the old, that its source lies in the Indian scriptures Za baozang jing, Xianyu jing and Fayuan zhulin, and that it reached Japan by way of China. On how far it is historical, the paper takes it that individual cases occurred, but holds that there is no evidence of it being widely practised as a social custom.

The "village rule" most people now picture is an image made by Shichiro Fukazawa's The Ballad of Narayama of 1956 and two films of it. Fukazawa himself wrote in the Asahi Shimbun in 1969 that "people seem to think the setting is Obasute Mountain in Shinshu", and stated plainly that the setting was Daikokuzaka in Sakaigawa village, Higashi-Yatsushiro county, Yamanashi. There is no record of an institution. What there is is a line of descent through tales and a novel.

made.label: 10th century Tales of Yamato, section 156
made.fact: The legend of abandoning the old first appears in section 156, "Ubasute", of the Tales of Yamato, held to have been put together in the Tenryaku era (947-957), and then in book 30, story 9, "How an Aunt Was Abandoned on a Mountain in Shinano Province", of the Konjaku monogatarishu, with the same content. The Kadokawa Dictionary of Japanese Place Names 20: Nagano states that "the first appearance of the legend of abandoning the old is the Tales of Yamato of the Tenryaku era", and the Nihon daihyakka zensho that "the legend appears first in the Tales of Yamato, then in the Konjaku monogatari, and further became Zeami's noh play Obasute". There is no historical source showing that it existed as a custom or as a rule.

restocked.label: 1956 The Ballad of Narayama
restocked.fact: Shichiro Fukazawa's The Ballad of Narayama (1956) and the film versions (Keisuke Kinoshita, 1958; Shohei Imamura, 1983) made the present image of ubasute as a village rule. The author himself denied the setting. In the Asahi Shimbun of 27 November 1969, in "Revisiting the setting: from my novels", Fukazawa wrote: "Because my Ballad of Narayama took its material from the ubasute legend, people seem to think the setting is Obasute Mountain in Shinshu, but the feelings and the landscape of that novel are here, at Daikokuzaka in Sakaigawa village, Higashi-Yatsushiro county, Yamanashi prefecture."

keyfacts.text: The plot of section 156, "Ubasute", of the Tales of Yamato is that a man who has abandoned his aunt on a mountain looks at the moon, composes the poem "I could not console my heart", and brings her back. It ends "and from then on they called it Obasute Mountain", taking the form of a tale of the origin of a place name.

Book 30, story 9 of the Konjaku monogatarishu, "How an Aunt Was Abandoned on a Mountain in Shinano Province", has the same content, and a note calls it "one of the so-called legends of abandoning the old, an account of the origin of the place name Obasuteyama". Obasute Mountain is Mount Kamuriki in Nagano, on the former boundary of Togura, Kamiyamada and Sakai.

The type of tale in which a parent is hidden and hard riddles solved by wisdom is imported. Yoshihiro Otani's "On the Obasuteyama Legend" (Japanese Journal of Ethnology, vol. 26, no. 2) argues that this type belongs with the Chinese legends of Yuan Gu and of Confucius and the curved jade, that its source lies further back in the Indian scriptures Fayuan zhulin, Xianyu jing and Za baozang jing, and that it reached Japan by way of China.

The same paper sets out the question of historicity as follows. From such things as the headnotes to elegies in the Man'yoshu and the record of the abandoning of the sick in a Grand Council document of 813 (Konin 4), "it is almost certain that the abandoning of the old did occur"; but whether "it was widely practised as a social custom" cannot be argued without more material.

As legend, the weight lies on the literary side. From Kunio Yanagita's material, records are counted at 39 places across the country, in types such as the broken branch, the falling ash, the hidden parent and the sowing of seed; in poetry, more than 150 verses appear in over 30 collections, imperial anthologies among them, through the Heian and Kamakura periods. The anonymous "I could not console my heart, seeing the moon that shines on Obasute Mountain in Sarashina" in the Kokinshu is taken to be the oldest record.

Dendera-no in Tono, Iwate, is recorded in such places as story 268 of the Tono monogatari shui as a place where people over 60 were abandoned. Kunio Yanagita's "The Mountain Where Parents Are Abandoned" is included in Obasute no keifu.

Shichiro Fukazawa stated plainly that the setting was Daikokuzaka in Sakaigawa village, Higashi-Yatsushiro county, Yamanashi (Asahi Shimbun, 27 November 1969, "Revisiting the setting: from my novels"). The village rule called "the pilgrimage to Narayama" in the novel is not a reproduction of the Obasute legend of Shinshu.

124.name: Droit du Seigneur
124.hitokoto: It did not exist in the Middle Ages. Voltaire gave it its name, in 1762.
body: The lord's right to the first night with a peasant's bride. It has long been known as a story showing the barbarity of feudalism, but no medieval law establishing it has been found. What can be confirmed is the taking of money: the marriage due (merchet, formariage) paid when a serf married off the lord's land, and the payment that bought exemption from the church rule forbidding intercourse on the wedding night.

The phrase "droit du seigneur" was first used in Voltaire's play Le droit du seigneur, written in 1762 and first performed in 1779. It is not a medieval term. Anti-clerical and anti-feudal writers of the nineteenth century swelled the story, and at about the same time invented a number of other fictitious feudal rights.

The denials are old too. Louis Veuillot denied its existence in 1854, and in 1881 the German jurist Karl Schmidt concluded that it was an assumption of scholars. The standard work is Alain Boureau's Le droit de cuissage: la fabrication d'un mythe (1995), which follows the making of the myth itself from the thirteenth century to the twentieth.

made.label: 1762 Named in Voltaire's play
made.fact: The phrase "droit du seigneur" is held to have been used first in Voltaire's play Le droit du seigneur (written 1762, first performed 1779). No medieval law established such a right, and it is not a medieval term. Anti-clerical and anti-feudal writers of the nineteenth century swelled the story and put it into circulation as "common knowledge about the Middle Ages".

discontinued.label: 1995 Settled as false history
discontinued.fact: Alain Boureau's Le droit de cuissage: la fabrication d'un mythe (XIIIe-XXe siècle) (Albin Michel, 1995; English translation The Lord's First Night: The Myth of the Droit de Cuissage, University of Chicago Press, 1998) showed that this "right" was not a medieval practice but a myth made between the thirteenth and the twentieth centuries. Earlier, Louis Veuillot had denied its existence in 1854, and in 1881 the German jurist Karl Schmidt concluded that it was an assumption of scholars.

keyfacts.text: Among the lord's rights in the Middle Ages, those touching marriage were the taking of money: the marriage due (merchet, formariage) paid when a serf married off the lord's land, and the payment that bought exemption from the church rule forbidding intercourse on the wedding night. These were later retold as a "right to the first night".
The phrase "droit du seigneur" itself is held to appear first in Voltaire's play (written 1762, first performed 1779). It is not a medieval term.

Louis Veuillot denied its existence in 1854, and in 1881 the German jurist Karl Schmidt concluded that it was an assumption of scholars. Even so, French writers of the later nineteenth century invented a number of other fictitious feudal rights.

Alain Boureau's Le droit de cuissage: la fabrication d'un mythe (XIIIe-XXe siècle) (Albin Michel, 1995; English translation 1998, University of Chicago Press) is taken as the standard work, showing both the absence of any documentary basis and the process by which the myth was formed.
Scholars today broadly deny that this "right" existed historically. What existed were the various monetary dues that feudal lords levied on marriage, not a sexual right.

001.name: Vendetta
001.meaning: Killing the killer of a senior relative, after filing notice with the authorities.
001.hitokoto: Avenging a parent became a crime with a single proclamation, on 7 February 1873.
body: Revenge in the Edo period was not an unchecked private feud but a licensed institution with a procedure set by the shogunate. A samurai obtained a licence from his lord, filed notice with the magistrate's office, and could set out after his enemy only once the entry stood in the town magistrate's revenge register. It applied only when a senior relative such as a father, mother or elder brother had been killed. Killing the avenger in self-defence was lawful, and juteki, a second round of revenge by that side, was forbidden. An unreported revenge killing was investigated, and punished as murder if it was not recognised as revenge.

The Meiji government at first carried the arrangement over in the Provisional Penal Code of 1868. Then, on 7 February 1873, Grand Council Proclamation No. 37, "Revenge Is Strictly Forbidden", was issued at the initiative of Justice Minister Shinpei Eto. Punishing those who kill is "the public authority of the government"; revenge is "an offence against public authority in the name of private duty". Bereaved kin were ordered from then on to "report to the authorities". The revenge clauses left the statute books entirely only with the Penal Code of 1880.

Seven years after the proclamation, on 17 December 1880, Rokuro Usui, a former retainer of the Akizuki domain, killed his father's enemy Naohisa Ichinose in Tokyo. On 22 September 1881 he was sentenced to life imprisonment for premeditated murder. An act that in Edo would have been entered in the register and praised was tried as murder in the same country. The licensed institution thus ended with a date attached.

made.label: Early-modern Licensed on notice
made.fact: Under the Tokugawa shogunate a procedure took hold: a samurai obtained a licence from his lord, filed notice with the magistrate's office, and pursued his enemy only after the entry was made in the town magistrate's revenge register and a copy issued. It applied only when a senior relative such as a father, mother or elder brother had been killed. Killing the avenger in self-defence was lawful; a second round of revenge by that side (juteki) was forbidden. An unreported revenge killing was investigated, and punished as murder if it was not recognised as revenge.

discontinued.label: 1873 Revenge strictly forbidden
discontinued.fact: 7 February 1873 (Meiji 6): Grand Council Proclamation No. 37, "Revenge Is Strictly Forbidden". Punishing those who kill is "the public authority of the government"; revenge is "an offence against public authority in the name of private duty" and was strictly forbidden. Bereaved kin were ordered instead to "set out the facts in full and report them promptly to the authorities".

keyfacts.text: On 7 February 1873, Grand Council Proclamation No. 37, "Revenge Is Strictly Forbidden", was promulgated. It forbade revenge as "an offence against public authority in the name of private duty" and ordered bereaved kin to report to "the authorities".

The proclamation was drafted on the strong initiative of Justice Minister Shinpei Eto. The new Meiji government had licensed revenge as before in the Provisional Penal Code of 1868, and the revenge clauses left the statute books entirely only with the Penal Code of 1880 (Meiji 13).

In the Edo period, revenge by a samurai required a licence from his lord and notice to the magistrate's office; the entry was made in the town magistrate's revenge register and a copy issued. Revenge without permission was investigated and punished as murder if it was not recognised as revenge. It applied only to senior relatives such as a father, mother or elder brother, and juteki, revenge taken in turn against the avenger, was forbidden.

On 17 December 1880, Rokuro Usui, a former retainer of the Akizuki domain, killed his father's enemy Naohisa Ichinose at the Tokyo residence of his former lord Kuroda. On 22 September 1881 the Tokyo Court sentenced him to life imprisonment in the form reserved for the privileged classes. The amnesty on the promulgation of the Constitution in 1889 reduced it to ten years' confinement, and he left prison on 22 September 1891.
In the Kogi on-cho register of the Edo town magistrate's office, ordinary revenge killings decline from the Genroku era (1688-1703) onward.

002.name: Loyalty & Filial Piety
002.hitokoto: Handed to every school in 1890; both houses ended it on 19 June 1948.
body: Teaching loyalty and filial piety together to ordinary people begins in early-modern times. In 1722 the shogunate had Muro Kyuso translate a Ming book of precepts, printed Rikuyu engi taii officially and spread it as a text in the terakoya schools. In 1801 it gathered and published the commendations of 8,610 filial children and others, reported from across the country, as Kankoku kogiroku. Loyalty and filial piety were virtues the shogunate distributed and rewarded.

The Imperial Rescript on Education of 30 October 1890 opened "Our subjects, being loyal, being filial, millions of hearts as one, have through the ages made this beauty complete", and placed loyalty and filial piety as "the glory of the national polity" and "the source of education". In the form of the imperial name and seal alone, without the countersignature of a Minister of State, it was read aloud on school ceremonial days and put before every citizen as the root norm of moral training.

After the defeat, the Ministry of Education removed the requirement to read it aloud by ministerial ordinance in 1946, but the decisive lapse is 19 June 1948. On that day the plenary session of the House of Representatives passed the Resolution on the Exclusion of the Imperial Rescript on Education and Other Rescripts, and the plenary session of the House of Councillors the Resolution Confirming the Invalidity of the Imperial Rescript on Education and Other Rescripts, both proposed jointly by all parties. The order of business and the text as read out remain in the record of Diet proceedings.

made.label: 1722 Rikuyu engi taii
made.fact: In 1722 the shogunate had Muro Kyuso render a Ming book of precepts into Japanese as Rikuyu engi taii, printed it officially and spread it as a text for the terakoya schools. In 1801 it recorded and published the commendations of 8,610 filial children and others, reported from across the country, in Kankoku kogiroku. The Imperial Rescript on Education of 30 October 1890 placed "being loyal, being filial" as the glory of the national polity and the source of education.

discontinued.label: 1948 Excluded by the Diet
discontinued.fact: On 19 June 1948 the plenary session of the House of Representatives passed the Resolution on the Exclusion of the Imperial Rescript on Education and Other Rescripts (submitted by Junzo Matsumoto and 34 others, jointly by all parties), and the plenary session of the House of Councillors passed the Resolution Confirming the Invalidity of the Imperial Rescript on Education and Other Rescripts (moved by Kotaro Tanaka and 25 others, jointly by all parties).

keyfacts.text: Promulgated on 30 October 1890, the Imperial Rescript on Education stated "Our subjects, being loyal, being filial, millions of hearts as one, have through the ages made this beauty complete; herein lies the glory of Our national polity, and herein too lies the source of education", placing loyalty and filial piety as the glory of the national polity and the source of education. It runs to 315 characters in all, in the form of the imperial name and seal alone, without the countersignature of a Minister of State.

On 19 June 1948 the plenary session of the House of Representatives took up, without committee examination, the draft Resolution on the Exclusion of the Imperial Rescript on Education and Other Rescripts, submitted by Junzo Matsumoto and 34 others, and passed it. The text states that the fundamental idea of the rescripts rests on "sovereignty residing in the monarch and a mythical view of the national polity".

The same day, the plenary session of the House of Councillors passed, as the second item on the order of business, the draft Resolution Confirming the Invalidity of the Imperial Rescript on Education and Other Rescripts, moved by Kotaro Tanaka and 25 others, confirming that the Imperial Rescript on Education, together with the Imperial Rescript to Soldiers and Sailors, the Boshin Rescript and others, "has already been abolished and has lost its effect".

Education Minister Tatsuo Morito explained in the House of Representatives that day that the Ministry of Education had, by ministerial ordinance of 3 March 1946, made void the provision that moral training be conducted on the basis of the purport of the Imperial Rescript on Education, and by ministerial ordinance of 9 October the same year deleted the provision for reading the rescript aloud on ceremonial days.

In 1722 the shogunate had Muro Kyuso translate the Ming work Liuyu yanyi into Japanese as Rikuyu engi taii, printed it officially and used it as a text in popular education such as the terakoya schools (the six maxims are the six articles of the Ming emperor Hongwu: filial obedience to parents, respect for elders and so on).

In 1789 the shogunate ordered reports from across the country of commendations of filial children and others, and 8,600 cases covering 8,610 people were compiled at the Shoheizaka Academy and published in 1801 as Kankoku kogiroku.

003.name: Shudo
003.hitokoto: Some acts between men were punishable under national law for less than ten years.
body: Relations between men of different ages, an older man and a youth not yet through his coming-of-age rite, were open culture in medieval temples and in early-modern samurai society. Ihara Saikaku's The Great Mirror of Male Love (1687) gives 20 of its 40 chapters to shudo among the samurai and the other 20 to the world of the young kabuki actors. It was spoken of as a bond, not a shame.

In the eleventh month of 1872 the Ministry of Justice, answering a query from Shirakawa Prefecture, issued the keikan regulation, and Article 266 of the Revised Criminal Regulations, in force from July 1873, set "90 days' penal labour for whoever commits sodomy". Peers and former samurai, however, were "dealt with as grossly shameless": the article ran differently by status. It was not carried into the Penal Code of 1880 and was gone when that code came into force on 1 January 1882.

What followed the end of the crime was pathology. Popular sexology, such as Hentai seiyokuron of 1915, retold male love as "perversion", and Makoto Furukawa argued that this turn was a change of codes. The American Psychiatric Association removed homosexuality from the DSM on 15 December 1973; the WHO removed it in ICD-10 on 17 May 1990. In Japan, Shibuya Ward passed its ordinance on 31 March 2015, and the first certificates were issued on 5 November that year.

made.label: 1687 The Great Mirror of Male Love
made.fact: Ihara Saikaku's The Great Mirror of Male Love (published in the fourth month of 1687, 8 volumes, 40 chapters) gives its first 20 chapters to shudo in samurai society and its last 20 to the world of the young kabuki actors. Earlier works exist, such as the chigo tales of the Muromachi period.

discontinued.label: 1873 Criminalised by statute
discontinued.fact: On 13 November 1872 the Ministry of Justice, answering a query from Shirakawa Prefecture, issued the keikan (sodomy) regulation. Article 266 of the Revised Criminal Regulations, in force from July 1873: "Whoever commits sodomy shall each serve 90 days' penal labour; peers and former samurai shall be dealt with as grossly shameless." It was not carried into the Penal Code of 1880 and disappeared when that code came into force on 1 January 1882. Popular sexology then pathologised it as "perversion", as in Hentai seiyokuron of 1915.

keyfacts.text: It began in the ninth month of 1872, when Shirakawa Prefecture (now northern Kumamoto) asked the Ministry of Justice about punishing "male love" in public schools and private academies. The ministry drafted the regulation in a document dated 15 October and issued the keikan regulation on 13 November: "Whoever entices another and commits sodomy shall receive 90 strokes; peers and former samurai shall be dealt with as grossly shameless…"

Article 266 of the Revised Criminal Regulations of 1873 read: "Whoever commits sodomy shall each serve 90 days' penal labour. Peers and former samurai shall be dealt with as grossly shameless. A child of 15 or under who is so used is not liable. Whoever commits rape shall serve ten years' penal labour." It set a different treatment for peers and former samurai: a provision of status law.

The sodomy provision was not included in the Penal Code enacted in 1880, and ceased to exist when that code came into force on 1 January 1882. This is held to be the only period in which some consensual sexual acts between men (keikan) were subject to criminal penalty under national law in Japan.

Hentai seiyokuron by Eiji Habuto and Junjiro Sawada (Shun'yodo, published 15 June 1915, 704 pages) is the representative work of "popular sexology". Furukawa (1994) argued that the turn in discourse on homosexuality in modern Japan was a change of three codes (U.S.-Japan Women's Journal, no. 17, pp.29-55).

The Board of Trustees of the American Psychiatric Association (APA) approved the decision to remove homosexuality from DSM-II on 15 December 1973, and the WHO approved ICD-10 at the 43rd World Health Assembly on 17 May 1990, dropping the classification of homosexuality.

On 31 March 2015 the Shibuya Ward assembly passed an ordinance including certification of same-sex partnerships. On 5 November that year, certificates and acknowledgements were issued to one couple in Shibuya Ward and seven couples in Setagaya Ward. The Act on the Promotion of Public Understanding of Diversity in Sexual Orientation and Gender Identity was enacted on 16 June 2023 and promulgated and in force on 23 June.

004.name: Inkyo Retirement
004.hitokoto: The Civil Code set inkyo at 60 or over. Its articles went on 1 January 1948.
body: Inkyo in the Edo period was a widely seen life plan: the head passed the headship on while still alive and stepped back from the front line. A samurai petitioned his lord and passed the headship to his son; a townsman left the shop and handed property and rights to his successor. Documents kept in Ranzan, Saitama, from 1802 and 1867 record inkyo-men arrangements, by which the new head promised the retired head an annual allowance of rice, money and fields.

The Meiji Civil Code, in force from 1898, wrote the custom into articles as a legal act with requirements of age and more. Article 752 made inkyo conditional on the house head being 60 full years or more and on the heir to the headship accepting the succession without reservation; Article 964 set inkyo, alongside the death of the house head, as a ground on which succession to the headship began. Notice went to the registrar. Inkyo became an institution whose requirements the state managed.

On 3 May 1947, Article 3 of the Emergency Measures Act, in force with the Constitution, provided that "the provisions on the house head, family members and otherwise concerning the house shall not apply", and the amended Civil Code promulgated on 22 December that year came into force on 1 January 1948, at which point the inkyo articles were gone. What decides the time to step back instead is the mandatory retirement age: in 1968, 69.0% of firms with 30 or more employees had one; in 2022, 94.4%. In March 2020, Quit Like a Millionaire, which argues for early retirement, appeared in Japanese.

made.label: Early-modern The standard life plan
made.fact: A samurai petitioned his lord and passed the headship to his son; a townsman left the shop and passed property and rights to his successor; a farmer handed his fields to his son and retired. Documents kept in Ranzan, Saitama, a bond of 1802 and a note of 1867, record inkyo-men arrangements, by which the new head promised the retired head an annual allowance of rice, money and fields.

discontinued.label: 1948 Abolished by the Civil Code
discontinued.fact: The Act on Emergency Measures concerning the Civil Code Accompanying the Enforcement of the Constitution of Japan (Act No. 74 of 19 April 1947), in force from 3 May 1947, provided in Article 3 that "the provisions on the house head, family members and otherwise concerning the house shall not apply", suspending the inkyo provisions. The Act Partially Amending the Civil Code (Act No. 222), promulgated on 22 December 1947, came into force on 1 January 1948 and deleted the articles.

restocked.label: 2020 FIRE
restocked.fact: Quit Like a Millionaire by Kristy Shen and Bryce Leung, translated by Masaaki Iwamoto (Diamond, Inc.), was published in Japanese in March 2020 and became a bestseller.

keyfacts.text: Article 752 of the Meiji Civil Code (in force 16 July 1898) provided that a house head could not retire unless he both was "60 full years or more" and had "an heir to the headship with full capacity accepting the succession without reservation"; Article 753 made special retirement for illness and the like subject to the permission of the court. Article 964 gives the grounds on which succession to the headship begins as "the death, retirement or loss of nationality of the house head".

Article 3 of the Emergency Measures Act (Act No. 74 of 1947), promulgated on 19 April and in force from 3 May 1947, provided that "the provisions on the house head, family members and otherwise concerning the house shall not apply". The provisions on inkyo and the house head lost their effect at the same moment the Constitution came into force.

The Act Partially Amending the Civil Code (Act No. 222 of 1947), promulgated on 22 December 1947, wholly revised the books on relatives and on succession, and its entry into force on 1 January 1948 deleted the articles on succession to the headship and on inkyo.

According to the Survey on Employment Management by the Ministry of Health, Labour and Welfare (firms of 30 or more employees), 69.0% of firms had a mandatory retirement age in 1968, when the survey began (about 95% among firms with 300 or more, 51.0% among those with 30 to 99). It passed 90% in 1991. As of 1968, 63.5% of uniform retirement ages were 55 or under.

In the 2022 General Survey on Working Conditions, 94.4% of firms had a mandatory retirement age, and 96.9% of those a uniform one. Under the Act on Stabilization of Employment of Elderly Persons as amended in 1994, a retirement age below 60 became unlawful from April 1998.

The oldest mandatory retirement age in Japan is held to be the 55 in the workers' regulations of the Tokyo Artillery Arsenal in 1887, and in the private sector the 55 in the rules on leave of absence at Nippon Yusen in 1902 (life expectancy for men was then about 43).

005.name: The House Name First
005.hitokoto: The "house" became law on 16 July 1898 and lost its effect on 3 May 1947.
body: The criterion that puts not letting the house name die out above all else had long been rooted in samurai society, but what made it law for every citizen was the books on relatives and on succession of the Meiji Civil Code, in force from 16 July 1898. Article 746: "The house head and the family members bear the surname of the house." Article 750 made the consent of the house head a requirement for a family member's marriage. Article 970 ranked heirs to the headship by male sex, legitimacy and seniority.

The lapse came in two stages. On 3 May 1947, Article 3 of the Emergency Measures Act (Act No. 74 of 1947), in force together with the Constitution of Japan, stopped the provisions concerning the house from applying, and the amendment to the Civil Code (Act No. 222) promulgated on 22 December that year came into force on 1 January 1948, at which point the articles on the house head and succession to the headship were gone. The ground for this is Article 24 of the Constitution: individual dignity and the essential equality of the sexes.

The law is gone, but the practice remains. Of the 474,741 marriages in 2023, 94.5% chose the husband's surname. Meanwhile reburials, moving the graves of ancestors, rose from 91,567 in fiscal 2015 to 166,886 in fiscal 2023. The apparatus for keeping up the house name is being taken apart, slowly, outside the law.

made.label: 1898 The Meiji Civil Code
made.fact: Books 4 and 5 of the Civil Code (Act No. 9 of 21 June 1898), promulgated on 21 June and in force from 16 July 1898, defined family members in Article 732 as "the relatives of the house head who are in his house, and their spouses", provided in Article 746 that "the house head and the family members bear the surname of the house", required the consent of the house head for a family member's marriage or adoption in Article 750, and in Article 970 ranked heirs to the headship by nearness of degree, male sex, legitimacy and seniority.

discontinued.label: 1948 The house system abolished
discontinued.fact: Article 3 of the Emergency Measures Act (Act No. 74 of 1947), in force from 3 May 1947, suspended the provisions concerning the house, and the entry into force on 1 January 1948 of the Act Partially Amending the Civil Code (Act No. 222), promulgated on 22 December 1947, deleted the provisions on the house head and succession to the headship.

keyfacts.text: Books 4 (Relatives) and 5 (Succession) of the Civil Code were promulgated as Act No. 9 of 21 June 1898, and under the Act on Enforcement of the Civil Code (Act No. 11 of the same year) the whole of them came into force on 16 July 1898.

Meiji Civil Code Article 746: "The house head and the family members bear the surname of the house." Article 749: "A family member may not fix his residence against the will of the house head." Article 750: "A family member who marries or adopts must obtain the consent of the house head." Article 970 ranked heirs to the headship by degree of kinship, male sex, legitimacy and seniority.

Article 3 of the "Act on Emergency Measures concerning the Civil Code Accompanying the Enforcement of the Constitution of Japan" (Act No. 74 of 1947), promulgated on 19 April 1947, provided that "the provisions on the house head, family members and otherwise concerning the house shall not apply". From 3 May, the day the Constitution came into force, the provisions of the house system lost their effect.

The "Act Partially Amending the Civil Code" (Act No. 222 of 1947), promulgated on 22 December 1947, came into force on 1 January 1948, abolishing succession to the headship and providing for the spouse's right of inheritance and for equal shares.
Of the 474,741 marriages in 2023, 448,397 (94.5%) chose the husband's surname and 26,344 (5.5%) the wife's. In 1995 the husband's surname was 97.4%.

The national number of reburials in the Report on Public Health Administration and Services by the Ministry of Health, Labour and Welfare rose from 91,567 in fiscal 2015 to 124,346 in fiscal 2019, 151,076 in fiscal 2022 and 166,886 in fiscal 2023 (these are reburial permits and do not equal the number of graves closed).

006.name: Born to One's Station
006.hitokoto: Samurai status privileges came off over six years, in proclamations from 1870 to 76.
body: Status in early-modern Japan was decided by birth, and the domains entered the stipends and posts of their retainers in a bungen-cho register. Bungen, a word that meant status and property from the late Heian period, gave "know your bun" and "one's station": the norm was to live within that range. Bearing a surname in public and wearing a sword were, as a rule, privileges of the samurai.

The Meiji government undid this not with one statute but with a run of proclamations. Grand Council Proclamation No. 608 of 1870 (19 September Meiji 3) permitted commoners to bear surnames in public; the order of 1871 (9 August Meiji 4) on cropped hair and the removal of swords left hairstyle and the wearing of swords "as one pleases"; on the 23rd of that month came "Marriage Is Permitted Between All from the Peerage Down to Commoners", and on the 28th the so-called Emancipation Edict. Wearing a sword was forbidden by the Sword Abolishment Edict of 28 March 1876 (Grand Council Proclamation No. 38).

The Jinshin household registers of 1872, however, entered the status designations of peers, former samurai and commoners, so the divisions themselves stayed in the register. "Born to one's station" came back under another name in 2021, when oya-gacha, the parent lottery, was chosen for the top ten of the U-Can New Words and Buzzwords Award and took the Daijisen New Word of the Year. What differs from 150 years ago is that it is spoken in the vocabulary of probability rather than of status.

made.label: Early-modern The status order
made.fact: Bungen is a word seen from the late Heian period, meaning social status, rank and property, that is, one's station. In the Edo period the domains entered the names, stipends, ranks and posts of their retainers in a bungen-cho register. Bearing a surname in public and wearing a sword were privileges of the samurai.

discontinued.label: 1871 Sword and hair edicts, etc.
discontinued.fact: Grand Council Proclamation No. 608 of 19 September Meiji 3 (13 October 1870) permitting commoners surnames; Grand Council Order No. 399 of 9 August Meiji 4 (23 September 1871) on cropped hair and the removal of swords; "Marriage Is Permitted Between All from the Peerage Down to Commoners" of 23 August Meiji 4; the so-called Emancipation Edict of 28 August Meiji 4; Grand Council Proclamation No. 38 of 28 March 1876, the Sword Abolishment Edict.

restocked.label: 2021 Parent Gacha
restocked.fact: Oya-gacha was chosen for the top ten of the U-Can New Words and Buzzwords Award for 2021 and took the grand prize in the Daijisen New Word of the Year for the same year. It had been current as the vocabulary of smartphone games from about 2015, and turned into a serious word for inequality from September 2021.

keyfacts.text: On 19 September Meiji 3 (13 October 1870), Grand Council Proclamation No. 608, permitting commoners surnames, allowed commoners to bear a surname in public. Registrations did not proceed, however, and an ordinance making surnames compulsory was to follow in 1875.

On 9 August Meiji 4 (23 September 1871), Grand Council Order No. 399 on cropped hair and the removal of swords provided that "cropped hair, uniform, informal dress and the removal of swords are all to be as one pleases", leaving hairstyle, and the removal of swords other than with formal dress, to each person's own choice.

On 23 August Meiji 4 the Grand Council permitted marriage across status lines, providing that "marriage between all from the peerage down to commoners is permitted; neither side need petition, and notice is to be given to the ward head at the time" (Collection of Laws No. 437). On the 28th of the same month it issued the so-called Emancipation Edict.

Compiled from 1 February Meiji 5 under the Family Register Act of 4 April Meiji 4 (Grand Council Proclamation No. 170), the Jinshin household registers were the first nationally uniform register, replacing the religious census registers, but they kept the status designations of the imperial family, the peerage, the former samurai and commoners as entry items, and so kept the status divisions themselves.

On 28 March 1876, Grand Council Proclamation No. 38, "Wearing a Sword Is Forbidden Except with Court Dress or the Uniform of Soldiers, Police and Officials" (the Sword Abolishment Edict), forbade the wearing of swords.

Bungen is a word from the late Heian period meaning social status, rank and property, one's station, and in the Edo period the daimyo houses compiled a bungen-cho register of their retainers' stipends and posts. Oya-gacha was in the top ten of the 2021 U-Can New Words and Buzzwords Award and took the grand prize in the Daijisen New Word of the Year for 2021. The word oya-gacha was first used in the Diet at a plenary session of the House of Councillors on 12 October 2021.

007.name: Impermanence
007.hitokoto: Buddhist meditation on impermanence became a US medical programme in 1979.
body: "The flow of the river never ceases, and yet the water is never the water of before." Hojoki by Kamo no Chomei was completed at the end of the third month of 1212, and The Tale of the Heike appears in a record of 1240 under the name "Jisho monogatari, six volumes, called Heike". In Mujo (1964), Junzo Karaki set out the passage by which the court's hakanashi became mujo in the medieval period and went on to the metaphysics of Dogen. Calling it the operating system of the medieval period is the received view in literary history.

No figures were found, however, to show that it "fell, driven out by the modern view of history as progress". No opinion survey asks about impermanence over time, so the fall remains an interpretation. That Karaki's book was written in 1964 itself shows that impermanence went on being read as a subject after the war. Not lapsed, only left unnoticed.

It came back under another name by way of the United States: MBSR, begun by Jon Kabat-Zinn at the University of Massachusetts in 1979, then "Search Inside Yourself", begun inside Google in 2007, and then the NHK Special "Killer Stress" of 18 and 19 June 2016, which introduced mindfulness. The Buddhist observation of impermanence was reimported as a meditation programme.

made.label: 1212 Hojoki
made.fact: Hojoki by Kamo no Chomei was completed at the end of the third month of 1212. The Tale of the Heike is noted in 1240 as "Jisho monogatari, six volumes, called Heike", so it existed by the first half of the 13th century at the latest. Mujo by Junzo Karaki (Chikuma Shobo, 1964) set out the passage from the court's hakanashi to mujo in the medieval period and on to the metaphysics of Dogen.

restocked.label: 2016 Mindfulness
restocked.fact: Jon Kabat-Zinn began MBSR (Mindfulness-Based Stress Reduction) at the University of Massachusetts in 1979; the in-house Google course "Search Inside Yourself" began in 2007; and the second part of the NHK Special series "Killer Stress", broadcast on 18 and 19 June 2016, introduced mindfulness as a way of coping.

keyfacts.text: Hojoki was completed by Kamo no Chomei on the last day of the third month of 1212 and begins "The flow of the running river never ceases, and yet the water is not the water of before".

The year The Tale of the Heike was written is unknown, but a record of 1240 speaks of "Jisho monogatari, six volumes, called Heike", and section 226 of Essays in Idleness relates that "Yukinaga, former governor of Shinano, made the Tale of the Heike and taught it to a blind man called Shobutsu to recite".

Mujo by Junzo Karaki (Chikuma Shobo, 1964) is in three parts, hakanashi (the court), mujo (Honen, Shinran, Ippen, Sogi, Basho) and the metaphysics of mujo (Dogen), setting out the changes in the Japanese sense of impermanence.
The in-house Google programme "Search Inside Yourself" was developed in 2007 by the engineer Chade-Meng Tan.
