016.name: Rising in the World
016.hitokoto: Risshin shusse is already in a kabuki play of 1753. What Meiji made was the content.
body: The four characters of risshin shusse are not a Meiji coinage. The first use in the Nihon kokugo daijiten is the kabuki play Osanago no katakiuchi of 1753, and in the Edo period it meant an ethic of life, keeping to one's station and living frugally in order to "come out into the world and make oneself". What Meiji made was not the word but the content, which was replaced by upward movement through learning and effort.

In 1872 (2 August Meiji 5) the Education System Order was issued with Grand Council Proclamation No. 214, and its preamble taught that "learning is the capital for making one's way" and called on every citizen to attend school. Saigoku risshihen (Smiles's Self-Help), translated by Masanao Nakamura and published two years earlier, and Yukichi Fukuzawa's An Encouragement of Learning, published that same year, became bestsellers, and Risshin shusse shugi by Yo Takeuchi (NHK Books, 1997) describes how this desire became the romance of modern Japan.

In a century and a half the notion has faded. In the Global Survey on Employment and Growth Awareness by Persol Research and Consulting (2022, 18 countries and regions), 19.8% of rank-and-file employees in Japan said they wanted to become managers, the lowest of all, against 90.5% in India, which came first. In 2021 oya-gacha, the parent lottery, entered the top ten of the New Words and Buzzwords Award. The notion that drove out being decided by birth is being driven back by being decided by birth.

made.label: 1872 The Education System Order
made.fact: Grand Council Proclamation No. 214 of 2 August Meiji 5, the preamble on the encouragement of learning: "Learning may be called the capital for making one's way." Saigoku risshihen (1870-71), translated by Masanao Nakamura, and Yukichi Fukuzawa's An Encouragement of Learning (1872) became bestsellers, and risshin shusse turned into the sense of upward movement through learning. The phrase itself is used in the kabuki play Osanago no katakiuchi (1753).

keyfacts.text: The first use of risshin shusse in the Nihon kokugo daijiten, selected edition, is the kabuki play Osanago no katakiuchi (1753): "if only you will hand over the certificate, rising in the world is in plain sight". The phrase exists from the middle of the Edo period.

Encyclopedia Nipponica: in the Edo period risshin shusse was an ethic of life, frugal and holding to one's station, of "coming out into the world and making oneself", but after the Meiji Restoration it was tied to upward social movement and later institutionalised through the school and the bureaucracy.

The preamble to the Education System Order, Grand Council Proclamation No. 214 of 2 August Meiji 5, states that "learning may be called the capital for making one's way" and called on every citizen to attend school.

Risshin shusse shugi: Romance and Desire in Modern Japan by Yo Takeuchi was published as NHK Books in November 1997, with an enlarged edition from Sekaishisosha in 2005. It expands the text of the NHK Ningen Daigaku series (January to March 1996), "Risshin shusse and the Japanese".

In the Global Survey on Employment and Growth Awareness by Persol Research and Consulting (surveyed February to March 2022, published November, 18 countries and regions), rank-and-file employees saying they wanted to become managers were 19.8% in Japan, the lowest of all (India first at 90.5%, Vietnam second at 87.8%).
Oya-gacha was chosen for the top ten of the 2021 U-Can New Words and Buzzwords Award, and took the grand prize in the Daijisen New Word of the Year 2021.

017.name: Bushido
017.hitokoto: Bushido was written in English; a Japanese reader had to wait eight years.
body: Inazo Nitobe's Bushido: The Soul of Japan came out in English in 1900, from Leeds & Biddle of Philadelphia (the copyright notice reads 1899). The Japanese translation, by Oson Sakurai, came in March 1908; until then it was read in the English reprint issued by Shokabo of Tokyo in 1900. The representative at home of the argument that identified bushido with national morality is Tetsujiro Inoue, who began with Bushido (Heiji Zasshisha) in 1901 and in 1905 edited the three-volume Bushido sosho with Sukemasa Arima.

The word itself, however, is not of 1900 make. Bushido first appears in Koyo gunkan, compiled in the early Edo period, where it was the technique by which an individual samurai made his name and survived. Hagakure (about 1716) was a secret book of the Saga domain and had never been in print until an abridgement edited by Ikuichi Nakamura appeared in 1906, and the Imperial Rescript to Soldiers and Sailors of 1882 preached not bushido but chusetsu, fidelity.

Bushido no gyakushu by Kakumyo Kanno (Kodansha Gendai Shinsho, 2004) argued that the "Meiji bushido" made in the years of the Sino-Japanese and Russo-Japanese wars is a different thing from the bushido of before modern times, and Oleg Benesch called the same process an invention in Inventing the Way of the Samurai (2014). The word existed in the 17th century; the meaning was made in the late Meiji period. It has been discussed as a textbook case of what Hobsbawm called an invented tradition.

made.label: 1900 Nitobe's Bushido
made.fact: Inazo Nitobe's Bushido: The Soul of Japan was published in 1900 by Leeds & Biddle of Philadelphia (copyright notice 1899). At home, writing on bushido was turned out in quantity from Tetsujiro Inoue's Bushido (Heiji Zasshisha, 1901) onward, and the three-volume Bushido sosho was edited in 1905. Nitobe's Japanese translation is that of Oson Sakurai (Teibi Shuppansha, March 1908). The word first appears in Koyo gunkan, compiled in the early Edo period.

keyfacts.text: The oldest edition held by the National Diet Library is Bushido; the soul of Japan, Philadelphia: Leeds & Biddle, 1900 (copyright 1899). It carries no statement that it is a first edition, and Nakajima, "On the confusion over the bibliographical details of Inazo Nitobe's Bushido" (2008), points out the confusion in the bibliography.
The first Japanese translation is Bushido, translated by Oson Sakurai (Teibi Shuppansha, March 1908).
The first book to write down the word bushido is Koyo gunkan, compiled in the early Edo period, where it was conceived as the technique by which an individual samurai made his name and survived.

Hagakure was a secret book of the Saga domain, and its first appearance in print was an abridgement, about a fifth of the original, edited by Ikuichi Nakamura and published in Tokyo on 23 March 1906. In February 1911 it was reissued, borrowing the fame of Maresuke Nogi, as Nabeshima rongo Hagakure.

The Imperial Rescript to Soldiers and Sailors of 1882 preached not bushido but chusetsu, fidelity. A "bushido boom" followed the Sino-Japanese War (1894-95), and from Bushido (Heiji Zasshisha) in 1901 onward Tetsujiro Inoue developed the argument identifying bushido with national morality, editing Bushido sosho in three volumes (30 March, 18 June and 25 November 1905).

Bushido no gyakushu by Kakumyo Kanno (Kodansha Gendai Shinsho, 20 October 2004) treats the bushido of the boom as an image made from Meiji onward, and argues in chapter 5, "Meiji bushido", for its break with early-modern times. Oleg Benesch, Inventing the Way of the Samurai (Oxford UP, 2014) and Yasushi Suzuki, "The creation of bushido in Meiji Japan", likewise treat Meiji bushido as a creation or invention.

018.name: Diligence as Virtue
018.hitokoto: Japanese diligence, Yasumaru argued, is a morality spread in the late Edo period.
body: Nihon no kindaika to minshu shiso (Japan's Modernisation and Popular Thought) by Yoshio Yasumaru (Aoki Shoten, 1974) argued that a "conventional morality" of diligence, thrift, filial piety and honesty spread from the late early-modern period through the years of the Restoration as a discipline the people laid on themselves, and became the spiritual base of modernisation. Its textbooks were the Shingaku of Baigan Ishida and the hotoku method of Sontoku Ninomiya, and Yasumaru drew this not as a virtue of the samurai but as a discipline farmers and townsmen imposed on themselves.

In a paper to the Socio-Economic History Society in 1976, "The formation of economic society and its characteristics" (published 1977), Akira Hayami named the agriculture of the Edo period, which raised output by cutting livestock and adding human labour, an "industrious revolution". It carries the year of establishment back to the 17th and 18th centuries, earlier than Yasumaru. On either account diligence is not an ancient national character but something that spread at a particular time in the Edo period.

The figures point downhill. In the Monthly Labour Survey, annual total hours actually worked per regular employee went from 2,432 in 1960 to 2,052 in 1990 and 1,693 in 2025. Much of that is the move to a 40-hour week under the 1987 amendment to the Labour Standards Act, and the rising share of part-time workers, whose hours are short; it is not a figure that shows a change in the sense of diligence directly.

made.label: Late Edo Conventional morality
made.fact: Nihon no kindaika to minshu shiso by Yoshio Yasumaru (Aoki Shoten, September 1974) argued that a "conventional morality" of diligence, thrift, filial piety and honesty spread from the late early-modern period to the years of the Restoration as the self-discipline of the people, and became the spiritual base of modernisation. The Shingaku of Baigan Ishida (1685-1744) and the hotoku method of Sontoku Ninomiya (1787-1856) are the representative cases. In a paper to the 1976 meeting of the Socio-Economic History Society, "The formation of economic society and its characteristics" (published 1977), Akira Hayami proposed an "industrious revolution" in the Edo period, carrying the year of establishment further back.

keyfacts.text: Nihon no kindaika to minshu shiso by Yoshio Yasumaru was published by Aoki Shoten on 1 September 1974 (reissued in the Heibonsha Library in 1999). It set out the process by which a "conventional morality" of diligence, thrift and self-denial took root in the minds of ordinary people and became the spiritual base of modernisation.

The term "industrious revolution" was first used explicitly by Akira Hayami in his paper "The formation of economic society and its characteristics", given at the 1976 meeting of the Socio-Economic History Society (common theme: "In search of a new picture of the Edo period") and published in 1977.

In the Monthly Labour Survey (establishments with 30 or more employees), annual total hours actually worked per regular employee averaged 2,432 in 1960, 2,239 in 1970, 2,052 in 1990, 1,859 in 2000, 1,685 in 2020 and 1,693 in 2025 (the series before 1969 excludes services). For establishments with 5 or more employees it is 1,621 in 2025.

Behind the fall in hours lie changes of rule such as the 1987 amendment to the Labour Standards Act, which cut statutory hours in stages from 48 to 40 a week, and from the late 1990s the rising share of part-time workers also tells; it is not an indicator of a change of attitude in itself.

The continuing question closest to "work is a virtue" is in the NHK Broadcasting Culture Research Institute's "Japanese Value Orientations" survey (every five years from 1973, the work-oriented and leisure-oriented answers under "work and leisure").

019.name: Family at the Table
019.hitokoto: The chabudai spread across Japan by early Showa and gave way to tables by 1980.
body: Calling the place where life is lived katei rose sharply, above all in the magazines, in the years from 1887, and was taken as the translation of the English home. In the Nihon kokugo daijiten the first attested use in the sense of the place where husband and wife, parents and children live is Koyo Ozaki's Konjiki yasha (1897-98) — the word katei itself has a use in Shinbun zasshi in 1871 — and until then kanai and ie were the main words. Soho Tokutomi's Min'yusha launched Katei zasshi in September 1892, and Senryaku toshite no kazoku (The Family as Strategy) by Kazue Muta (Shin'yosha, 1996) argues that the ideology of katei appeared around 1887.

The word came first, however, and the table after. The chabudai, the single low table a family sits round, appeared about 1887, and spread across the country from the end of Taisho into the early Showa years; before that each person had a hakozen, an individual tray (Chabudai no Showa, edited by Kazuko Koizumi, Kawade Shobo Shinsha). With individual trays the father took the head place and the mother the lower one, and "it was not an atmosphere for talking during a meal", while after the change to the chabudai "it became easier to talk", one witness recalls (interviews in Seika, Kyoto).

The word danran itself has a use, "the whole house in a circle", in Sodoshu, a collection of Chinese poems of 1816, so it is not of Meiji make. What Meiji made was the idea that katei is home, and what spread from the end of Meiji into the early Showa years was the shape of the table that reproduced it every evening. The chabudai was replaced by the chair-height table from the late 1950s, and the changeover was complete in the 1980s. The traditional scene of the family in a circle was on sale for about 60 years.

made.label: 1892 Katei zasshi
made.fact: From the language note in the Nihon kokugo daijiten (Selected Edition): until the early Meiji years kanai and ie were the main words, while in the years from 1887 katei appeared often, above all in the magazines, and the sense of it as the translation of home arose (the first attested use in the sense "the place where husband and wife, parents and children live" is Koyo Ozaki's Konjiki yasha, 1897-98; the word itself has a use in Shinbun zasshi in 1871). Soho Tokutomi's Min'yusha launched Katei zasshi in September 1892. Kazue Muta argues that the ideology of katei appeared around 1887. The reality of a family sitting round one table came about when the chabudai spread across the country from the end of Taisho into the early Showa years (Kazuko Koizumi).

keyfacts.text: In the Nihon kokugo daijiten (Selected Edition), the first attested use of katei in sense 2, the place of life centred on husband and wife and on parents and children, is Koyo Ozaki's Konjiki yasha (1897-98); sense 1, the inside of a household or the family, first appears in Shinbun zasshi (1871). The language note: until the early Meiji years kanai and ie were used, and in the years 1887-96 katei appeared often, above all in the magazines, with a sense of it as the translation of home arising too.
Soho Tokutomi's Min'yusha launched Katei zasshi in September 1892 (Meiji 25) and closed it in 1898.

Senryaku toshite no kazoku: kindai Nihon no kokumin kokka keisei to josei (The Family as Strategy: The Formation of the Modern Nation-State in Japan, and Women) by Kazue Muta (Shin'yosha, 1996) argues that the ideology of katei appeared around 1887 and was formed in the years of the Imperial Constitution, the Civil Code and the Imperial Rescript on Education, tied to the view of the state as a family.

In the Nihon kokugo daijiten (Selected Edition), the first attested use of danran, the gathering of family or intimates to pass the time pleasantly, is Sodoshu (1816), "the whole house in a circle, talking", with a modern example in Shusei Tokuda's Kabi (1911), "the family in a circle". The word itself is not of Meiji make.

Chabudai no Showa, edited by Kazuko Koizumi (Kawade Shobo Shinsha, 2002, and a new edition): the chabudai came into use from about 1887, spread across the country from the end of Taisho into the early Showa years, and from the late 1950s the chair-height table spread, taking its place by the 1980s.

In the days of the hakozen, the individual tray, the father took the head place and the mother the lower one and "it was not an atmosphere for talking during a meal", while witnesses who lived through it say that with the chabudai "it became easier to talk". Shokuji no bunmeiron by Naomichi Ishige (Chuko Shinsho, 1982) also discusses the turn from individual trays to a shared table.

020.name: Lifetime Employment
020.hitokoto: Employers called for a rethink, yet support rose from 72% in 1999 to 88% in 2015.
body: The word "lifetime employment" goes back to 1958, when the American management scholar James C. Abegglen called the employment relation in the Japanese factory a "lifetime commitment" in The Japanese Factory; the Japanese translation of the same year, Nihon no keiei, rendered it "a lifetime relationship", and this is held to have become the name shushin koyo. Lifetime employment first appears in the record of Diet proceedings in 1961: a practice with no name was named from outside.

The OECD report on manpower policy in Japan of 1972 listed lifetime employment, seniority wages and enterprise unions as the three elements of Japanese employment, and the name "the three sacred treasures" stuck. Employers have announced a rethink twice. In 1995 Nikkeiren proposed an "employment portfolio" dividing employment into three types in Japanese-Style Management in a New Era, and in May 2019 the chairman of Keidanren and the president of Toyota said in turn that "there is a limit to running a company and thinking about business on the premise of lifetime employment" and that it was "hard to keep".

Workers moved the other way. In the Survey on Working Life by the Japan Institute for Labour Policy and Training, the share supporting lifetime employment, staying with one firm until the retirement age, rose broadly from 72.3% in 1999 to a high of 87.9% in 2015, and stands at 82.0% even in 2021. Workers have not let go of what employers kept saying they would end.

made.label: 1958 Abegglen
made.fact: James C. Abegglen's The Japanese Factory (Free Press, 1958) characterised the employment relation in the Japanese factory as a lifetime commitment, and the Japanese translation of the same year, Nihon no keiei (translated by Kuniyoshi Urabe, Diamond, Inc.), rendered it "a lifetime relationship", from which the name shushin koyo is held to have spread. Lifetime employment first appears in the record of Diet proceedings on 15 February 1961 (House of Representatives Budget Committee); there is no hit between 1947 and 1960.

keyfacts.text: In 1958 James C. Abegglen's The Japanese Factory: Aspects of Its Social Organization (Glencoe: Free Press) was published, and the Japanese translation Nihon no keiei came out from Diamond, Inc. the same year. The original words are lifetime commitment (also permanent employment), and shushin koyo settled in as the translation.

The OECD report on manpower policy in Japan, published in 1972, listed lifetime employment, seniority wages and enterprise unions as the three main elements of the Japanese employment system, and they came to be called "the three sacred treasures" (the account crediting the name to Masao Matsunaga, Vice-Minister of Labour, is poorly sourced).

In May 1995 Nikkeiren published Japanese-Style Management in a New Era, proposing an "employment portfolio" combining three types: long-term accumulated ability, high-level specialist ability, and flexible employment.

On 7 May 2019, Hiroaki Nakanishi, chairman of Keidanren, said at his regular press conference that "with working lives expected to lengthen, there is a limit to running a company and thinking about business on the premise of lifetime employment".

On 13 May 2019, Akio Toyoda, president of Toyota and chairman of the Japan Automobile Manufacturers Association, said at a press conference that "unless rather more incentive comes to firms that keep people on, we have entered a phase in which keeping lifetime employment is quite hard".

In the 8th Survey on Working Life by the Japan Institute for Labour Policy and Training (24 September to 17 October 2021, drop-off and pick-up, 2,388 valid replies), the share supporting lifetime employment, staying with one firm until the retirement age, is 82.0%. It went 72.3% in 1999, 86.1% in 2007, 87.9% in 2015 (the high) and 82.0% in 2021, falling after the 2015 peak.

curve.note: Support = "a good thing" plus "on the whole a good thing". Lifetime employment = "the Japanese lifetime employment of staying with one firm until the retirement age"; seniority wages = "the Japanese seniority wages in which pay rises with length of service". 4,000 men and women aged 20 and over across the country, including those not in work; rounds 1 to 7 were face-to-face interviews (round 7 in November-December 2015, 2,118 valid replies). Round 8 (2021) was changed to drop-off and pick-up by the interviewer because of Covid (JILPT report).

Question 9(c), "the view closest to your own", option 1, "I mean to stay at this company for life". The other options are "I would not mind changing jobs given the occasion or the chance", "I want to change jobs right now" and "none of these / don't know".

021.name: Seniority Pay
021.hitokoto: The seniority curve was steeper in 1995, the year of performance pay, than in 1976.
body: Seniority pay is another of the Japanese employment practices Abegglen described in 1958, and it first appears in the record of Diet proceedings in May 1960. Notice of the lapse came early: in 1969 the Study Group on Ability-Based Management at Nikkeiren published Noryokushugi kanri (Ability-Based Management), setting out a course of treating people by ability while keeping the merits of the seniority system.

The wage curve actually flattened only after 1995. In the Basic Survey on Wage Structure by the Ministry of Health, Labour and Welfare, scheduled cash earnings for men aged 50 to 54, with men aged 20 to 24 at 100, stood at 185.7 in 1976, 212.2 in 1995 and 178.1 in 2025: of the three points the curve was steepest in 1995. That overlaps with the years in which Fujitsu brought management by objectives to its managers in 1993 and Nikkeiren called in 1995 for a shift from pay based on age and length of service to pay based on ability and performance.

Attitudes, meanwhile, moved the other way. In the surveys of the Japan Institute for Labour Policy and Training the share supporting seniority wages rose from 60.8% in 1999 to 76.3% in 2015, and stands at 70.4% even in 2021. The wage curve flattened and support thickened. Institution and value moved separately in this product.

made.label: 1958 Abegglen
made.fact: Abegglen (1958) described treatment by seniority, along with lifetime employment, as a feature of the Japanese factory. Seniority pay first appears in the record of Diet proceedings on 6 May 1960 (House of Representatives Committee on Local Administration).

keyfacts.text: In 1969 the Study Group on Ability-Based Management at Nikkeiren published Noryokushugi kanri: sono riron to jissen (Ability-Based Management: Theory and Practice), proposing an "ability-based management" that treated people by ability while keeping the merits of the seniority system.

Fujitsu introduced appraisal by management by objectives for its managerial ranks in 1993, and in 1994 extended annual salaries to managers and management by objectives to the supervisor grade. NEC had introduced a divisional performance-sharing scheme for managers in 1990.
Nikkeiren's Japanese-Style Management in a New Era of 1995 called for a shift from pay resting mainly on age and length of service to a system rising with the growth of ability and performance.

In the Basic Survey on Wage Structure by the Ministry of Health, Labour and Welfare, scheduled cash earnings of male full-time workers aged 50 to 54, with men aged 20 to 24 in the same year at 100, stood at 185.7 in 1976, 212.2 in 1995 and 178.1 in 2025 (the peak in 2025 is 181.4, at 55 to 59). Of the three points the seniority curve was steepest in 1995, and 2025 is flatter than that.

In the Basic Survey on Wage Structure for 2023, men's pay peaks at 427.4 thousand yen at 55 to 59 (186.4 with pay at 20 to 24 at 100). The index for 45 to 49 with 25 to 29 at 100 fell from 157.8 in 2003 to 138.8 in 2023 (tabulated by the Recruit Works Institute).

In the Survey on Working Life by JILPT the share supporting seniority wages went 60.8% in 1999, 71.9% in 2007, 76.3% in 2015 (the high) and 70.4% in 2021. The wage curve flattened, but attitudes stand higher than in 1999.

022.name: Breadwinner & Housewife
022.reading: otto wa soto de hataraki, tsuma wa katei o mamoru
022.hitokoto: Women's participation bottomed in 1975. This household spread in the boom years.
body: "The husband works outside and the wife keeps the home" looks like tradition, but its statistical heyday falls at the end of the high-growth years. In the Labour Force Survey the labour force participation rate of women aged 15 and over fell from 50.7% in 1968 and bottomed at 45.7% in 1975. Emiko Ochiai discussed this postwar turning of women into housewives from the side of family sociology, and in Toward the Family of the 21st Century (Nijuisseiki kazoku e) of 1994 named it "the postwar family system".

Household numbers say the same. In 1980, where the series of the Special Survey of the Labour Force Survey begins, there were 11.14 million full-time-housewife households against 6.14 million dual-earner households, about 1.8 times as many; dual-earner households passed them for the first time in 1992, and have been in the majority without a break since 1997. In 2025 there are 13.33 million dual-earner households against 4.76 million full-time-housewife households.

Agreement with the norm has fallen too. In the Cabinet Office's Public Opinion Survey on a Gender-Equal Society, those who agree with the view came to 33.5% in the survey of November 2022 and 33.1% in that of September 2024, with 64.8% against. In the National Survey on Family by the National Institute of Population and Social Security Research the share of wives who agree fell from 47.7% in 2008 to 29.5% in 2022, below three in ten for the first time.

made.label: 1975 Women's participation bottoms
made.fact: In the Labour Force Survey the labour force participation rate of women aged 15 and over fell from 50.7% in 1968 and hit its postwar low of 45.7% in 1975 (56.4% in 2025). Emiko Ochiai argued that women in postwar Japan did not go out into the labour market but were turned into housewives, and in Toward the Family of the 21st Century (Nijuisseiki kazoku e, Yuhikaku, 1994) named this "the postwar family system".

keyfacts.text: In 1980, where the series of the Special Survey of the Labour Force Survey begins, full-time-housewife households numbered 11.14 million against 6.14 million dual-earner households, nearly twice as many. Dual-earner households passed them for the first time in 1992 (9.14 million against 9.03 million), fell behind again in 1995-96, and have been in the majority without a break since 1997. In 2025 there are 13.33 million dual-earner households against 4.76 million full-time-housewife households.
The labour force participation rate of women aged 15 and over was at its lowest in 1975, at 45.7% (46.5% in 1974, 45.8% in 1976).

Toward the Family of the 21st Century: How to See and Go Beyond the Postwar Family System (Nijuisseiki kazoku e) by Emiko Ochiai (Yuhikaku, first edition 1994, fourth edition 2019). In the chapters "Were women always housewives?" and "The birth of housework and the housewife" she argues that the housewife is a product of modern times and spread to the mass of people in the postwar years of high growth.

In the Cabinet Office's Public Opinion Survey on a Gender-Equal Society (survey of November 2022, by post), 33.5% agreed with "the husband should work outside and the wife should keep the home" (4.0% agree plus 29.4% on the whole agree) and 64.3% disagreed.

In the survey of September 2024 (26 September to 3 November 2024, by post, 2,673 people), 33.1% agreed (4.5% plus 28.6%) and 64.8% disagreed. Because the 2022 survey changed from individual interview to post, the figures for 2019 and before (35.0% in 2019, 40.6% in 2016, 44.6% in 2014) are treated as reference values.

In the 7th National Survey on Family by the National Institute of Population and Social Security Research (as of 1 July 2022, 8,910 valid returns), the share of wives agreeing that "after marriage the husband should work outside and the wife should devote herself to the home" went 47.7% in 2008, 44.9% in 2013, 38.1% in 2018 and 29.5% in 2022, below three in ten for the first time.

curve.title: Agree and disagree: ◆"the husband should work outside and ◆the wife should keep the home"
curve.subtitle: Opinion surveys of the Prime Minister's Office ◆and the Cabinet Office
curve.note: In 1979 the wording was the view that "the husband works outside and the wife keeps the home". The totals of 72.6 agreeing and 20.4 disagreeing are the plain sums of the separate options in the original source (31.8 agree plus 40.8 on the whole agree; 16.1 on the whole disagree plus 4.3 disagree); the White Paper on Gender Equality sometimes gives 72.5/20.4, a difference of rounding.

extraCurves.subtitle: Full-time-housewife household = a male employee ◆and a wife not in work
extraCurves.note: A "full-time-housewife household" is one in which the husband is an employee outside agriculture and forestry and the wife is not working (not in the labour force, or wholly unemployed; from 2018, "unemployed"). A "dual-earner household" is one in which both husband and wife are employees outside agriculture and forestry. The definitions are those of "numbers of dual-earner and other households" in the White Paper on Gender Equality (which also carries a series limited to wives aged 64 and under).

023.name: Arranged Marriage
023.hitokoto: The love match drove arranged marriage out; now the internet is closing on it.
body: The miai is not "the way it always was". The Japanese edition of the Encyclopaedia Britannica treats the miai as a custom that arose from the late Edo period, and the Nihon dai-hyakka zensho holds that the practice of setting a miai in a theatre or a dining room in the cities began in the middle Meiji years. Folklore studies have long held that in the villages choice by the couple themselves, through the youth group, was widely seen (Kunio Yanagita, Konin no hanashi).

By year of marriage in the National Fertility Survey, 69.0% of the couples who married in the 1930s married by miai. Love marriage passed the miai among those who married in 1965-69: 48.6% love against 44.9% miai. It fell in a straight line after that, down to 5.3% among those who married in 2005-09.

In the latest, 16th survey (2021), however, 15.2% of the couples who married in 2019-21 met "online", through social media or a dating app, above the 9.9% who married by miai. The arrangement by which a third party brings two people together can be said to have revived in another shape, from the nakodo to a service on the internet.

made.label: Middle Meiji Spread in the cities
made.fact: The Japanese edition of the Encyclopaedia Britannica treats the miai as "a custom that arose from the late Edo period", and the Nihon dai-hyakka zensho (entry by Akira Takeda) holds that the practice of setting a miai in a city theatre or dining room began in the middle Meiji years. In the National Fertility Survey, 69.0% of the couples who married in the 1930s married by miai.

restocked.label: 2021 Meeting online overtakes
restocked.fact: In the 16th National Fertility Survey (2021), 15.2% of the couples who married between 2019 and 2021 met "online", through social media, a dating app or the like, above arranged marriage at 9.9%. In Meiji Yasuda Life's survey, "a dating app" has led the ways couples married within the past year met for three years running from 2023 (30.4% in 2025).

keyfacts.text: Figure 5-2-1 of the 16th National Fertility Survey (National Institute of Population and Social Security Research, 2021): the share of arranged marriages was 69.0% for those who married in 1930-39, 54.0% in 1950-54, 49.8% in 1960-64, 44.9% in 1965-69, 33.0% in 1970-74, 17.7% in 1985-89, 5.3% in 2005-09, 8.1% in 2015-18 and 9.8% in 2019-21 (9.9% in the text of the summary). Love marriage passed the miai for the first time in 1965-69, at 48.6%.

Couples who met "online" (on the internet), an option newly set in this survey, were 6.1% of those who married in 2015-18 and 15.2% of those who married in 2019-21 (text of the summary), above arranged marriage in the latest years. Couples who met online had been together 2.8 years on average, shorter than the 4.9 years of love marriages.

The Japanese edition of the Encyclopaedia Britannica treats the miai as "a custom that arose from the late Edo period; before that the settling of a match was left to the will of the head of the house", and the Nihon dai-hyakka zensho (entry by Akira Takeda) holds that the practice of setting a miai in a theatre or dining room began in the cities in the middle Meiji years.

In the record of Diet proceedings, a public hearing of the House of Representatives Judicial Affairs Committee on 20 August 1947 reports "whether marriage by miai is better" as a topic of the street recordings. On 22 July 1949, before the House of Representatives Special Committee on Investigation, a witness, a conductor of Japanese National Railways, said "until now it was marriage by miai, but this time it became love marriage".

Meiji Yasuda Life's "Good Couples' Day" survey: among couples married within the past year, "a dating app" was the way they met for 25.0% in 2023 (level with "a colleague, senior or junior at work", the first time it led), 29.8% in 2024 and 30.4% in 2025, leading three years running. The 2023 survey covered 1,620 married men and women aged 20 to 79, online, from 12 to 16 October 2023.

024.name: Love-Marriage Ideal
024.hitokoto: Love marriage peaked in the 2000s. Its heyday was not the Showa era.
body: Follow the sense that a marriage made by love is the real thing through the figures for behaviour, and love marriage passed the miai in the second half of the 1960s. In the National Fertility Survey the share of love marriages went on rising, reaching 88.0% among the couples who married in 2005-09. The heyday is not the Showa era but the 2000s.

The fall after that is quick: 87.9% among those who married in 2010-14, 84.9% in 2015-18, and down to 74.6% in 2019-21. What filled the gap is couples who met "online", 15.2% of those who married in 2019-21. Couples who met that way had been together 2.8 years on average before marrying, shorter than the 4.9 years of love marriages.

Private surveys point the same way. In the Survey on Marriage-Hunting by the Recruit Bridal Research Institute, the share of people who married through a marriage-hunting service rose from 1.4% of those who married in 2000 to 15.3% of those who married in 2023, of which the online kind was 11.4%, the highest yet. In Meiji Yasuda Life's survey, "a dating app" has led the ways couples married within the past year met for three years running from 2023.

made.label: 1967 Overtakes the miai
made.fact: Among couples in a first marriage on both sides, love marriage passed arranged marriage for the first time among those who married in 1965-69 (48.6% love, 44.9% miai). It kept rising after that, reaching 88.0% among those who married in 2005-09.

keyfacts.text: Figure 5-2-1 of the 16th National Fertility Survey: the share of love marriages was 48.6% for those who married in 1965-69, 80.2% in 1985-89, 87.2% in 1995-99, 88.0% in 2005-09 (the high), 87.9% in 2010-14, 84.9% in 2015-18 and 74.8% in 2019-21 (74.6% in figure 5-2 of the summary).

In the same survey, 15.2% of the couples who married in 2019-21 met "online". Tabulated by round of survey, the share who met "at work or through work" fell from 28.2% in the previous survey to 21.4% among those who married between July 2018 and June 2021, and "online" was 13.6% among those who married in that Covid period, July 2018 to June 2021. Couples who met online had been together 2.8 years on average (4.9 years for love marriages).

"Survey on Marriage-Hunting 2024" by the Recruit Bridal Research Institute (announced 24 September 2024, men and women aged 20 to 49 across the country, online): 15.3% of those who married in 2023 married through a marriage-hunting service (a marriage agency, an online marriage-hunting service or a marriage-hunting party), of which 11.4% through the online kind, the highest yet. For those who married in 2000 the figures were 1.4% and 0.1%.

Meiji Yasuda Life's "Good Couples' Day" survey: among couples married within the past year, "a dating app" was the way they met for 25.0% in 2023 (level with "a colleague, senior or junior at work"), leading for the first time, then 29.8% in 2024 and 30.4% in 2025, leading three years running. In 2025 the second was "introduced by a friend or acquaintance" at 19.2% and the third "a colleague, senior or junior at work" at 17.6%.

"Love marriage" first appears in the record of Diet proceedings on 22 July 1949, before the House of Representatives Special Committee on Investigation, where a witness, a conductor of Japanese National Railways, said "until now it was marriage by miai, but this time it became love marriage".

025.name: Marriage Resignation
025.hitokoto: A 1966 ruling voided marriage resignation, 20 years before the statute did.
body: Company rules requiring women to resign on marriage were voided in court before they were voided by statute. Sumitomo Cement had women submit, on hiring, a written undertaking to "resign on marriage or on reaching the full age of 35", but the Tokyo District Court judgment of 20 December 1966 held the marriage resignation rule void, as a restriction on freedom to marry and discrimination by sex.

What cut the ground from under the rule was the Equal Employment Opportunity Act. Promulgated on 1 June 1985 (Act No. 45 of 1985) and in force from 1 April 1986, it forbade from enactment in 1985 both discrimination by sex in retirement age and dismissal and any provision making marriage, pregnancy or childbirth a ground for resignation (Article 11); the 1997 amendment (in force April 1999) turned discrimination by sex in recruitment and hiring, and in assignment and promotion, from a duty to endeavour into a prohibition. "Marriage resignation" appears in the record of Diet proceedings from 1964, but the word kotobuki taisha first appears in October 2001.

The curve of the practice can be followed in the National Fertility Survey. The share of wives who were working when they decided to marry and were out of work immediately after it fell from 37.3% for marriages of 1985-89 to 25.1% for 2000-04 and to 14.0% for 2015-19, while continuing in work across marriage reached 79.8%. When the word kotobuki taisha was born could not be confirmed from the dictionaries.

made.label: Showa The marriage resignation rule
made.fact: The first appearance of the word kotobuki taisha could not be fixed from the dictionaries or the record of Diet proceedings (in the Diet record the first is 26 October 2001, House of Representatives Committee on Health, Labour and Welfare, Tomoko Nakagawa). The marriage resignation rule itself was common enough to be litigated in the 1960s: Sumitomo Cement had women submit, on hiring, a written undertaking to "resign on marriage or on reaching the full age of 35". "Marriage resignation" first appears in the Diet record on 3 December 1964 (House of Councillors Committee on Social and Labour Affairs).

discontinued.label: 1966 Marriage resignation void
discontinued.fact: 20 December 1966: the Tokyo District Court (the Sumitomo Cement case, Rominshu vol. 17 no. 6 p. 1407) held a marriage resignation rule applying to women only void, as a restriction on freedom to marry and discriminatory treatment by sex. The Equal Employment Opportunity Act (Act No. 45 of 1 June 1985, in force 1 April 1986) cut the ground from under the rule, forbidding in Article 11 as enacted discrimination by sex in retirement age and dismissal and provisions making marriage and the like a ground for resignation; the 1997 amendment (Act No. 92 of 18 June 1997, in force 1 April 1999) made discrimination by sex in recruitment and hiring, and in assignment and promotion, a prohibition too.

keyfacts.text: The Sumitomo Cement case: filed in 1964, judgment of the Tokyo District Court on 20 December 1966. The company had women submit on hiring a written undertaking to "resign on marriage or on reaching the full age of 35", and dismissed a woman employee who did not resign after marrying; the judgment held the marriage resignation rule void as contrary to public order and good morals, and ordered confirmation of her status under the employment contract and payment of unpaid wages.

The Equal Employment Opportunity Act was promulgated on 1 June 1985 (Act No. 45 of 1985) as an amendment to the Working Women's Welfare Act (Act No. 113 of 1972), and came into force on 1 April 1986 under Article 1 of its supplementary provisions.

The 16th National Fertility Survey, figure 9-1-2: the share of "marriage resignation" wives, who were working when they decided to marry and out of work immediately after it, was 37.3% for marriages of 1985-89, 34.5% for 1990-94, 31.2% for 1995-99, 25.1% for 2000-04, 24.1% for 2005-09, 17.6% for 2010-14 and 14.0% for 2015-19. Continuing in work rose from 56.6% to 79.8%.

The rate at which wives who had been working before pregnancy continued in work across the birth of a first child rose from 57.7% for first births in 2010-14 to 69.5% in 2015-19, and 79.2% of those who continued used the childcare leave system.

In the record of Diet proceedings "marriage resignation" appears from the House of Councillors Committee on Social and Labour Affairs of 3 December 1964, with 239 instances to September 2026. The first appearance of kotobuki taisha is the House of Representatives Committee on Health, Labour and Welfare of 26 October 2001, with 33 in all to September 2026.

026.name: Three Years on a Rock
026.reading: ishi no ue ni mo sannen
026.hitokoto: More of the 2004 graduates quit within three years than of the 2022 graduates.
body: "Three years on a rock" is a proverb current since the early Edo period. The Nihon Kokugo Daijiten, concise edition, gives as its first appearance the haikai collection Kefukigusa (1638), and Saikaku oridome (1694) has "three years on a rock, as the common saying has it". There is no settled account of its origin, and the reading that ties it to Bodhidharma's nine years facing a wall is not taken up by the dictionaries.

Evidence that the proverb has fallen out of use is, unexpectedly, absent from the statistics. In the Ministry of Health, Labour and Welfare's tabulation, the share of new university graduates leaving their job within three years begins at 28.4% for those graduating in March 1987; the lowest is 23.7% for 1992 graduates, the highest 36.6% for 2004, and 2022 graduates are at 33.8%. It rose from the middle 20s in the early 1990s to the 30s in the middle of that decade, and has run a little above 30% since.

Job changers numbered 3.51 million in 2019 (3.53 million in the figures adjusted for the time series), the most since 2002, and stand high at 3.31 million in 2024 and 3.30 million in 2025, but that is a movement of the whole workforce, the middle-aged included. The story that more young people fail to keep to "three years" is not borne out by the three-year separation rate for university graduates, at least not from the 2000s on.

made.label: 1638 Kefukigusa
made.fact: The dictionaries give as its first appearance the haikai collection Kefukigusa (1638), and volume four of the ukiyozoshi Saikaku oridome (1694) has "merchant or artisan, do not change the place you have grown used to; three years on a rock, as the common saying has it". In the early Edo period the form was "sit three years on a rock and it warms", and the second half was later dropped. There is no settled account of its origin.

keyfacts.text: The Nihon Kokugo Daijiten, concise edition, and others: the first appearance is the haikai collection Kefukigusa (1638), and Saikaku oridome (1694) has "three years on a rock, as the common saying has it". The reading that ties it to Bodhidharma's nine years facing a wall is not taken up by the dictionaries and is not the settled view.

Ministry of Health, Labour and Welfare, "Job Separation of New School Graduates", appendix 1: the rate of leaving within three years of starting work, for university graduates, was 28.4% for those graduating in March 1987, 23.7% for 1992 graduates (the lowest), 36.5% for 2000, 36.6% for 2004 (the highest), 28.8% for 2009, 32.3% for 2020, 34.9% for 2021 and 33.8% for 2022.

Statistics Bureau of the Ministry of Internal Affairs and Communications, Labour Force Survey (Detailed Tabulation): job changers peaked at 3.46 million in 2006 and 2007, fell after the Lehman shock, rose from 2011, and reached 3.51 million in 2019, the most since 2002, the first year comparable. 2024 was about 3.31 million, a third straight rise.
In JILPT's 8th Survey on Working Life (2021), 82.0% supported "staying with one company until retirement age".
In the record of Diet proceedings "three years on a rock" is quoted only as a proverb, and is no index of the rise or fall of the norm.

027.name: Fight 24 Hours?
027.hitokoto: The same jingle was sung again 25 years later, as "24 hours is too hard".
body: Sankyo's energy drink Regain went on sale in June 1988, and at the end of May 1989 came the commercial in which Ushiwakamaru Saburota, played by Saburo Tokito, sings 24-jikan tatakaemasu ka ("Can you fight for 24 hours?"). The jingle Yuki no shirushi ("Sign of Courage") was released as a single on 22 November that year, and the phrase took the bronze prize in the buzzword division of the 6th New Words and Buzzwords Award for 1989. The copy itself dates from the launch in 1988, and the month the craze caught can be fixed.

The lapse can be followed by date too. In 1991, after the bubble burst, the copy was changed to 24-jikan, tatakau anata ni ("For you, fighting 24 hours"), and the copy and the song came back once with Regain 24 in 2007; then on 1 July 2014 a commercial for Suntory Beverage & Food's Regain Energy Drink sang the same song again as 24-jikan tatakau no wa shindoi ("Fighting 24 hours is rough"), with the copy 3, 4-jikan tatakaemasu ka ("Can you fight for three or four hours?"). In 2018 a manager at Daiichi Sankyo Healthcare said it "has become a dead word".

The law moved the same way. Under the Work Style Reform Act, in force from 1 April 2019, the cap on overtime was set at 45 hours a month and 360 hours a year as a rule, and came to carry a penalty (1 April 2020 for small and medium firms). The new Regain product released in February 2019 was pitched at the "age of the hundred-year life". The norm of fighting 24 hours had its contents swapped while the product name stayed.

made.label: 1989 The Regain commercial
made.fact: Sankyo's energy drink Regain went on sale in June 1988. The commercial Yuki no shirushi ("Sign of Courage"), in which Saburo Tokito, as Ushiwakamaru Saburota, sings 24-jikan tatakaemasu ka ("Can you fight for 24 hours?"), began broadcasting at the end of May 1989, and the single Yuki no shirushi: Regain no thema was released on 22 November 1989. It took the bronze prize in the buzzword division of the 6th New Words and Buzzwords Award the same year.

discontinued.label: 2014 The "three or four hours" ad
discontinued.fact: On 1 July 2014 the commercial for Suntory Beverage & Food's carbonated drink Regain Energy Drink (featuring Sumire, sung by Makoto Kawamoto) sang the same song again as 24-jikan tatakau no wa shindoi ("Fighting 24 hours is rough") and made the copy 3, 4-jikan tatakaemasu ka ("Can you fight for three or four hours?"). Under the Work Style Reform Act, in force from 1 April 2019, the cap on overtime (45 hours a month and 360 hours a year as a rule) came to carry a penalty (1 April 2020 for small and medium firms).

keyfacts.text: Regain went on sale from Sankyo in 1988 (June). From the end of May 1989 commercials using Yuki no shirushi began, and the single CD was released in November that year. At the 6th New Words and Buzzwords Award for 1989, "24-JIKAN TATAKAEMASU KA" took the bronze prize in the buzzword division.

In 1991, after the bubble burst, the catchphrase was changed to 24-jikan, tatakau anata ni ("For you, fighting 24 hours"). In 2018 Masaaki Hanawa of the product strategy department of Daiichi Sankyo Healthcare said that "'24-jikan tatakaemasu ka' has become a dead word".

On 1 July 2014, in the television commercial for Regain Energy Drink released by Suntory, Sumire appeared as a live-action Lum, with the lyric 24-jikan tatakau no wa shindoi ("Fighting 24 hours is rough") over an arrangement of Yuki no shirushi sung by Makoto Kawamoto, and the catchphrase became 3, 4-jikan tatakaemasu ka? ("Can you fight for three or four hours?").

I'm, a group company of Daiichi Sankyo Healthcare, released Regain Triple Force (a quasi-drug, 60 tablets, 4,200 yen) on 27 February 2019, turning from "Can you fight for 24 hours?" to "health first" and "recovering youthfulness" (WWD JAPAN, 5 December 2018).

The cap on overtime under the Work Style Reform Act came into force on 1 April 2019 for large firms and 1 April 2020 for small and medium ones. The cap is 45 hours a month and 360 hours a year as a rule; even under a special clause, within 720 hours a year, an average of 80 hours over any several months, under 100 hours in a month, and above 45 hours in no more than six months a year. Breach carries imprisonment of up to six months (imprisonment with labour until May 2025) or a fine of up to 300,000 yen.
In the record of Diet proceedings, "can you fight for 24 hours" first appears on 15 June 1990 (Special Committee on Disaster Countermeasures, Seiichiro Murakami), with nine instances in all.

028.name: Guts
028.hitokoto: Konjo was a Buddhist term. Sports konjo is held to date from the 1964 Olympics.
body: Konjo was originally a Buddhist term, for the capacity of one who receives the Buddha's teaching. It became a doctrine of spirit in sport after the war, and the time can be fixed. Hirofumi Daimatsu, coach of Nichibo Kaizuka, published Ore ni tsuite koi! Watashi no shobu konjo ("Follow Me! My Fighting Guts") in June 1963, and at the Tokyo Olympics of October 1964 the "Oriental Witches" took the gold medal. The oldest instance of the word konjoron in the record of Diet proceedings is "I am in favour of the doctrine of guts", said by the Director-General of the Defence Agency at the House of Councillors Budget Committee of 19 March 1969.

Yusuke Okabe's The Birth and Transformation of the Doctrine of Guts in Sport (Junposha, 2021) argues that the doctrine took shape around the Tokyo Olympics of 1964 and settled in as a view of sport that put victory above all. Hideto Suzuki reads Daimatsu's idea of coaching as the making of a thought out of the "war experience" of surviving the Imphal campaign (Japan Journal of Physical Education, Health and Sport Sciences, vol. 66, 2021). Star of the Giants (Weekly Shonen Magazine, no. 19 of 1966 to no. 3 of 1971) made the mould of supokon.

There is no date of lapse, but there is a turning point. On 23 December 2012 the captain of the basketball team at Sakuranomiya High School in Osaka killed himself over corporal punishment by his teacher-coach, and the coach was convicted at the Osaka District Court on 26 September 2013. In March 2018 the guidelines of the Japan Sports Agency set at least two rest days a week and stated that corporal punishment "is not permitted in any case". Guts remain, but the way of it, training without rest and under blows, was denied again, this time from the side of the institutions.

made.label: 1964 The Tokyo Olympics
made.fact: Hirofumi Daimatsu's Ore ni tsuite koi! Watashi no shobu konjo ("Follow Me! My Fighting Guts") was published in June 1963 in the Kodansha How-To Books series (238 pages), and at the Tokyo Olympics of October 1964 Daimatsu's Japan women's volleyball team, the "Oriental Witches", took the gold medal. Yusuke Okabe argues that the "doctrine of guts in sport" took shape around the Tokyo Olympics of 1964. The oldest instance of the word konjoron in the record of Diet proceedings is the House of Councillors Budget Committee of 19 March 1969 (Kiichi Arita, Director-General of the Defence Agency: "I am in favour of the doctrine of guts").

keyfacts.text: Hirofumi Daimatsu's Ore ni tsuite koi! Watashi no shobu konjo was published in June 1963 in the Kodansha How-To Books series (238 pages). The sequel, Naseba naru! Zoku ore ni tsuite koi, appeared in 1964.

Hirofumi Daimatsu (12 February 1921 to 24 November 1978) became coach of Nichibo Kaizuka in 1954, beat the Soviet Union to win the world championship in 1962, and led the Japan women's team to the gold medal at the Tokyo Olympics of 1964. Hideto Suzuki analyses his idea of coaching as the making of a thought out of the "war experience" of surviving the Imphal campaign.

Yusuke Okabe's The Birth and Transformation of the Doctrine of Guts in Sport: The Will to Excellence, the Pursuit of Victory (Junposha, November 2021) argues that the doctrine of guts in sport took shape around the Tokyo Olympics of 1964 and thereafter settled in as a view of sport that put victory above all.
Star of the Giants (story by Ikki Kajiwara, art by Noboru Kawasaki) ran in Weekly Shonen Magazine from no. 19 of 1966 to no. 3 of 1971, and is held to be the first of the supokon baseball comics.

On 23 December 2012 the captain (aged 17) of the basketball team at Sakuranomiya High School in Osaka killed himself over corporal punishment by his teacher-coach. The coach was dismissed for misconduct on 12 February 2013 and, on 26 September 2013, given one year's imprisonment suspended for three years by the Osaka District Court for assault and bodily injury. On 24 February 2016 the Tokyo District Court found a causal link between the corporal punishment and the suicide and ordered the City of Osaka to pay about 75 million yen in damages.

The Japan Sports Agency's "Comprehensive Guidelines on Extracurricular Athletic Club Activities" (March 2018) set at least two rest days a week during term (at least one weekday and at least one weekend day), and held corporal punishment to be "not permitted in any case".

curve.note: Counted year by year as the number of speeches containing the word in the National Diet Proceedings Search System. The record for the most recent years comes in late, so the chart runs to 2024.
curve.subtitle: Includes uses other than the doctrine of guts, such as shimaguni konjo, "island mentality". ◆To 2024

029.name: Nominication
029.hitokoto: In Nippon Life's survey, "unnecessary" first became the majority in 2021.
body: The coinage joining nomi, drinking, to "communication" is oldest, in the National Diet Library's index of magazine articles, in "A History of Nominication" in Ushio for August 1982, and the spelling with the character for drinking goes back to Gekkan Somu for November 1983. In the Diet, a witness said "communication, nominication" at the House of Representatives Committee on Agriculture, Forestry and Fisheries on 23 April 1992. It spread as a name for the workplace culture of the late Showa period.

In the survey on Labour Thanksgiving Day that Nippon Life has published each November since 2017, those calling nominication at work "necessary" were 62.0% in 2017, 53.6% in 2018, 57.3% in 2019 and 54.3% in 2020. In 2021 (1-13 October, 7,774 respondents) it fell to 38.2%, and "unnecessary" at 61.9% was the higher for the first time since the survey began. It has stayed in the 40s since: 45.6% in 2022, 44.7% in 2023, 43.5% in 2024.

In the surveys of 2023 and 2024, about seven in ten said they did not want to work at a place with nominication (67.4% and 70.2%). Meanwhile 34.1% had had nominication in fiscal 2023, back up from 14.3% the year before, so the drinking itself has not gone. What has fallen is the share who think it necessary.

made.label: 1982 First in the magazine index
made.fact: The oldest article containing nominikeshon in NDL Search (the index of magazine articles) is "Sansuijin suikyo mondo 8: A History of Nominication" in Ushio for August 1982; the oldest with the spelling using the character for drinking is Gekkan Somu for November 1983, and for nomyunikeshon, Senken Romu Kanri for November 1983. There are no hits before 1980. In the record of Diet proceedings, "communication, nominication" appears at the House of Representatives Committee on Agriculture, Forestry and Fisheries on 23 April 1992 (witness Ryuzo Kigasawa), and the spelling with the character for drinking at the House of Councillors Committee on Audit on 2 September 1994 (Arinobu Morizumi).

keyfacts.text: In Nippon Life's "Nissay Internet Survey: On Labour Thanksgiving Day" for 2021 (surveyed 1-13 October, 7,774 respondents, announced 17 November), those answering that nominication at work was "necessary" or "rather necessary" were 38.2% (down 16.1 points on the year), and "unnecessary" or "rather unnecessary" 61.9%. For the first time since the survey began in 2017, unnecessary was higher than necessary.

The "necessary" share over time in the same survey: 62.0% in 2017 (5,901 respondents), 53.6% in 2018 (8,021), 57.3% in 2019 (4,644), 54.3% in 2020 (25,062). From 2017 to 2019 the question offered necessary or unnecessary; from 2020 it offered four options, and the figure is "necessary" plus "rather necessary".

2022 (9,553 respondents) was 45.6% (up 7.4 points on the year), 2023 (7,400) 44.7% against 55.2% unnecessary, and 2024 (8,953) 43.5% against 56.4%. In both 2023 and 2024 about seven in ten (67.4% and 70.2%) answered that they did not want to work at a place with nominication.

Those who had "had nominication with people from work" in fiscal 2023 were 34.1%, a sharp rise from 14.3% in fiscal 2022. In the 2024 survey, those saying the frequency had "risen compared with last year" were 12.2%, half the 24.3% of the year before. The drinking itself has come back, but the side that thinks it necessary is still in the 40s.

First appearances of the word: in the NDL index of magazine articles, "A History of Nominication" in Ushio for August 1982 is the oldest. The spelling with the character for drinking dates from Gekkan Somu for November 1983. In the record of Diet proceedings the first appearances are 23 April 1992 (in katakana) and 2 September 1994 (with the character for drinking).

030.name: Aim for Number One
030.hitokoto: "You need not be No. 1" sold 3.14 million copies and became No. 1.
body: Shito goraku is a phrase about how long a candidate sleeps: four hours and you pass, five and you fail. It comes from the pre-war election phrase "X to pass, Y to fail" (a newspaper of the 1930s has go-to san-raku, 50,000 yen to win and 30,000 to lose), and its transfer to entrance examinations is found in use from about the end of the 1950s. The norm of aiming for number one circulated in quantity in the 1960s, when the phrase "examination war" settled into the press.

The answer to it came out on 5 March 2003. SMAP's Sekai ni hitotsu dake no hana ("The Only Flower in the World"), written and composed by Noriyuki Makihara, sings "You need not be No. 1; you were always a special Only one"; it passed two million on 4 August that year and three million on 19 December 2016, and at 3.140 million copies in all became the biggest single of the Heisei era. The "yutori" Course of Study, which cut the content taught by about 30%, had come into effect in primary and lower secondary schools in April 2002, the year before.

"Crossing the finish line hand in hand at sports day" has been told and retold in the Diet as the emblem of this turn. It was mentioned as a case in Hiroshima Prefecture at the House of Councillors Committee on Education, Culture and Science on 24 September 1998, and at the House of Councillors Special Committee on the Basic Act on Education on 22 November 2006 Prime Minister Shinzo Abe said that "it was in fact being done"; the same day, however, Chief Cabinet Secretary Yasuhisa Shiozaki answered that "I have never myself seen anyone cross the line hand in hand on the spot, though I have heard the story in various places". No survey showing where and how much it was done was found within what this catalogue looked at.

made.label: Late 1950s The examination race
made.fact: Shito goraku, on how long a candidate sleeps (four hours and you pass, five and you fail), is found in use from about the end of the 1950s. Its origin is the pre-war election phrase "X to pass, Y to fail"; a newspaper of the 1930s has go-to san-raku, 50,000 yen to win and 30,000 to lose.

keyfacts.text: Shito goraku is found in use as an examination phrase from the end of the 1950s, transferred from the pre-war election phrase "X to pass, Y to fail". The writer at Kanji Cafe (2020) notes that cutting sleep dulls the head instead, so it is probably out of fashion now.

SMAP's Sekai ni hitotsu dake no hana (written and composed by Noriyuki Makihara) was released on 5 March 2003 as their 35th single. The lyric runs "You need not be No. 1; you were always a special Only one". It passed two million in its 21st week, on 4 August 2003, and three million on 19 December 2016; at 3.140 million copies in all (as at 27 January 2025) it is the biggest single of the Heisei era. It was first on Oricon's annual chart for 2003.

The Course of Study announced in December 1998 for primary and lower secondary schools, which cut the content taught by about 30% and set out "zest for living", came into effect from April 2002, as did the full five-day school week. The 2008 revision turned away from yutori, phased in from 2011.

"Crossing the finish line hand in hand at sports day" is recorded in the proceedings of the Diet. At the House of Councillors Committee on Education, Culture and Science on 24 September 1998, Noriko Hayashi said, of primary schools in Miyoshi, Shobara and Fukuyama in Hiroshima Prefecture, that "to rank people first and second is discrimination; let us all cross the line together hand in hand". At the House of Councillors Special Committee on the Basic Act on Education on 22 November 2006, Prime Minister Shinzo Abe said "it was in fact being done", while Chief Cabinet Secretary Yasuhisa Shiozaki answered that "I have never myself seen anyone cross the line hand in hand on the spot".

031.name: Own Your Home
031.hitokoto: Home ownership has held at 60% for 50 years. What fell is belief in land.
body: The view of life that takes owning a home as proof of being a full adult was established together with post-war housing policy. Under the Government Housing Loan Corporation Act (Act No. 156 of 6 May 1950) the corporation opened on 5 June that year; with the Public Housing Act (Act No. 193 of 4 June 1951) and the Japan Housing Corporation Act (Act No. 53 of 8 July 1955) the three pillars of loans, public housing and the housing corporation were in place, and the Housing Construction Planning Act (Act No. 100 of 30 June 1966) bound them into five-year plans. The housing construction five-year plans ran from the first to the eighth, fiscal 1966 to 2005.

The home ownership rate itself, however, has not fallen. In the Ministry of Internal Affairs and Communications' Housing and Land Survey it was 59.2% in 1973 and 60.9% in 2023, flat at about 60% for half a century. What fell is on the side of attitudes. In the Ministry of Land, Infrastructure, Transport and Tourism's Public Opinion Survey on Land Issues, those who think "land is a more advantageous asset than savings or shares" fell from 61.8% in fiscal 1993 to 37.0% in fiscal 1998, 27.1% in fiscal 2019 and 21.8% in fiscal 2023 (by post from fiscal 2020).

"I want to own both the land and the building" also fell, from 83.3% in fiscal 1993 to 73.5% in fiscal 2019 and 65.0% in fiscal 2023, taken by post. On the side of the institutions, the Basic Act for Housing (Act No. 61 of 8 June 2006) repealed the Housing Construction Planning Act, and the Government Housing Loan Corporation too was abolished on 31 March 2007, its business passing to the Japan Housing Finance Agency. The policy of building quantity is over, and the owned home is returning from an "advantageous asset" to a place to live.

made.label: 1950 The Housing Loan Corporation
made.fact: The Government Housing Loan Corporation was established on 5 June 1950 under the Government Housing Loan Corporation Act (Act No. 156 of 6 May 1950). With the Japan Housing Corporation Act (Act No. 53 of 8 July 1955) and the Housing Construction Planning Act (Act No. 100 of 30 June 1966), the three pillars of the corporation's loans for owned homes, the housing corporation and public housing were in place, and the housing construction five-year plans ran from the first (fiscal 1966) to the eighth (to fiscal 2005).

discontinued.label: 2007 The corporation abolished
discontinued.fact: The Basic Act for Housing (Act No. 61 of 8 June 2006, in force the same day) repealed the Housing Construction Planning Act, and the housing construction five-year plans ended with the eighth (fiscal 2005). The Government Housing Loan Corporation was abolished on 31 March 2007, its business passing on 1 April 2007 to the Japan Housing Finance Agency, an incorporated administrative agency. The institutional end point of the "policy of owned homes by quantity".

keyfacts.text: The Government Housing Loan Corporation Act is Act No. 156 of 6 May 1950, the Japan Housing Corporation Act is Act No. 53 of 8 July 1955, and the Housing Construction Planning Act is Act No. 100 of 30 June 1966.

The home ownership rate in the Ministry of Internal Affairs and Communications' Housing and Land Survey was 59.2% in 1973 and 60.9% in 2023 (rented 35.0%), flat at about 60% for half a century. The "fall" is not a matter of the ownership rate.

In the Ministry of Land, Infrastructure, Transport and Tourism's Public Opinion Survey on Land Issues, those answering "I think land is a more advantageous asset than savings or shares and the like" went 61.8% in fiscal 1993, 37.0% in fiscal 1998, 39.3% in fiscal 2008, 27.1% in fiscal 2019, 21.5% in fiscal 2020, 17.4% in fiscal 2021, 17.9% in fiscal 2022 and 21.8% in fiscal 2023. From fiscal 2020 the method changed from interview to post, so the ministry does not compare simply with earlier years.

In the same survey, "as for land and building, I want to own both" went 83.3% in fiscal 1993, 79.2% in fiscal 2000, 80.9% in fiscal 2010, 75.7% in fiscal 2017, 73.5% in fiscal 2019 and 65.0% in fiscal 2023. "Renting is fine" went from 9.4% to 17.5%.

The Basic Act for Housing is Act No. 61 of 8 June 2006 (in force the same day). The Government Housing Loan Corporation was abolished on 31 March 2007 and its business passed to the Japan Housing Finance Agency on 1 April.

032.name: Credentialism
032.hitokoto: Thirty-odd years after "no credentials asked", university entry is at a record.
body: The phrase gakureki shakai, "credential society", came into wide use from around the start of the 1960s (Heibonsha World Encyclopedia). It was a period in which the rate of going on to university kept rising, and the OECD education mission that came to Japan in January 1970, Johan Galtung among them, noted in its report that entry to university was decided by a single examination taken at 18. Criticism concentrates in the second half of the 1970s: Makoto Aso and Morikazu Ushiogi, eds., On the Utility of Credentials (Yuhikaku, 1977), and Ushiogi's The Turn of the Credential Society (University of Tokyo Press, 1978).

There have been moments when it was called over. In 1991 Sony launched hiring "with no credentials asked", in which applicants need not write the name of their university, and Shukan Post reported "we don't want deviation-score students any more". Yet the rate of going on to university (undergraduate) is at a record level, 57.1% in fiscal 2023, 58.6% in fiscal 2024 and 58.6% in fiscal 2025 (the School Basic Survey, on the formula revised in December 2025 and applied retrospectively), and the graduate has become, rather, the majority of the cohort.

The words change, but the sorting goes on. On 1 June 2015 an image was posted on Twitter claiming that the display on the application screen for Japan Post Bank's recruitment seminars switched between "full" and "places available" according to the university registered, and on 6 December 2021 Mynavi apologised after sending students in error an email whose subject line read "Daitoa and below" (both companies deny that any credential filter exists). What the phrase "credential filter" shows is not that credentials have stopped being everything, but that the judgment is now made quietly at the door.

made.label: 1960s "Credential society"
made.fact: The Heibonsha World Encyclopedia (revised edition) says the term gakureki shakai, "credential society", "came into wide use in Japan from around the start of the 1960s", and Nipponica too says "the name settled in in the 1960s". Johan Galtung, a member of the OECD education mission that came to Japan in January 1970, diagnosed that in Japan the rest of one's life is decided by an entrance examination on a single day at 18. The chief works of criticism are Makoto Aso and Morikazu Ushiogi, eds., On the Utility of Credentials: The Road from a Credential Society to an Ability Society (Yuhikaku, February 1977), Morikazu Ushiogi's The Turn of the Credential Society (University of Tokyo Press, January 1978), and Ronald Dore's The Diploma Disease (Iwanami Shoten, 1978).

keyfacts.text: The term gakureki shakai came into wide use in Japan from around the start of the 1960s (Heibonsha World Encyclopedia). Criticism of the credential society began in earnest from the 1960s, as the examination race grew fierce, its main themes being "credentials as a new status order" and "the reproduction of class".

Makoto Aso and Morikazu Ushiogi, eds., On the Utility of Credentials: The Road from a Credential Society to an Ability Society, was published by Yuhikaku in February 1977, and Morikazu Ushiogi's The Turn of the Credential Society by the University of Tokyo Press in January 1978.

In 1991 Sony launched hiring "with no credentials asked", not requiring the name of the university on the application, and Shukan Post of 3 May 1991 reported "the hiring revolution Sony has carried through: we don't want deviation-score students any more". Among those joining in 1992, the first intake, the Sankin Koryu group went from none the year before to five, and the Nittokomasen group rose by four.

The rate of going on to university (undergraduate), including those who left upper secondary school in earlier years, was 57.7% in fiscal 2023 and 59.1% in fiscal 2024 (up 1.4 points on the year, a record; final figures of 18 December 2024). The rate for universities and junior colleges together is 62.3%.

1 June 2015: the "full / places available" question on Japan Post Bank's seminar application screen. 6 December 2021: Mynavi's email in error reading "Daitoa and below". Both companies denied that any credential filter existed. There is no instance of "credential filter" in the record of Diet proceedings (as at September 2026).

curve.title: Rate of going on to university (undergraduate)
curve.note: Definition: entrants to university (undergraduate), including those who left upper secondary school in earlier years, divided by those leaving lower secondary school and the like three years before. Men and women together. Annually from 1954. Values on the formula that the Ministry of Education, Culture, Sports, Science and Technology revised in December 2025 and applied retrospectively.

033.name: Self-Responsibility
033.hitokoto: Much used in financial administration, it was turned on three hostages in April 2004.
body: "The principle of self-responsibility" first appears in the record of Diet proceedings on 17 December 1952, where a division director of the Banking Bureau of the Ministry of Finance was explaining finance for small and medium enterprises. In 1970 the chairman of the Regional Banks Association of Japan used the same phrase, and in 1972 a division director of MITI used it of petroleum. The collocation was, first of all, a term of finance and industrial policy. In 1991, over the covering of client losses by securities houses, the Director-General of the Securities Bureau of the Ministry of Finance said again and again that it was "an act contrary to the principle of self-responsibility in securities dealing", and in that year alone 72 statements containing the phrase are recorded. Between 1995 and 1999 they reached 586.

On 7 April 2004 three Japanese were taken hostage by an armed group in Iraq. On 13 April, before their release, Yoichi Masuzoe said in the House of Councillors that "going to a place under an evacuation advisory is, I think, self-responsibility", and on 21 April Chief Cabinet Secretary Yasuo Fukuda answered in plenary session that "it cannot be denied that they were not careful enough". The U-Can New Words and Buzzwords Award for that year put "self-responsibility" in its top ten, but recorded "no recipient".

What is interesting is that the first report of the National Council on Educational Reform in 1985 defined "the principle of emphasis on individuality" as "the dignity of the individual, respect for individuality, freedom and self-discipline, and the principle of self-responsibility". Individuality and self-responsibility are twins born of the same sentence, and 2004 was the year one of them alone was turned on the hostages.

made.label: 2004 Into general use
made.fact: On 7 April 2004 three Japanese were taken hostage in Iraq (Al Jazeera broadcast the footage on the 8th) and released on the 15th. In the Diet, on 13 April, Yoichi Masuzoe told the House of Councillors Committee on Foreign Affairs and Defence that "going to a place under an evacuation advisory is, I think, self-responsibility", and on 21 April Chief Cabinet Secretary Yasuo Fukuda told the plenary session of the House of Councillors that "it cannot be denied that they were not careful enough. Self-responsibility is … the care any member of society naturally takes."

keyfacts.text: 21 April 2004, plenary session of the House of Councillors, the answer of Chief Cabinet Secretary Yasuo Fukuda: "Close to thirty evacuation advisories and items of warning information had been issued. … It cannot be denied that they were not careful enough. Self-responsibility means weighing what effect the action one is about to take will have on society and on the people around one, and it is the care any member of society naturally takes."

13 April 2004, the House of Councillors Committee on Foreign Affairs and Defence, Yoichi Masuzoe: "To begin with, going to a place under an evacuation advisory is, I think, self-responsibility." On 20 April, in a plenary session of the House of Representatives, Yukihisa Fujita said "the catchword in Japan is self-responsibility", and quoted US Secretary of State Colin Powell's remark that he was glad there were Japanese who had taken risks upon themselves.

The grand prize of the 21st New Words and Buzzwords Award for 2004 went to "cho kimochi ii" (Kosuke Kitajima). "Self-responsibility" made the top ten, but with "no recipient". The official note: "It properly means that whoever takes a risk and acts bears the 'responsibility for the result' himself, but lately it is often used when shifting responsibility onto others."

The first appearance of "the principle of self-responsibility" in the Diet is 17 December 1952, in the subcommittee on small and medium enterprises of the House of Councillors Committee on Commerce and Industry, where Hisao Fukuda, Director of the General Affairs Division of the Banking Bureau of the Ministry of Finance, was explaining lending by financial institutions and the bearing of losses. Takashi Ihara, chairman of the Regional Banks Association of Japan, used the same phrase on 3 September 1970, and the Director of the Petroleum Planning Division of MITI on 21 March 1972.

Statements in the Diet containing "the principle of self-responsibility" rose sharply from 17 in 1985-89 to 175 in 1990-94 and 586 in 1995-99. There were 72 in 1991 alone, when, over the covering of client losses by securities houses, the Director-General of the Securities Bureau of the Ministry of Finance (Nobuhiko Matsuno) said again and again that it was "an act contrary to the principle of self-responsibility in securities dealing" (17 December 1991, House of Councillors Committee on Audit).

"The principle of emphasis on individuality" in the first report of the National Council on Educational Reform (26 June 1985) was defined as "the dignity of the individual, respect for individuality, freedom and self-discipline, and the principle of self-responsibility, that is, the principle of emphasis on individuality": self-responsibility had entered the vocabulary of education reform as well.
