One Manifesto did not end it. In April 1904, President Joseph F. Smith issued the Second Manifesto, meeting any new plural marriage with excommunication. Utah became a state in 1896, and its state constitution forbade plural marriage.

086.name: Bear and Multiply
086.hitokoto: The target: 100 million at home by 1960, five children a couple, wed at 25 and 21.
body: In January 1941 the second Konoe cabinet adopted the Outline for Establishing a Population Policy. The target was 100 million people in the home islands twenty years on, in 1960. The mean age at first marriage was then 28.39 for men and 24.41 for women; it was to be brought forward by three years within the decade, to 25 for men and 21 for women. Births per couple were to rise from an average of four to five. What the numerical targets were set for was not people but population.

The means were listed too: cheaper weddings and a loan scheme for the cost of marrying, favourable treatment for families with many children, lighter burdens for those with many dependants and heavier ones for the unmarried, more maternity homes and infant homes. And a ban on artificial birth control, contraception and abortion among it. The National Eugenic Law of 1940 handled "quality", the Outline "quantity". Bearing children stopped being a private matter and became an item of state policy.

The turn came seven years later. The Eugenic Protection Law (Act No. 156, promulgated 13 July 1948) made induced abortion lawful. The bill was introduced by members of the Diet, and Shidzue Kato, who spoke to it, called the National Eugenic Law "a law made out of a militarist spirit of bear and multiply". Seven years, no more, separate the Outline that proclaimed a prohibition from the statute that lifted it.

made.label: 1941 Population Policy Outline
made.fact: In January 1941 (Showa 16) the second cabinet of Fumimaro Konoe adopted the Outline for Establishing a Population Policy as part of the Outline of Basic National Policy. The target was 100 million people in the home islands twenty years on, that is in Showa 35 (1960). The mean age at first marriage was then 28.39 for men and 24.41 for women, and this was to be brought forward by three years within the decade to make 25 for men and 21 for women the proper age of marriage, with births per couple raised from an average of four to five. Alongside these it set out a loan scheme for the cost of marrying, favourable treatment for families with many children, heavier burdens on the unmarried (a bachelor tax), and a ban on artificial birth control such as contraception and abortion.

discontinued.label: 1948 Abortion made lawful
discontinued.fact: The Eugenic Protection Law (Act No. 156, promulgated 13 July 1948, now the Maternal Health Act) made induced abortion lawful, turning national policy right about. The bill was introduced by members of the Diet, and Shidzue Kato, speaking to it in the Committee on Health and Welfare of the House of Representatives on 1 December 1947, criticised the wartime National Eugenic Law of 1940 as "a law made out of a militarist spirit of bear and multiply".

keyfacts.text: In Kaji to eisei, vol. 18, no. 7, of 1942, Kujuro Fujiwara, director of the Osaka city health bureau, wrote that "our government is for the present aiming at a population of 100 million in the home islands in Showa 35", and summarised the Outline as "bringing the age at first marriage forward by three years, to roughly 25 for men and 21 for women" and "raising births, now an average of four, to an average of five over the next ten years".

The Outline carried the words "birth control to be forbidden and suppressed", and a bachelor tax and a loan scheme for marriage funds were among the items under consideration (explained by Hiroshi Obuchi as an expert witness before the House of Councillors Research Committee on National Life and the Economy on 16 April 1999).

In the Committee on Health and Welfare of the House of Representatives on 16 October 1947, Shinkichi Nomoto described the Outline as "100 million in the home islands by Showa 25", "the hope that about five children be born to a couple" and "lowering the age of marriage". Understanding of the target year was already unsteady at the time.

Inside the Outline, two policies that pulled against each other stood side by side, increasing the population and solving rural overpopulation; on the one hand it aimed at "maintaining a fixed number in the farming population of the home islands" (Fifty Years of the Ministry of Health and Welfare, 1988, p.418).

The National Eugenic Law, enacted in 1940, managed "quality" as the counterpart to the Outline's "quantity". On 1 December 1947, Shidzue Kato, who introduced the Eugenic Protection Bill, said of the National Eugenic Law that "the spirit of that bill was a law made out of a militarist spirit of bear and multiply".

087.name: The Potlatch Ban
087.hitokoto: From 1885 to 1951, a ceremony of giving away was a punishable offence.
body: On 19 April 1884 the federal government amended the Indian Act, and the amendment came into force on 1 January 1885. The text provided that everyone who took part in, or helped to celebrate, "the Indian festival known as the 'Potlatch' or in the Indian dance known as the 'Tamanawas'" was guilty of a misdemeanour and liable to imprisonment. A ceremony of sharing out goods became a crime in law.

The provision did not define "potlatch". At the first prosecution, Chief Justice Matthew Begbie of British Columbia found it unenforceable. It stayed on the books all the same, and people were arrested for dancing. At the potlatch held by Chief Dan Cranmer on 25 December 1921, those present were prosecuted: about half were imprisoned for two or three months, and the rest agreed to hand over their ceremonial regalia. Some 600 items are estimated to have been taken, and they went to three museums.

The major revision of the Indian Act in 1951 deleted the prohibition. The next year, in 1952, Chief Mungo Martin held the first "legal" potlatch since 1885, at Victoria. Sixty-six years on, the side that had been forbidden was still there and the article that forbade it was gone. The work of returning what was taken began in the 1970s and is not finished.

made.label: 1885 The potlatch forbidden
made.fact: The federal government amended the Indian Act on 19 April 1884 and brought the amendment into force on 1 January 1885. The text: "Every Indian or other person who engages in or assists in celebrating the Indian festival known as the 'Potlatch' or in the Indian dance known as the 'Tamanawas' is guilty of a misdemeanour, and shall be liable to imprisonment."

discontinued.label: 1951 The Indian Act revised
discontinued.fact: The major revision of the Indian Act in 1951 deleted the provision forbidding the potlatch.

restocked.label: 1952 The first legal potlatch
restocked.fact: The year after the ban was lifted, Chief Mungo Martin of the Kwakwaka'wakw held the first "legal" potlatch since 1885, at Victoria, British Columbia.

keyfacts.text: The ban was enacted as an amendment to the Indian Act on 19 April 1884 and came into force on 1 January 1885. The Indian Act itself was made in 1876 and was replaced by the 1951 version.

Because the provision did not define the word "potlatch", Chief Justice Matthew Begbie of British Columbia found it unenforceable at the first prosecution. It stayed on the books all the same, and people were arrested for dancing.

On 25 December 1921, Chief Dan Cranmer held a potlatch at Village Island ('Mimkwa̱mlis) that gathered about 300 people, and those present were prosecuted. About half were imprisoned for two or three months; the remaining twenty or so avoided prison by agreeing to hand over their ceremonial regalia.

Some 600 items are estimated to have been confiscated, most of them going to the National Museum in Ottawa (now the Canadian Museum of History), the Royal Ontario Museum in Toronto and the National Museum of the American Indian in New York. Efforts to have them returned began in the 1970s.

The reasoning of those who imposed the ban was that the songs and dances of the ceremony were incompatible with Christianity, and that Indigenous culture, society and politics were a threat to authority.
